paragraphs.text: 1. With a man of Mauretania the lion shares the road and drinks the water of the same spring. And I hear that the lions even visit the houses of the Mauretanians, when they meet with no game and a strong hunger seizes them. And if the man is present, he wards the lion off and drives it back, chasing it with all his might; but if he is away and only the woman is left, she holds it from advancing with reproachful words and brings it to order, admonishing it to master itself and not to flame up with hunger. And the lion understands the Mauretanian speech, and the sense of the woman's rebuke to the beast is, as they say, of this kind: "Are you not ashamed, being a lion, the king of the animals, to come to my hut and to need a woman to be fed, and, like a man maimed in body, to look to a woman's hands, that by her pity and mercy you may obtain what you need? You, who ought to hasten to the mountain haunts after deer and antelopes and all the rest that is the lion's glorious dinner. Yet you are content to be fed on scraps like a wretched little dog." And while she chants such things, the lion, as though stricken in soul and filled with shame, quietly and with downcast eyes departs, overcome by what is just. And if horses and dogs, through being reared with us, understand and cower when men threaten, I should not wonder that the Mauretanians, being reared and brought up together with lions, are understood by the very lions. For they testify of their own infants that they think the lions' cubs worthy of the same and like fare, of one bed and one roof; and that from this the beasts understand the aforesaid speech is neither incredible nor strange.

2. About the Libyan mare I hear the Libyans say such things. They are the swiftest of horses, and either feel weariness little or not at all. They are lean and not well-fleshed, yet fit also to endure their master's neglect. For their masters give them no tending — neither stroking them, nor making a rolling-place, nor cleaning out their hooves, nor combing their coats, nor plaiting their manes, nor washing them when weary — but as soon as they have finished the appointed course, they dismount and turn them loose to graze. And the Libyans are lean and squalid, and on such horses they ride. But the Medes are stately and luxurious, and so too are their horses. You would say that they live softly along with their masters, both in the size of their body and in their beauty, and now too in their finery and the tending from without. These same things come to my mind too about dogs. The Cretan hound is light and good at leaping and bred to mountain-ranging; and indeed the Cretans show themselves to be such men, as the report sings. The most spirited of dogs is the Molossian, since the men too are most spirited. And the Carmanian man and his dog are both most savage and unbendingly fierce, they say.

3. These too, it seems, were peculiarities of the nature of animals. Ctesias says that neither a wild nor a tame pig is found among the Indians, and he says somewhere that their sheep have tails a cubit broad.
4. The Indian ants that guard the gold

5. would not cross the river called Campylinus. And the Issedones who dwell with these ants are so called, and are so. A tortoise that has eaten a serpent and then bitten off some marjoram is freed from the harm which would otherwise have destroyed it utterly. And the dove I hear men say is the most chaste of birds and most restrained in love; for they are never torn from one another, neither the female, unless by some chance she is bereft of her mate, nor the male, unless he is widowed. But partridges are without self-control in love; and so they destroy the eggs that are laid, that the females may not, by rearing their young, bring a distraction from intercourse with them.

6. Wolves swimming a river, that they may not be violently overturned by the rush of the stream, nature, devising a peculiar ballast for them, has taught a salvation easy out of difficult straits. Biting one another's tails, they then resist the current, and so swim across painlessly and safely.

7. To she-asses nature did not assign braying, they say. But the same nature granted that dogs are made voiceless by hyenas. Sweet scent and perfume are causes of death to vultures. To swans hemlock is destruction. And how the horse fears the camel both Cyrus and Croesus learned, as they say.
8. When horses' foals are left by their mothers before their rearing, like orphans, the other mares rear them together with their own young, taking pity on them.

9. Crows are most faithful to one another, and when they come together into partnership they are exceedingly fond of each other, and one would not see these creatures mating loosely and at random. And those who are exact about these matters say that if one of them dies, the other remains widowed. And I hear that the ancients in their marriages, after

10. the wedding-song, used to sing the crow, giving this as a token of concord to those who come together for the begetting of children. But those who watch the seats and flights of birds say it is an ill omen for a single crow to answer. And since the owl is its enemy, and by night plots against the crow's eggs, the crow by day does this same thing to the owl, knowing that the owl's sight is then weak. The land-hedgehog nature has made not unwise nor unlearned in storing up for use. For since it needs food for the whole year, but not every season gives the fruits in season, it rolls itself, they say, in the drying-floors, and the dried figs that get stuck on it — many fix themselves on its spines — it quietly carries off, and having laid them up in store keeps them, and can take from its den, at a time when it is not possible to procure them from outside.

11. Indeed even the fiercest of animals are at peace and at truce with those that can help them, their inborn malice being loosed for the sake of need. The crocodile, for instance, swims and at the same time gapes. So the leeches fall upon it and trouble it. Knowing this, it needs a physician, the plover; for when it has become full of them, it comes forth to the bank and gapes toward the sunbeam. Then the plover, inserting its beak, draws out the said leeches, and the crocodile, being helped, endures and keeps still. And the one has the leeches for its dinner, the other is benefited, and reckons it the plover's wage that it does it no harm.

12. The Thessalians and the Illyrians and the Lemnians count jackdaws benefactors, and have voted them public maintenance, since the jackdaws destroy and ruin the eggs and the offspring of the locusts, which damage the crops of the aforesaid peoples. So the clouds of locusts are greatly diminished, and the fruits in season remain unharmed for the aforesaid peoples.

13. Cranes are born in Thrace, which is the most wintry of regions and the most frosty of those I hear of. So they love the land in which they were born, but they love themselves too, and assign part to their ancestral haunts and part to their own safety. For in the summer they stay in their place, but when autumn is already half over they depart to Egypt and Libya and Ethiopia, as though they knew the circuit of the earth and the natures of climates and the differences of seasons. And having passed a spring-like winter, again, when the air begins to be calm and peaceful, they turn back. They make as leaders of the flight those already experienced in the journey; and these would naturally be the elder ones. And to bring up the rear they appoint birds of like age; and the young are stationed in the middle of them. Having watched for a wind favourable and friendly to them and flowing behind, using it as an escort and one that thrusts them forward, they then form the figure of their flight into an acute-angled triangle, so that, striking the air, they may cleave it most easily, and they hold to their course. So do cranes summer and winter. But men have thought the wisdom of the king of the Persians wonderful in his knowledge of the mixture of climates, singing of Susa and Ecbatana and the much-talked-of removals of the Persian to this place and that. And when the cranes see an eagle coming on, forming a circle and gathering into a hollow mass they threaten as though to set themselves against it; and it is beaten back, wing and all. And resting their beaks on one another's rumps, they then in a way bind their flight together, and make their toil easy toil for themselves, the same birds sparingly resting upon one another. And when, in a long stretch of land, they chance upon a spring, they rest by night and sleep; but three or four keep guard over the rest, and, that they may not let their watch fall asleep, they stand on one leg, while with the lifted foot they hold a stone in their claws very firmly and carefully, so that if ever they should without knowing it slip into sleep, the stone, falling and striking, may force them to throw off slumber. And the stone which a crane swallows to have ballast is a touchstone of gold, when, having as it were come to anchor and put in, it then brings it up again.

14. A helmsman, seeing in the midst of the open sea cranes turning back and flying the other way, understood that they had given up going forward at the assault of a contrary wind; and becoming, as one might say, a pupil of the birds, he sailed back and saved his ship. And this, having happened first, was handed down to men by these birds as at once a lesson and a teaching.

15. Doves in the cities herd together with men, and are most gentle, and crowd about their feet; but in desolate places they run away, and do not endure men. For they take courage in their numbers, and know very well that they will suffer nothing harsh. But where there are fowlers and nets and plots against them, they no longer dwell fearlessly, to use what was said of those very birds by Euripides.

16. When partridges are about to lay, they prepare for themselves out of certain twigs what is called the threshing-floor. It is a hollow plaited thing, very suitable to sit in. And pouring in dust, and making, as it were, a soft bed, and creeping in, then covering themselves above with twigs so as to escape the notice both of the rapacious birds and of the hunters among men, in great peace they lay; then they do not entrust the eggs to the same place, but to another, as though removing house; for they fear lest they be detected. And in their nesting they warm the tender young and keep them warm with their own feathers, wrapping them as in swaddling-clothes with their plumage; they do not wash them, but make them brighter by dusting. And if a partridge sees someone approaching and plotting against both itself and its young, then it rolls itself before the feet of the hunter, and gives him hope of being able to catch it as it tumbles. And he stoops to the prey, while the partridge unrolls itself; and it escapes, and the young get on their way. And when the partridge perceives this, taking courage now it relieves the fowler of his vain occupation by flying up, and leaves the man gaping. Then the mother, being in safety and standing in a good place, calls her young. And they fly to her, recognizing the cry. The partridge, when about to be delivered of her eggs, tries to escape her mate's notice, lest he break the eggs; for being lustful, he does not let the mother have leisure for rearing the young. So unbridled is the race of partridges. When the females have left them and are brooding, the males deliberately kindle one another to anger, and strike and are struck most bitterly; and the one defeated is mounted like a hen, and the victor does this without restraint, until he too, defeated by another, then falls into the same holds.

17. Euripides says that envy bears an ill name; and this, it seems, dwells also in some of the animals. The gecko, for instance, as Theophrastus says, when it has cast off its old age, turning round then swallows it and makes it disappear; for it seems that the old skin of this creature is a remedy against epilepsy. And the deer too knows that its right horn is good for many things, and indeed buries it and hides it out of grudging that anyone should enjoy so great a benefit. And the mare knows the love-charms she brings forth with her foal; and so, as soon as the young is born, she bites off the bit of flesh on its forehead. Men call it the horse-frenzy. And the sorcerers say that such things provide and kindle certain impulses that draw toward uncontrollable union and an amorous frenzy. So the mare is not willing that men should share in this charm, grudging it as a very great good. Is it not so?

18. In the Red Sea Leonides of Byzantium says there is a fish, no smaller at all than a full-grown goby; but it has neither eyes nor a mouth in the manner of fish. There are attached to it gills and the shape of a head, as one might guess, yet it is not formed into a clear shape; and below, under its belly, there is impressed a gently hollowed mark, and it sends out the colour of an emerald. This, he says, is its eye and its mouth too. And whoever tastes it has hunted it to his own hurt. And the manner of the destruction: the one who has tasted it swells, then his belly bursts, and the man perishes. And the fish too, when caught, pays its penalty. First, on being out of the wave, it swells; and if anyone touches it, it is inflamed still more. And if one continues handling it, it becomes, by putrefaction, wholly transparent, like a man with dropsy; then at last it bursts. And if one should wish to let it back into the sea while still alive, it floats like a bladder lifted by air. And he says that from this affliction they called it the puffer.
19. The seal, as I hear, vomits out its own rennet,

20. that it may not be a cure for those subject to epilepsy. A spiteful creature, then, the seal, indeed by Heaven. The pelicans in the rivers gape round the mussels and then swallow them, and warming them within in the recess of the belly, vomit them up; and the shells have parted by the heat, like those of boiled things, and the birds dig out the flesh and have their dinner. And indeed the gulls too, as Eudemus says, raising the snails on high and lifting them up, dash them most violently against the rocks.

21. Eudemus says that on Thracian Pangaeum a bear, finding a lion's lair empty of its guard, destroyed the lion's cubs, because they were still small and unable to defend themselves. And when the father and the mother came back from some hunt, and saw their young amid the slaughter, they grieved, as was likely, and rushed at the bear; but it, in fear, ran up into a tree as fast as its feet could carry it, and sat there trying to avoid the plot from them. And when they seemed to come there to avenge themselves on the ravager, then the lioness did not leave the watch, but sat under the trunk lying in wait and looking up with bloodshot eyes, while the lion, distressed and wandering in his grief, roamed in the mountains and met a woodcutter. The man was afraid and dropped his axe, but the lion fawned on the beast and, raising himself, embraced him, as best he could, and brightened the man's face with his tongue. And the man took courage, and the lion, throwing his tail about him, led him on, and would not let him leave the axe behind, but signalled with his foot to take it up. And as the man did not understand, the lion took it with his mouth and held it out to him, and the man followed, and the lion led him to the lair. And the lioness, when she saw him, herself coming up fawned too, and looked piteous, and gazed up at the bear. So the man, perceiving and inferring that these had been wronged in some way by the bear, with all his strength and the work of his hands cut down the tree. And it was overturned, and the bear was brought down; and the beasts tore it to pieces. But the man the lion led back unharmed and unhurt to the place where he had first met him, and restored him to his original woodcutting.

22. The battle of the Egyptian beasts, the asp and the ichneumon. And the ichneumon comes to the contest against its adversary not without plan nor in panic, but as a man arms himself with full armour, so that creature, rolling itself in the mud and filling itself with what has caked on, seems to have a sufficient and water-tight defence. And if there is a lack of mud, washing itself in water and throwing itself, still wet, into deep sand, from this device drawing a means of defence out of difficult straits, it goes to the battle. And it will keep guard over the tip of its nose, somewhat exposed to the asp's bite, by bending back its tail and stopping the nose up with it. And if the asp succeeds in striking this, it has brought down its antagonist; but if not, it wears out its teeth in vain on the mud, and again the ichneumon, creeping up unexpectedly and seizing it by the neck, throttles

23. the asp. And the one that strikes first wins. To feed their fathers grown old storks both wish and have made their practice; and no human law bids them do this, but the cause of it is nature. And these same birds love their own offspring too; and the proof: when the full-grown bird is in want of food to set before its still unfledged and tender nestlings in the nest, a scarcity having come upon it by chance, it vomits up its own food of the day before and feeds them. And I hear that herons do the same, and pelicans too. I learn besides that the storks themselves flee together with the cranes and run away from the winter; and when the frosty season is over, when both these and those return to their own homes, each recognizes its own nest, as men recognize their house. And Alexander of Myndus says that when they come to old age, passing to the islands of the Ocean they change their shapes into a human form, and have this as a prize of their piety toward their parents — and besides, if I understand anything, the gods wishing thereby to suggest that at least the race of men there is pious and holy, since it was not possible for such a one to live out his life in the rest of the world under the sun. And it does not seem to me a fable. For with what end in view would Alexander have invented this marvel, gaining nothing at all? And besides, it would not befit a sensible man to set falsehood before truth, not even for the greatest gain, much less when about to fall into holds most profitless concerning such matters.

24. The swallow, when it has plenty of mud, carries it with its claws and builds up the nest; but if there is a lack, as Aristotle says, it wets itself, and falling into dust mingles it with its feathers, and when the mud has caked on, then scraping it off with its beak it works the building it has in hand. And knowing well that, the nestlings being tender and bare of plumage, they will be hurt and pained if they rest on bare twigs, it perches on the backs of sheep, and tears off some of the wool, and from this strews a soft bed for its young.

25. The swallow as a mother makes her nestlings just, keeping equality among them through equal feeding; she does not bring one thing for all, since indeed she cannot; but the things she brings are small and few, and she feeds the first hatched first, the second the one after it, and feeds third the one of the third birth, and so proceeds up to the fifth in this manner; for the swallow neither conceives nor bears more. And she herself takes down only so much of the food as she can gain in the nest from what slips by her. And her young see late, as do the pups of dogs; she brings and applies a certain herb, and they look up, and then, having kept still a little, being now able to fly, they leave the nest for pasture. To get possession of this herb men thirst, and have not yet attained their desire.

26. Hoopoes are the most harsh of birds, and they seem to me, in memory and also in hatred of the former wrongs of mankind toward the race of women, to weave their nests in deserts and on the high crags; and so that men may not come near their young, they smear their nests instead of with mud, casting around human dung, warding off and checking by the stench and foul smell the creature hostile to them. And once this bird, having raised young in a more deserted part of a wall, in a cleft of stone parted by time — so the keeper of the wall, seeing the young within, smeared over the hole with mud. And the hoopoe, returning, when it saw itself shut out, brought a herb and applied it to the mud; and the mud flowed off, and it came to its own young, then went to pasture. So again the same man smeared it over, and the bird with the same herb opened the hole; and a third time the same things were done. Then the guardian of the wall, seeing what was being done, took up the herb and used it, not for the same purpose, but to open up treasures that in no way belonged to him.

27. The Peloponnese is barren of lions; and Homer, as was likely, perceiving this with an instructed mind, said, when he sang of Artemis hunting there, that she ranges over Taygetus and Erymanthus delighting in boars and swift deer. And since these mountains are empty of lions, very reasonably he did not mention them.

28. There is a fish born in the Red Sea, and, as far as I know, the natives gave it the name Perseus. And the Greeks call it so, and the Arabs likewise with the Greeks; for they too sing of Perseus as the son of Zeus, and they celebrate the fish as named after him. In size it is like the largest anthias, and to look at it is like a sea-bass; it is slightly hook-nosed, and is variegated with bands likened to gold; the bands begin from the head, slanting, and end at the belly. It is fenced with large and close-set teeth. And it is said to surpass fishes in strength of body and force; nor does it lack daring. Its hunting and catching I have told elsewhere.

29. The pinna is a sea-creature, and is of the shellfish. It gapes by the parting of the shells that lie about it, and holds out a bit of flesh from itself like a bait to the fish swimming by. And a crab stays with it, reared together and feeding together. So when one of the fish swims up, the crab gently pricks it; and the pinna opens itself wider, and receives within the head of the approaching fish — for it lets it down as if for food — and eats it.

30. These things too, it seems, were proper for the educated man to know. The cuckoo is most wise and most clever at weaving easy contrivances out of difficult straits. For it is conscious of itself that it cannot brood and hatch, on account of the coldness of the constitution in its body, as they say. So when it lays, it neither weaves a nest itself nor tends the young, but watches for the owners of the nests being away and wandering, and slipping into a stranger's lodging lays its eggs there. And it does not pounce on the nests of all birds, but of the lark, the wood-pigeon, the greenfinch, and the pappus; for it knows these lay eggs like its own. And when the nests are empty, it would not enter; but when there are eggs within, then it mingles in its own. And if those are many, it rolls some out and makes them disappear, and leaves its own, which cannot be discerned and detected because of the likeness. And the aforesaid birds hatch what in no way belongs to them, but those young, as they set firm, being conscious to themselves of their spurious birth, fly off and go to the parent that bore them; for when the feathers have grown about them they are recognized as alien, and are most bitterly maltreated. The cuckoo is seen one season of the year, the best; for at the beginning of spring it appears, until the rising of Sirius, and then withdraws from the sight of the many.

31. A lion fears a cock. And the basilisk too dreads the same bird, as they say, and trembles on seeing it, and hearing it crow is convulsed and dies. For this reason those who travel through Libya, the nurse of such creatures, in fear of the aforesaid basilisk take with them as a fellow-traveller and companion of the road a cock, which will rid them of so great an evil.

32. Crete is most hostile both to wolves and to creeping beasts. And I hear Theophrastus saying that on Macedonian Olympus too there are places impassable to wolves. The Cephallenian goats, it seems, do not drink for six months. And the sheep of Budinum you will not see white, as they say, but all black. A difference too and peculiarity of animals would lie in this: some of them are biters and inject poison from their tooth, while those are strikers which, having struck, then likewise inject such an evil.
33. The Libyan asp, I hear, blinds the sight of one who looks back against its breath; but the other kind does not blind, but kills most easily.

34. Epirote cows are said to be milked in very great abundance, and Scyrian goats to give the most plentiful milk, as much as no other goats. And some Egyptian goats bear five at a birth, and most bear twins. And the Nile is said to be the cause, providing water most productive of offspring. Whence indeed the herdsmen who are very fond of fine beasts and careful of their own flock bring water from the Nile to their own herds by every possible device, and to the barren ones still more. To Ptolemy the Second, they say, a horn was brought from the Indians, and it held three amphorae. What sort of ox, then, that one was, to have grown so great a horn!

35. You would never hear one single cry from all partridges, but they are different. And at Athens those beyond the deme of the Corydallians sound one note, and those on this side another. And what the names of these cries are, Theophrastus will tell. But in Boeotia and the Euboea opposite they are of like voice and, as one might say, of like tongue. Wholly voiceless are the frogs in Cyrene, and the swine in Macedonia. And there is a kind of cicada, these too voiceless.

36. There is, they say, a kind of venomous spider, and they call the spider rhax, either because it is black and truly resembles a grape-berry and somehow looks round too, or for another reason. It is found in Libya, and has small feet; and it has been allotted a mouth in the middle of its belly, and it is very swift to kill.

37. In Seriphus there are frogs, of which you would not at all hear any utterance; but if you carry them elsewhere, they sound piercing and most harsh. And in Pierus of Thessaly there is a lake, not ever-flowing, but in winter it is formed from the waters that run together into it. So if one throws frogs into it, they keep silent, though they utter their voice elsewhere. And concerning the Seriphian frogs the Seriphians boast that Perseus, coming from his contest against the Gorgon, after going round much land, and being weary, as was likely, rested near the lake and lay down needing sleep. And the frogs cried out and mocked the hero and broke his sleep; and Perseus prayed to his father to silence the frogs. And he listened, and to please his son condemned the frogs of that place to everlasting silence. But Theophrastus, throwing out the fable and freeing the Seriphians from their boasting, says that the coldness of the water is the cause of the silence of the aforesaid frogs.

38. In moist places, and where the air is exceedingly damp, cocks do not crow, says Theophrastus. And the lake in Pheneus is barren of fish. And cicadas, being cold in their constitution, then, being heated by the sun, sing — so he says.

39. The boldest of creatures, it seems, was the goatsucker; for it despises the small birds, but attacks the goats by force, and indeed, flying onto their udders, sucks out the milk, and does not fear the punishment from the goatherd, though it pays them a most wicked wage for its fill; for it blinds the teat and quenches the flow from there.

40. Metrodidactus, the son of Arete, the sister of Aristippus, the many celebrate; but Aristotle says that he himself saw the nestlings of the nightingale being taught to sing by their mother. The nightingale was, it seems, of birds a strong lover of freedom; and for this reason the full-grown one, when caught and shut up in a little cage, refrains from song, and avenges itself on the fowler for its slavery by silence. Of this men, having experience, let the older ones go, but are eager to hunt the nestlings.

41. The land of India bears one-horned horses, they say, and the same land rears one-horned asses, and from these horns drinking-cups are made. And if one should put into them a deadly poison, the man who drinks will suffer no harm from the plot; for the horn, both of the horse and of the ass, seems to be a defence against the evil.

42. The purple coot is at once the most beautiful and the most aptly named of creatures, and it delights in dusting itself, and now too it takes the bath of doves; but it does not give itself to the dust-baths and the washings before it has walked a certain number of paces sufficient for it. And eating before witnesses it dislikes, and for this reason withdraws, and eats secretly. It is strongly jealous, and watches the married women, and if it judges the mistress of the house to be committing adultery, it strangles itself. It does not fly high. Men delight in it, and rear it sparingly and carefully. And it seems either to be a plaything of a stately and very rich house, or a temple receives it, and it wanders free within the enclosure. The peacock, being beautiful, the prodigal both slaughter and eat; for of that bird the feathers are an adornment, but the body is little or nothing. But I do not know of anyone who has slaughtered a purple coot for dinner — not Callias nor Ctesippus the Athenians, not Lucullus nor Hortensius the Romans; and I have named a few out of many prodigal and most intemperate men, both otherwise and indeed about the belly.

43. The raven, when now grown old and unable to feed its young, offers itself to them as food; and they eat their father. And from this, they say, the proverb took its origin which says, "Of a bad raven a bad egg."

44. The wood-pigeons are sung as the most chaste of birds. For the male and the female, having paired and, as it were, breathed together into marriage, cling to one another and are chaste, and neither of these birds would touch a stranger's bed. And if they cast amorous eyes on others, the rest go round upon them, and the male the males of its kind tear to pieces, the females the female. This law of chastity reaches also to the turtle-doves and remains unchanging, except that each bird is not put to death; for the male they kill, but the female they pity and leave unharmed, and it goes about widowed.

45. Aristotle says that of doves the males share the labour of the females in giving birth, and when these wander outside the nest thrust and drive them back, and when they have laid force them to brood. And the same author says that the males too warm the young and rear them together with the females, and that, so the young may not be ill-fed, the parents give the infants as their first food salty earth, which when they have tasted, then they readily feed on the rest. And doves seem somehow to be at truce with the other rapacious birds, but to dread, they say, the sea-eagles and the hawks. And what they contrive against the falcons is worth hearing. When the one that is high up and made to fly aloft pursues them, they slip down and draw themselves lower and try to press in their wing; but when the one that has by nature its flight lower pursues, they rise and travel aloft, and flying above it take courage, since it cannot lead higher.

46. An Indian horse-trainer met with a white elephant-foal, and taking it reared it while still young, and little by little made it tame, and rode upon it, and loved the possession and was loved in return, receiving from it the recompense for having reared it. So the king of the Indians, learning of it, asked to take the elephant. But the man, as a lover jealous, and indeed greatly grieved if another were to be master of it, said he would not give it, and went off into the desert, mounting the elephant. The king was angered, and sent men against him to take it away and at the same time to bring the Indian to justice. And when they came, they tried to use force. So the man too pelted them from above, and the beast, as though wronged, joined in defending him. And at first it was so; but when the Indian, being struck, slipped down, the elephant bestrode his foster-father, like a man shielding him in arms, and killed many of the assailants, and put the rest to flight; then, throwing its trunk about its foster-father, it lifted him up and carried him to the lair, and stayed by him as a faithful friend by a friend, and showed its goodwill. O wicked men, ever about the table and the clatter of the frying-pan, and dancing toward your dinner, but in dangers traitors, and to no purpose and to no end gaping with the name of friendship!

1. The partridge is the most lascivious of birds. They love the females fiercely, and being overcome by lust they couple most constantly. So when those who keep fighting partridges goad them on to battle against one another, they set beside each one its mate, having discovered this device against cowardice and weakness in the contest. For the partridge will not endure to appear beaten before either his beloved or his wife; he will rather die under blows than, when his adversary comes against him, turn away and shamefully let her see this, before whom he wishes to win esteem. This was just what the Cretans had in mind concerning their beloved boys. For I am told that a certain Cretan, a good lover and brave in war and in all else, had as his favourite a noble youth of outstanding beauty, manly in spirit and well and finely endowed by nature for the noblest studies, but on account of his age not yet called to arms (I have given elsewhere the name both of the lover and of the boy). The Cretans say that this young man displayed great deeds of valour in the battle, but that when the enemy's phalanx pressed upon him in a mass he stumbled over a corpse lying there, and they say he was overturned. One of the enemy, the nearest, raised his weapon and was about to strike the man across the back; but he turned and said, "Do not deal me a shameful and unmanly blow, but strike me full in the breast, so that my beloved may not convict me of cowardice and refuse to lay out my corpse, not daring to approach me when I lie disgraced." That a man should be ashamed to be seen a coward is no great wonder; but that a partridge should partake of shame—this is a most august gift of nature. Yet Aristodemus the trembler, and Cleonymus who threw away his shield, and Pisander the coward, felt no shame before their fatherlands, nor before their wives, nor before their children.

2. At Eryx in Sicily there is a festival which the people of Eryx themselves, and indeed all who dwell in Sicily, call the Anagogia, the Departure. The reason given is that on those days they say Aphrodite sets out from there to Libya. They infer this from the following evidence. There is a very great multitude of doves in that place. Now during those days they are not to be seen, and the people of Eryx say that the goddess has departed with them as her escort; for that doves are the playthings of Aphrodite both they sing and all men believe. After nine days have passed, one of surpassing beauty is seen flying in from the sea that brings her from Libya—not like the rest of the common pigeons, but purple, just as Anacreon of Teos sings of Aphrodite to us, calling her somewhere "the purple one." And she might be likened to gold as well, in keeping with Homer's goddess of the same name, whom he hymns as golden. The clouds of the remaining doves follow her, and again there is a festival and a great gathering for the people of Eryx, the Katagogia, the Homecoming—this name too taken from the event.

3. Wolves go in pairs, and so do horses; but lions no longer do so. For the lioness and the lion do not take the same path, whether they go to the hunt or to drink. The reason, as the older authorities say, is that each, trusting in its own bodily strength, has no need of the other.

4. Wolves do not loose themselves from the pangs of birth easily, but only in twelve days and as many nights, since the Delians say that it took Leto just so long to come from the Hyperboreans to Delos.

5. The tortoise and the partridge are creatures at war; so too the stork and the corncrake against the gull, and the falcon and the heron against the seagull; the lark regards the goldfinch as its enemy, and there is enmity between the turtledove and the redstart; the kite and the raven are foes; the siren against the hawk, and the hawk against the buzzard are found to differ not only in kind but also in nature. The channa is a most lustful fish. And white ants may be heard of at Pheneus in Laconia.

6. That horses delight more in marshes and meadows and windy places, men skilled in the rearing of horses and foals agree. Hence too Homer—being, as it seems to me, clever at observing such things—said somewhere that "three thousand mares pastured along the marsh." And horse-keepers testify that mares are often made pregnant by the wind and flee before the south wind or the north. So the same poet, knowing this, said, "Of these even Boreas grew enamoured as they grazed." And Aristotle too, as I understand it, taking his cue from this, said that they, stung by the aforementioned winds, run off.

7. I am told that the king of the Scythians (I know his name but pass it by; for what profit is it to me?) had a mare of high quality possessing every excellence that mares are required to have and to show, and that he had also a son of that very mare surpassing all the others in excellence. Now not finding any worthy mate to pair with her, nor any good mare to bring to the son so as to take seed from him, for these reasons he brought the two together to the act. They for their part welcomed and showed affection to each other in every other way, but would not come together. So since the animals were wiser than the Scythian's scheme, he covered both the male and the female with cloaks, and they performed that lawless and unjust act. But when both perceived what had been done, then indeed they atoned for the impiety by death, leaping over a cliff.

8. Eudemus relates that a groom fell in love with a young mare, the best of the herd, as one might with a beautiful girl, the loveliest in the whole estate; and that at first he held himself in check, but at last ventured upon the strange union and had intercourse with her. She had a foal, itself also beautiful, which, seeing what was being done, was grieved, as though its mother were being tyrannized by its master, and it leapt upon the man and killed him; and afterwards it watched where he was buried, and going there it dug him up and outraged the corpse and mangled it with all manner of mutilation.

9. Most fish during the spring are eager for love, and they betake themselves rather to the Black Sea; for it has, in a way, chambers and resting-places—these being nature's gifts to fishes—and moreover it is free of such beasts as the sea feeds. Dolphins alone roam there, slender and weak; and indeed it is barren of the octopus and produces no crab, and

10. it does not breed the lobster; but these are the destruction of small fish. I learn that when the new moon first appears, the elephants, by some natural and mysterious instinct, take freshly plucked branches from the wood in which they pasture and then raise them aloft, and look up toward the goddess, and gently wave the branches, as though holding out to the goddess this supplication on behalf of her being gracious and kindly to them.

11. I am told that of all animals only mares endure the union of the males even when pregnant; for they are the most lustful. For this reason the more dissolute among women are called "mares" by those who censure them in more dignified terms.

12. Partridges, while still dwelling within their eggs and confined by the shells that have grown about them, do not wait to be hatched out by their parents, but by their own efforts, as though knocking at a door, break out of the eggs, and peeping forth then push themselves up, and having shattered the shell of the egg they at once run, and if the half toward the tail clings to them they shake it off and cast it away, and they seek for food and leap most swiftly.

13. Among partridges, the clear-voiced and tuneful trust in their own fine singing; and the warlike and contentious ones likewise are confident that they are not fit to be wasted once caught; and for this reason, when taken, they struggle less against their captors in order not to be caught. But the others, and still more the Cirrhaean partridges, conscious of being good neither at fighting nor at singing, and knowing well that once caught they will become dinner for their captors, contrive by a certain natural cunning to render themselves uneatable; and they abstain from all other food that gratifies and fattens them, and eat garlic most eagerly. Now those who have learned this beforehand make a willing truce of non-pursuit with them; but whoever has not previously encountered the catch of these birds, having taken and boiled one, wastes both his time and his pains upon it, finding that he has got a wretched piece of meat.

14. The weasel is a wicked beast, and so is the snake. So when a weasel is about to fight a snake, it first chews rue and then comes to the fight as though fenced and armed. The reason is that rue is most hateful to the snake.

15. When the wolf has filled itself to satiety, it will not taste even the smallest morsel thereafter; for its belly is stretched, its tongue swells, and its mouth is blocked, and it is most gentle to meet, like a lamb, and it would not plot against either man or beast, not even if it walked through the middle of the flock. But its tongue diminishes quietly and little by little, then returns to its original shape, and it becomes a wolf again.

16. Cocks in a flock all mount the newcomer. And tame partridges do the same to the one that has just arrived and is not yet subdued. And in return for those who rear them, the partridges themselves lure the free and wild ones, doing this just as the pigeons do. Now the decoy partridge attracts and holds out its siren-song to draw the others on in this way. It stands singing, and its song is a challenge, goading the wild bird to battle; and it stands in ambush by the snare. The leader of the wild birds, answering the song, comes forward to fight in front of the flock. Then the tame one retreats step by step, pretending to be afraid; but the other advances proudly, as if already victorious, and is caught fast in the snare. Now if the one that has fallen into the trap is a male, his companions try to come to the rescue of the captive; but if it is a female, they strike at the one caught, one from one side and one from another, as having fallen into slavery through lust. And I shall not pass over this, since it too is worth hearing. If the decoy is female, then, so that the male may not fall in, the females outside sound an answering song and rescue the one who would have fallen into the snare, since he gladly stays beside his many mates, as though drawn by some erotic spell, by Zeus indeed.

17. The land-hedgehog too is believed to be one of the envious, malign creatures. At any rate, whenever it is caught, it at once wets its own skin with urine and renders it useless—though the skin seems serviceable for many purposes. The lynx too hides its urine; for when it congeals it becomes a stone, and is suited for engraving, and serves, they say, as an ornament for women.
18. A lion that has eaten of the "lion-killer" dies. Insects are destroyed if one smears them with oil. Perfume is the death of vultures. And you will destroy a beetle if you throw roses upon it.

19. Indian dogs—these too are wild beasts, mighty in strength, most spirited in soul, and the largest of dogs anywhere. They look down on all other animals; but the Indian dog goes to meet the lion, and endures its onset, and barks back when it roars, and bites in return when bitten; and having greatly distressed and wounded it, in the end the dog is overcome. Yet a lion might also be overcome by an Indian dog, and indeed once the dog has bitten it holds on most firmly. Even if you come and cut off the dog's leg with a knife, it has no leisure in its pain to relax its bite, but the leg is cut off first and only as a corpse does it let go its mouth, and it lies there, forced to release its hold by

20. death. What is fitting I shall tell elsewhere. Of man alone and of the dog does the food rise up again when they are full. And in man the heart is attached to the left breast, but in other animals it is set in the middle of the chest. No crook-taloned bird drinks or makes water or herds together with others.

21. There is an Indian beast violent in strength, in size like the largest lion, red in colour so as to seem like cinnabar, and shaggy like dogs, named in the Indian tongue the martichoras. Its face is such as to seem to belong not to a beast but to a man. It has three rows of teeth set in above and three rows below, exceedingly sharp at the point, larger than the teeth of dogs. Its ears resemble a man's, but are larger and shaggy. Its eyes are grey, and these too resemble a man's. Imagine its feet and claws to be like a lion's. To the tip of its tail is attached a scorpion's sting, and this would be more than a cubit long, and on either side the tail is set with stings. The tip of the tail stings whomever it meets to death, and destroys him at once. If anyone pursues it, it shoots its stings sideways like arrows, and the creature is a far-darter. When it discharges its stings forward, it bends back its tail; but when backward, after the manner of the Sacae, it stretches it out straight. Whatever the missile strikes it kills—the elephant alone it does not destroy. The stings it hurls are a foot in length and the thickness of a rush. Ctesias says, and affirms that the Indians agree with him, that in the places where those stings are discharged others grow up beneath, so that there is a whole crop of this evil. It delights, as the same author says, above all in eating men, and it kills many men, and lies in wait not for one alone, but would attack two or even three, and overpowers so many single-handed. It masters the rest of the animals too, but could never bring down a lion. That this animal takes the greatest delight in glutting itself with human flesh, its very name proclaims; for in the Greek tongue it means "man-eater," and from this deed it is named. In speed it is like the deer. The Indians hunt the young of these beasts while their tails are still without stings, and they crush the tails with a stone so that they cannot grow stings. Its voice it sends forth as nearly as possible like a trumpet. Ctesias says he has also seen this animal among the Persians, brought as a gift from the Indians to the king of the Persians—if indeed Ctesias is a sufficient witness in such matters. At any rate, having heard the peculiar features of this animal, let one then give heed to the writer of Cnidus.
22. The sea-scolopendra, they say, bursts asunder when a man spits upon it.

23. If one were to give the crushed fruit of the willow to drink to dumb animals, they are not harmed at all, but rather are even nourished by it; but a man who drinks it destroys his power to beget children and bear fruit. And it seems to me that Homer, having tracked out even the secrets of nature, then said in his verses "and willows that lose their fruit," hinting at this. And a man who drinks hemlock dies through the congealing and chilling of his blood, but a pig gluts itself on hemlock and stays healthy.

24. The Indians cannot easily capture a full-grown elephant, but going to the marshes that border the river they take the young of them. For the elephant loves dewy and soft places, and is fond of water, and wishes to live in such haunts,

25. and is, as one might say, a marsh-dweller. So having taken them tender and tractable, they rear them with flattery of the belly and tending of the body and a coaxing voice (for elephants understand even the human speech of the country), and, to put it briefly, they rear them as children and bestow upon them care and various kinds of training. And they obey. When it is threshing-time and the oxen turn about the threshing-floor, and the floor is full of the sheaves, to keep the oxen from tasting the ears they smear their nostrils with dung, having devised this stratagem most aptly. For this animal, loathing the aforesaid smearing, would not taste anything, not even if it were pressed by the heaviest hunger.

26. The Indians hunt hares and foxes in the following way. They have no need of dogs for the hunt, but taking the nestlings of eagles and ravens and kites besides, they rear them and train them in hunting. And the lesson is this: they fasten meat to a tame hare and a domesticated fox, and let them run, and sending the birds after them at their heels they allow them to snatch away the meat. The birds pursue with all their might, and having caught the one or the other they hold it as the prize of their capture, the meat. And this is a bait for them, and a most enticing one. So when they have perfected the hunting skill, they let them loose upon the mountain hares and the wild foxes. And the birds, in hope of their accustomed meal, whenever one of these appears, give chase and seize it most swiftly, and carry it back to their masters, as Ctesias relates. And that in place of the meat formerly fastened to them the entrails of the captured prey serve them as dinner, this too we learn from him.

27. I am told that the griffin, the Indian animal, is four-footed like the lions, and has claws of the greatest strength, and these very like a lion's; and that it is winged, and the feathers of its back they sing of as black in colour, those of its front they say are red, but the wings themselves no longer such, but white. Ctesias records that its neck is variegated with dark-blue feathers, and that it has an eagle-like beak and a head such as artists draw and model. Its eyes, he says, are fiery. It makes its nest upon the mountains, and to take a full-grown one is impossible, but they catch the young. And the Bactrians, who are neighbours of the Indians, say that the griffins are guardians of the gold in those parts, and that they dig it up and weave it into their nests, and the Indians take what flows off. But the Indians deny that they are guardians of the aforesaid gold—for the griffins have no need of gold (and if they say this, they seem to me to speak credibly); rather the Indians themselves come to gather the gold, while the griffins, in fear for their young, fight with those who approach. And they contend with the other animals and overpower them most easily, but do not withstand the lion or the elephant. So the natives, dreading the strength of these beasts, do not set out for the gold by day, but come by night; for at that hour they seem more likely to escape notice. This region, where the griffins live and the gold is found, is dreadfully desolate. The seekers of the aforesaid wealth come a thousand and twice as many strong, armed, and they bring mattocks and sacks, and they dig, watching for a moonless night. Now if they escape the notice of the griffins, they gain a double profit; for they are saved and they carry their freight home, and those who have learned to refine gold, by a certain skill of their own, have very great wealth in return for the aforesaid dangers; but if they are caught in the act, they perish. And they return home, as I learn, every third or fourth year.

28. The severed head of a sea-tortoise sees and closes its eyes when a hand is brought near; and it would even bite if you brought your hand nearer. And for a long time it keeps its eyes shining; for its pupils are very white and very conspicuous, and when taken out they are set in gold and necklaces. Hence indeed they seem marvellous to women. These tortoises, as I learn, are found in the sea that men call the Red Sea.

29. The cock, when the moon rises, is filled with rapture, they say, and frolics. And the rising sun could never escape its notice, and at that hour it is most musical of all. I am told too that the cock is a bird dear to Leto. The reason is that they say it stood by her when she was in the double and blessed throes of childbirth. Hence even now the cock attends women in labour, and seems somehow to make their delivery easy. And when the hen has died, the cock himself broods upon the eggs, and hatches out his own chicks in silence; for he does not sing then, from some wondrous and secret cause—no, by heaven; for he seems to me to be conscious that he is then doing the work of a female and not of a male. And a cock defeated in battle and in the contest against another will not sing; for his spirit is cast down, and he sinks away in shame. But the victor is proud and holds his neck high, and

30. is like one exulting. And this too is surely worthy of wonder in the creature: when going under a doorway, even a very high one, it stoops, performing this most boastfully; for it seems to do so out of regard for its comb. Jackdaws love their own kind dreadfully. This is just what often destroys them, and the thing done is as follows. Whoever has a mind to hunt jackdaws contrives thus. Where he knows their feeding-grounds and pastures and sees them gathering in flocks, there he sets out basins full of oil. Now the oil is clear, and the bird is curious, and it comes and sits on the rim of the vessel, and bends down and sees its own reflection, and thinks it sees another jackdaw, and is eager to come down to it. So it descends and flaps its wings and covers itself with oil, and is least able to flutter up again, and without nets or snare or cords the creature remains, as one might say, fettered.

31. The elephant—some say it has tusks projecting, others horns. It has on each foot five toes, showing the beginnings of separation, but not divided. Hence indeed it is least able to swim. Its hind legs are shorter than its front ones; its breasts are by the armpits; it possesses a trunk more all-useful than a hand, and a short tongue; its gall, they say, is not by the liver but by the intestine. I learn that the elephant is pregnant for two years. Others say not so long, but agree it is eighteen months. It brings forth one as large as a yearling calf, and the calf draws the teat with its mouth. When inflamed to mating and burning with frenzy, it falls upon a wall and overturns it, and bends palm-trees, dashing its forehead against them after the manner of rams. It drinks water neither clear nor pure, but when it has muddied and stirred it. It sleeps standing upright; for to lie down and rise up again is laborious for it. The prime of an elephant is sixty years. It is least able to bear frost. It prolongs its life even to two hundred years.

32. The sheep-rearing of the Indians is worth learning what it is like. I am told that their goats and sheep are larger than the largest asses, and that each bears four; indeed an Indian goat or sheep would never bear fewer than three. The tails of the sheep reach to the foot, but the goats have very long ones, so as almost to touch the ground. Now from the sheep that are good at bearing the herdsmen cut off the tails, so that they may be mounted, and from their fat they press out oil too; but of the males they cut through the tails and take out the fat and sew them up again, and the cut grows together once more, and the traces of it disappear.

33. Alexander of Myndus says that the chameleon harasses snakes and brings them to starvation in the following way. Biting on a broad, firm twig, it turns itself about and comes face to face against the enemy. The snake is unable to lay hold of it, having no way to gape wide enough to take in the breadth of the twig. So the snake remains, as far as the chameleon is concerned, without its dinner; for biting the rest of its limbs it accomplishes nothing, since the chameleon has a firm hide, and feels nothing at all of the snake's teeth.

34. The lion's neck is composed of a single bone, not of many vertebrae. And if anyone cleaves the lion's bones, fire leaps out from them. They have no marrow; for they are not hollow after the manner of pipes. No season of the year holds it back from mating. It is pregnant for two months. It bears five times: at the first birth five, at the second four, three at the next, two at the one after, and one at all the last. The newborn cubs are small and blind like puppies; they begin to walk when they have lived two months from birth. The story that says they tear apart the womb is a myth. A hungry lion is hard to meet, but a sated one is most gentle; and they say it is then fond of play. A lion would never flee turning its back, but quietly retreats step by step, looking the foe in the face. When old age begins, it comes to the steadings and the huts and the cave-dwellings of the herdsmen, and with reason; for it can no longer take heart for the hunts on the mountains. It dreads fire. Now whichever of them is rounder and more compact and shaggier in mane seems more faint-hearted and less daring; but the one well-grown in length and straight-haired is believed more manly and more spirited. Being a glutton, it would, they say, swallow whole limbs by gulping. So when filled with these it often does not eat for three days, until what it first took has been consumed and digested. It drinks little.

35. The gentle ox would never forget the one who strikes and chastises it, but remembering, it takes vengeance even after an interval of time. For while under the yoke and in a way penned up, it is like a prisoner and keeps quiet; but when released, often it has struck with its leg and crushed some limb of the herdsman, and often, growing angry, has fallen upon him with its horn and killed him. Yet toward the others it is gentle, and comes into the stall quietly; for it is not savage toward those against whom it has no cause for anger.

36. The land of the Indians—the historians say it is rich in drugs and dreadfully prolific of such growths. Some of them preserve and rescue from danger those who, through bites, are at death's door (and there are many such things there), while others destroy and kill most swiftly—among which would be that produced from the purple snake. Now this snake is about a span long to look at, and in colour resembles the deepest purple. They describe its head as white and no longer purple, and white not, so to speak, ordinarily, but beyond snow and milk. This snake is toothless. It is found in the most fiery regions of India. It is least apt to bite, and in this respect you would say it is tame and gentle; but whomever it vomits upon, as I hear, whether man or beast, that limb must wholly rot away. So when it has been caught they hang it up by the tail, and as is natural it has its head down and looks toward the ground; and beneath its very mouth they place a vessel made of bronze. And through the mouth drops trickle from it into this, and what flows down sets and congeals, and on seeing it you would say it was the gum of an almond. And the snake dies, and they take away the vessel and set another in its place, of bronze too; and from the dead snake there flows again a watery ichor, and it resembles water. They leave it three days, and this too sets. And there would be a difference between the two in colour; for the one is dreadfully black, while the other is like amber. Now of this, if you gave to anyone as much as a sesame seed mixed into wine or food, first a convulsion will seize him, and a very strong one, then his eyes are distorted, and his brain slips out, trickling through his nostrils, and he dies most pitiably; but if he takes less of the drug, from then on his case is hopeless, yet he perishes only in time. And if you offer the black, which flowed from the dead snake, this too the size of a sesame seed, the man who takes it grows full of pus, and consumption seizes him, and within a year he is wasted away in decay; but many have gone on even to two years, dying little by little.

37. The ostrich lays many eggs, but does not hatch them all; rather it sets aside the infertile ones, and broods upon the fruitful. And from these it hatches out its chicks, while those that have been rejected it sets before them as food. If anyone pursues it, it does not venture upon flight, but runs with its wings spread; and if it is about to be caught, it slings with its feet the stones that lie in its way back at the pursuer.

38. The small sparrows, conscious of their weakness because of the smallness of their bodies, build their nests upon the slender tips of the branches that can bear them, and thus for the most part escape the plots of the hunters, who cannot climb out upon the twig; for it does not bear them, owing to its thinness.

39. Foxes, having reached the height of cunning and crafty ways, whenever they see a thriving wasps' nest, themselves turn aside from the hollow, swerving away and guarding against the wounds of the stings; but they let down their tail, which is very thick and long, and shake the wasps with it. The wasps cling to the thickness of the hairs. And when they have become entangled in it, the foxes dash the tail against a tree or wall or stone fence; and the wasps, being struck, die. Then the foxes come again to the same spot, and having gathered up and killed the rest just as they did the first, when at last they perceive that there is peace and freedom from the stings, they put down their mouth and eat the wasp-grubs, neither disturbed nor any longer wary of the stings.

40. A dog's skull has no suture. And one that has run a great deal becomes more lustful, they say. As a dog grows old its teeth grow blunt and turn black. It is so keen of scent that it would never taste roast dog's flesh, not even if it were bewitched with the most varied and crafty sauce. Three diseases, and no more, are allotted to the dog: quinsy, madness, and gout; but to men there are countless ones. Everything that is bitten by a mad dog dies. And a dog that has gout you will rarely see recover. The longest life of a dog is fourteen years. Argus, the dog of Odysseus, and the tale about him, seem to be a fancy of Homer's.

41. There is also a kind of very small Indian birds. It nests on the high crags and on the rocks called "leprous," and the little birds are in size about as big as a partridge's egg; imagine their colour to be that of realgar. The Indians in their own tongue like to call it dikairon, and the Greeks, as I hear, dikaion. If one were to take of its droppings as much as a millet seed dissolved in drink, he is dead by evening. And the death resembles sleep, and a most sweet and painless one, such as the poets like to call "limb-loosing" or "gentle"; for it too would be free of pain and therefore most pleasant to those who need it. The Indians set the highest value on obtaining it; for they consider it truly a remedy that brings forgetfulness of evils; and so among the most precious gifts to the king of the Persians the king of the Indians sends this too. And he, receiving it, prizes it above all the rest and lays it up in store as an adversary and defence against incurable evils, should necessity overtake him. So no one else among the Persians has it, save the king himself and the king's mother. And so let us, comparing them, examine of the two drugs, the Indian and the Egyptian, which was the more to be prized; since the Egyptian held back and checked the tears for a day, but the Indian provided eternal forgetfulness of evils; and the one was a woman's gift, the other a bird's, or rather of a mysterious nature that releases one from the truly heaviest of bonds through the aforesaid servant. And the Indians have had the good fortune to possess it, so as to be released from their watch here whenever they wish.

42. The bird called the attagas (Aristophanes too mentions it in his play the Birds) utters and sings out its own name with such voice as it has. They say that the birds called Meleagrides do the same, and that they are most fittingly attested to be related by descent to Meleager, the son of Oeneus. The myth says that all the women who were kin to the young son of Oeneus fell into uncontrollable weeping and unbearable grief and lamentation, admitting no remedy for their sorrow, and that through the pity of the gods they were changed in form into these creatures. And there is in them an image and a seed of that ancient grief, fixed deep within, and even now they sing of Meleager, and they sing too that they are his kin. And whoever reveres the divine would never touch these birds for food. And what the reason is, both the inhabitants of the island of Leros know, and it may be learned elsewhere.

43. I have learned this too about ants. So present in them is the love of toil and the willingness to labour, without any excuse and without any malingering pretext and pretence behind which sloth lurks, that even at the full moon they do not even by night grow idle or rest, but cling to their work. O men, who devise countless excuses and pretexts for taking your ease! And what need is there to recount and pour forth so great a crowd of them? For Dionysia have been proclaimed, and Lenaea, and Chytri, and Gephyrismi, and when one passes to Sparta there are other festivals, and to Thebes others, and in every city countless ones, some barbarian, some Greek.

44. As evidence of the nature of animals—that they are not altogether hard to manage, but, when well treated, are good at remembering the kindness—there are in Egypt the cats and the ichneumons and the crocodiles and still the race of hawks. Each is taken by flattery of the belly, and being thence tamed remains thereafter most gentle; and it would never attack its own benefactors, once the anger inborn and kindred to it has been loosed. But a man—a creature endowed with reason and deemed worthy of intelligence and granted a sense of shame and entrusted with the power to blush—becomes a grievous enemy to his friend, and the secrets entrusted to him, for the slightest and most casual cause, he spits out to the ruin of the one who trusted him.

45. Eudemus says there is a tale worthy of wonder, and this is the man's tale. A young hunter, able to live among the wildest of animals—reared, that is, from young and from cubs—had as his fellow-nurslings and messmates a dog and a bear and a lion that had grown up together. And these, Eudemus says, kept peace with one another for a time and were friendly in their feelings; but one day it happened that the dog, playing with the bear and fawning upon it and teasing it, the bear was contrary to custom turned savage and fell upon the dog, and tore the belly of the poor creature with its claws and rent it apart. The same author says that the lion was indignant at what had happened, and as it were hated the implacable and unfriendly act of the bear, and longed for the dog as a comrade, and came to a just anger, and laid upon the bear its punishment, and did to it the very things that it had done to the dog. Now Homer says that it is good that even a son of one who has perished should be left behind; but nature seems to show that to leave behind a friend to avenge oneself, dear Homer, is also a gain. Something of the like we think too about Zeno and Cleanthes, if we hear aright.

46. Among the Indians there are creatures as large as beetles might grow, and they are red; you would liken them to cinnabar, if you first beheld them. These have very long legs, and are soft to the touch. They grow upon the trees that bear amber, and feed on the fruit of these plants. The Indians hunt them and press them out, and from them dye their scarlet cloaks and the tunics beneath them and whatever else they wish to turn and dye to this colour. And such clothing is brought also to the king of the Persians. And the beauty of the clothing seems marvellous to the Persians, and when set beside the native Persian dyes it far surpasses and astonishes them, as Ctesias says; since it is keener and more brilliant than the famous Sardian dyes. There are produced too, in that part of India where the beetles are, the so-called Cynocephali, "Dog-heads," to whom the appearance and nature of their body gave the name; for in all else they have the features of men, and they walk clad in the skins of wild beasts. And they are just, and harm no man, and they utter no speech, but howl, yet they understand the language of the Indians. Their food is wild animals; and they catch these most easily, for they are very swift, and having caught them they kill them, and roast them not with fire, but tear them into pieces and dry them in the heat of the sun. They also rear goats and sheep. And they make the wild animals their food, but drink the milk of the flocks they rear. I have made mention of them among the irrational creatures, and with reason; for they have no articulate, distinct, and human voice.

47. Chloris is the name of a bird, which would make its nest from nothing else but the so-called comfrey; and comfrey is a root hard to find and to dig up. For bedding it spreads under itself hairs and wool. And the female bird is so called, but the male they call chlorion, and it is ingenious in its life, good at learning whatever you will and steadfast in enduring the trial that comes with learning, whenever it is caught. And through the winter one would not see it free and at liberty, but when the spring turnings of the year begin, then it would appear. When Arcturus rises, it withdraws to its own haunts, whence it set out hither.

48. A bull whetted by anger and rampaging with its horn and borne along by an uncontrollable rush—neither does the herdsman check it, nor fear restrain it, nor anything else of the kind; but a man stops it and looses it from its onset by binding fast his own right knee with a band and meeting it.

49. The leopard has five toes on its front feet, but four on its hind feet. The female is stronger than the male. And if it tastes unknowingly of the so-called leopard's-bane (it is a plant), having tracked out human excrement from somewhere, it saves itself.

50. Horses, they say, have no lower eyelashes. So they say that Apelles of Ephesus is blamed, since in painting a certain horse he failed to observe this peculiarity of the animal. But others say that it was not Apelles who incurred this charge, but Micon, a good man at painting this animal, who erred only in the thing mentioned.

52. I have learned that wild asses no smaller than horses in size are found among the Indians. And they are white over the rest of the body, but have the head somewhat purple, and the eyes send forth a dark-blue colour. They have a horn on the forehead about a cubit and a half in length, and the lower part of the horn is white, the upper crimson, but the middle exceedingly black. From these variegated horns I am told the Indians drink—and not all of them, but the most powerful among the Indians—pouring gold around them at intervals, as though adorning with bracelets the fair arm of a statue. And they say that the one who drinks from this horn becomes a stranger and unacquainted with incurable diseases; for he would not be seized by convulsions, nor by the so-called sacred disease, nor be destroyed by poisons. And if he has previously drunk something harmful, he vomits it up and becomes whole again. It is believed that the other asses over all the earth, both tame and wild, and the other solid-hoofed beasts, have no anklebones, nor any gall by the liver; but Ctesias says that the Indian asses which have the horn possess anklebones and are not without gall; and the anklebones are said to be black, and if one were to crush them, they are such within as well. And these are the swiftest not only of asses, but of horses and deer; they begin their running quietly, but gather strength little by little, and to pursue them is, in the poet's phrase, "to chase the uncatchable." When the female has given birth and leads about her newborn, the fathers, pasturing with them, guard the young. The haunts of these asses are the most desolate of the Indian plains. When the Indians go out for their capture, they let the tender and still young ones graze behind, while they themselves fight in their defence, and go to meet the horsemen, and strike with their horns. And so great is the strength of these creatures that nothing struck withstands them, but yields and is cut through, and if it chances is crushed and rendered useless. Already too they have fallen upon the flanks of horses and split them open and poured out their entrails. Hence indeed the horsemen dread to come near them; for the price of coming near is for them a most pitiable death, and they perish, both they and their horses. They are dangerous at kicking too. And their bites reach so deep that they tear away all they have grasped. A full-grown one alive you could not take, but they are shot with javelins and arrows, and the Indians strip the horns from them when dead and treat them as I have said. The flesh of the Indian asses is uneatable; the reason is that it is naturally most bitter.

53. Eudemus says that there are irrational animals which have a natural arithmetic without being taught, and he adduces as evidence the following about the animals in Libya. The name he does not give; but what he says is this. Whatever it catches, it makes into eleven portions, and eats ten of them, but leaves the eleventh (for whom, and with what notion, is worth considering) as a kind of first-fruits or a tithe, as one might say. So it is right to be amazed at this self-taught wisdom; for an irrational animal knows the unit and the dyad and the numbers that follow. But for a man, how many lessons are needed, and how many blows, that he may either learn these things well and rightly or often not learn them at all?

54. The Egyptians say (and philosophers do not lightly disregard them) that in a certain nome of Egypt, which they name after Heracles the son of Zeus, a beautiful boy, beautiful as an Egyptian, a keeper of geese, was loved by an asp, and indeed the love was marvellous on her part. Then, visiting her beloved, she would foretell to him in a dream the plots being craftily devised against him by another snake, which was, as one might say, her mate, the male trying to do this out of jealousy of the boy over his bride; and the boy, heeding her, was persuaded and kept on his guard. Now Homer gave a horse a voice, but nature gave one to the asp, "which cares nothing for laws," as Euripides says.

55. I have heard that camels live even fifty years, but I am told that those from Bactria go on even to twice that span. And the males being warlike, the Bactrians geld them, taking away their wantonness and lasciviousness, but preserving their strength. The females have the parts that kindle them to heat cauterized.

56. Eudemus says that a seal fell in love with a man accustomed to hunt sponges, and coming forth from the sea to where there was a hollow rock would consort with him. Of his fellow-craftsmen this man was the ugliest, but to the seal he seemed most beautiful. And there is perhaps nothing to wonder at, since men too have often fallen in love with the less beautiful, feeling nothing for the most beautiful, but neglecting them.

57. Aristotle says that one struck by the water-snake at once gives off a most heavy smell, so that no one can come near him. The same author says that forgetfulness is poured over the one struck, and indeed a great mist over his eyes, and madness comes upon him and a very strong trembling, and he dies on the third day.

58. One must know that the oinas is a bird, and not, as some think, a vine. Aristotle says that it is larger than the ringdove, but smaller than the pigeon. There are, as I hear, certain "oinas-hunters" even at Sparta. It might also be said that the female hawk differs from the male hawk not only in kind but also in nature.

59. Cyanus is its name, a bird by nature, unsociable in its ways, hating the haunts of the city and the lodgings in houses, and shunning too the haunts in the fields and wherever there are huts and the steadings of men, but delighting in solitudes and taking pleasure in mountain peaks and sheer crags. Nor does it take delight in mainlands or in goodly islands, but in Scyros and any other like it that is exceedingly wretched and barren and for the most part bereft of men.

60. Finches, indeed, are wiser even than men at foreknowing the future. At any rate they know when winter is coming, and they have most providently guarded against the snow that is to be. And for fear of being caught they flee to the wooded places, and the thickets are, as one might say, their refuges.

1. They say that there are black birds, dark to look at, which inhabit the land of the Parians and neighbouring Cyzicus; you would call them hawks by their shape. They do not taste flesh, and are temperate as to the belly, and seeds suffice them for a meal. When autumn begins, a flock of these birds (they call them Memnons) goes straight to the Trojan land, to the tomb of Memnon. Those who still dwell in the Troad say that there is a mound consecrated to Memnon the son of Eos; and that his very corpse, carried by his mother to Susa—the place so famously hymned as Memnonian—was raised on high from the field of slaughter and received the burial befitting him, while the monument there bears his name in another sense. So the birds named after the aforesaid hero come every year, and they divide and split into enmity and difference, and they fight a fierce battle, until half of them die, and the others, the victors, go off whence indeed they came. Now how this is done, and whence, I have no leisure now to philosophize, nor to track out the secrets of nature; but this shall be said. The aforesaid birds wage this contest every year as a funeral game for the son of Eos and Tithonus. The Greeks honoured Pelias once with a contest, and Amarynceus, and indeed Patroclus too, and Achilles, the rival of Memnon.

2. They say that in Crete the owl is not bred at all, but that if one is brought in from outside it dies. Euripides seems to have written without examination when he made Polyidus, seeing this bird and inferring from it that he would find Glaucus. For my part I learn that the Cretans sing and teach stories besides those already related. The Cretan land received a gift from Zeus, since it was, of course, his nurse and concealed him in the famous hiding-place: that it should be free of every wicked beast born for harm, and should neither breed such itself nor rear one brought from outside. And it displays the power of the gift; for it is barren of the aforesaid creatures. And if anyone, by way of test or proof of the favour from Zeus, should bring in one of those foreign beasts, it dies the moment it merely touches the land. So those who hunt snakes in nearby Libya contrive as follows. These charmers tame and bring as a spectacle many of the venomous beasts, and bring with them a load of Libyan earth, enough for their need. They do this through forethought for the snakes, so that they may not perish; and for this reason, whenever they come to the aforesaid island, they do not set down the animals before they have first scattered beneath them the foreign earth they bring.
