And upon this they gather the crowds, and indeed they astonish the foolish and the many. Now so long as each of them remains in its place, coiled and settled, and rises up but does not pass beyond its own familiar dust, so long it lives; but if it ventures out onto the foreign earth that is strange to it and hostile, it dies, and with reason. For if the nod of Zeus was not unfulfilled toward Thetis, nor would be toward anyone else, it will surely not appear void toward his own nurse.

3. The river Indus is without beasts, but in it alone, they say, is bred a worm. And its form is such as those that are born and bred in wood; but those of that river grow to seven cubits in length, though larger and smaller might be found; and their thickness is such that a boy of ten years would scarcely be able to clasp them with his arms. They have one tooth growing above and another below, and both are square, a span in length. So great is the strength of their teeth. Whatever they take in them they crush most easily, whether it be a stone or a tame or wild animal. By day they remain below in the depth of the river, delighting in the mud and slime, and so are not visible; but by night they come out onto the land, and whatever they meet—horse or ox or ass—they crush it, then drag it to their own haunts and eat it in the river, and gnaw all its limbs except the belly of the animal. And if hunger presses them even by day, when a camel or ox drinks at the bank they creep up beneath and seize it very warily by the tip of the lips, and by a most violent rush and a firm pull drag it into the water, and make it their dinner. A hide of two fingers' thickness covers each of them. The taking and hunting of them is contrived in this way. They let down a stout and strong hook fastened to an iron chain, having tied to it a rope of white flax a talent in weight, and wrapped both with wool here and there so that the worm may not gnaw through them; and having fixed a lamb or kid upon the hook, they then let it down into the water of the river. As many as thirty men hold the rope, each with a javelin slung ready and a sword at his side. And there lie at hand serviceable clubs to strike with if need be; these are of cornel-wood, exceedingly hard. Then, when the worm is caught upon the hook and has swallowed the bait, they haul it up, and having caught it they kill it and hang it in the heat for thirty days. And from it a thick oil drips into earthenware vessels; each animal yields ten cotylae. This oil they bring to the king of the Indians, sealed with seals; for no one else is permitted to have so much as a drop of it. The rest of the creature's carcass is useless. The oil has this power. Whatever heap of wood you wish to set ablaze and reduce to embers, you will kindle it by pouring on a cotyle of this, without first putting under it any seed of fire; and if you wish to burn a man or animal, you pour it on, and at once he is consumed. With this, they say, the king of the Indians takes the cities that have come into enmity with him, and waits for neither rams nor tortoises nor the other siege-engines, since he has taken them by burning; for he fills earthenware vessels, each holding about a cotyle, with the oil, and stops them up above, and slings them at the gates. And when they hit the windows, the vessels are dashed and broken, and the oil pours down, and fire is poured over the gates, and is unquenchable. It burns armour too, and men in battle, and its strength is boundless. It is put out and made to vanish by a great quantity of rubbish thrown over it. So Ctesias of Cnidus says.

4. The porpoise is an animal like the dolphin, and it too has milk. In colour it is not black, but resembles the deepest dark-blue, and it breathes not by gills but by a blowhole; for so they call the passage of its breath. Its haunt is the Black Sea and the sea there; and the porpoise is least apt to wander beyond those haunts.

5. The hen that has conquered the male in battle grows proud with pleasure and lets down its wattles—not so far as the cocks do, yet it lets them down, and is filled with spirit, and steps out more largely.

6. The dolphin is believed to be a creature that loves its own kind. And the proof is this. Aenus is a Thracian city. It happened that a dolphin was caught and wounded, not to death, but so that life was still possible for the captive. So blood flowed, and the others not yet taken perceived it, and a whole shoal came to the harbour, and leaped about, and seemed bent on doing something not good. So the people of Aenus were afraid and released the captive. And the others, having recovered it as one of their kindred, went off and departed. But rarely is a man a partner in zeal and care for a kinsman or kinswoman in misfortune.

7. In Egypt, as Eudemus says, a monkey was being pursued, and cats were the pursuers. So fleeing with all its might it made straight for a certain tree, and they too sprang up most swiftly; for they cling to the bark, and trees are climbable for them too. But when it was being caught, being one against many, it leaped from the trunk, and seized with its hands the tip of a branch that hung overhead, and held on firmly for no short time; and the cats, since it was no longer within their reach, ran off to another hunt. And it, with much effort, was saved, owing to itself, as was fitting, its rescue.

8. Aristotle says that the land of the Astypalaeans is hostile to snakes, just as the same author agrees with us that Rheneia is hostile to weasels. And the crow cannot climb up to the Athenian acropolis. And you will not call Elis the mother of mules—or what is said is false.

9. For the people of Rhegium and the Locrians it is by treaty allowed to pass into each other's land and till it. Yet the cicadas of the one and of the other do not agree with these terms, nor are they of one and the same mind; for you will find the Locrian cicada most silent in Rhegium, and the Rhegian most

10. voiceless among the Locrians. And what the reason for such an exchange is, I do not know, nor does anyone else, unless he is idly bold; but Nature alone knows, O men of Rhegium and Locri. At any rate a river runs between the land of the Rhegians and Locris, and the banks are not parted even by the distance of a plethron, and yet neither kind flies across it. And in Cephallenia there is a river which is the cause of the fruitfulness of the cicadas on one side and their barrenness on the other. As for their king, the bees, when he leaves them—being gentle and tame and very nearly stingless—pursue and chase him as a fugitive from his rule. They track him by scent in a secret way, and seize him from the smell about him, and bring him back to his kingship, willingly and of their own desire, admiring his character. But the Athenians drove out Pisistratus, and the Syracusans Dionysius, and others others, since they were tyrants and lawless and unable to display the kingly art, which is indeed humanity and the protection of subjects.

11. It is the king's care among the bees that the swarm be ordered in this way. Some he commands to carry water, others within to mould the honeycombs, while the third part goes out to forage; and then they change their tasks in rotation, having most beautifully divided them. But the king himself—it is enough for him to have taken thought for these things and to legislate as I have said, after the manner of the great rulers whom the philosophers like to name the same men, statesmen and kings—as for the rest he rests and is exempt from working with his own hands. And if it is better for the bees to move, then the ruler too departs. And if he is still young, he leads, and the rest follow; but if he is older, he goes carried, borne by other bees. The bees turn to sleep at a signal. When it seems time to sleep, the king commands one to sound the signal for slumber. And she, obeying, has proclaimed it, and the others turn thereupon to rest, having until then been humming. So long as the king survives, the swarm prospers, and all disorder is banished; and the drones rest contentedly in their own cells, and the older bees dwell apart, and the young apart, and the king by himself, and the larvae are by themselves, and their food and their evacuations are kept separate. But when the king perishes, all is full of disorder and anarchy; for the drones lay eggs in the bees' cells, and the rest, being thrown into confusion among one another, no longer permit the swarm to prosper; and they die out at last for lack of a ruler. The bee lives a pure life, and would never feed upon any animal; and it needs no Pythagoras as counsellor, but the flowers suffice it as food. It is also of the highest temperance. At any rate it has hated luxury and softness. And the proof is this: it pursues and drives away one anointed with perfume as an enemy who has done it deadly harm. And it knows too one who has come from licentious intercourse, and pursues him also as a deadly foe. And they are well endowed with courage and are not to be turned. They flee no animal at all, nor yield in cowardice, but go to meet it. And toward those who do not trouble them nor begin unjust acts nor approach the swarm with mischief and treachery, they are peaceful and at truce; but a truceless war, as the saying is, is kindled against those who harm them, and whoever comes to ravage their honey is reckoned among their enemies. They smite the wasps badly too. And Aristotle says that once, meeting a horseman near the swarm, the bees killed him, falling upon him in force, horse and all. Yet at times they differ even among themselves, and the stronger overcome the weaker. And there overcome them, as I hear, both the toads and the frogs from the marshes and the bee-eaters and the swallows, and often the wasps too. But whoever overcomes them wins, so to speak, a Cadmean victory; for being struck and stung they come off badly; for the bees are armed no less with spirit than with stings. Nor are they without a share of providential wisdom, and Aristotle gives proof of what I say. It is this. Some bees came to a swarm not their own but another's, and then plundered the honey that in no way belonged to them. But the others, although robbed of their own labour, nevertheless endured quietly, keeping still, and then waited firmly to see what would come. And when the beekeeper had killed most of the enemy, those within, judging that they could be a match for an equal fight, came forth and then defended themselves, and exacted a vengeance for what they had been robbed of that was by no means to be blamed.

12. This too is a proof of the industriousness of bees. In the most wintry of places, from the setting of the Pleiades to the spring equinox, the bees keep continually within doors and rest indoors quietly, out of longing for warmth and flight from cold; but all the rest of the year they hate idleness and rest, and are good at toil. And you would never see a bee loitering outside that season in which their limbs are numbed.

13. Geometry, and beauty of shapes, and lovely formations the bees display without art or rule or what the wise call the compass. And when there is increase and the swarm thrives with bees, they send out colonies just as the greatest and most populous of cities do. The bee knows too when rain threatens to visit, and when a harsh wind is to come. And if the wind should come upon it contrary to its expectation, you will see each carrying a stone with the tips of its feet for ballast. And what the divine Plato says about the cicadas and their love of song and of music, one might say also about the choir of bees. At any rate, whenever they frisk about or stray, then the beekeepers clap a certain rhythmic and harmonious clapping; and the bees, as though drawn by a Siren, indeed turn back to their own haunts again.

14. In the island of Gyaros, Aristotle says, there are mice, and indeed they eat the iron ore of the earth. And Amyntas says that those in Teredon (this is a land of Babylonia) feed on the same. In Latmus in Caria, I hear, there are scorpions which sting their own citizens to death, but the strangers only gently and just enough to cause an itch—Zeus the protector of strangers, it seems to me, having assigned this gift to those who come there.

15. Wasps too, then, are ruled by a king, but not tyrannized as men are. And the proof is that these also are stingless. And the subjects have it for a law to mould the works, while the rulers are double the size, but gentle and such as can harm neither willingly nor unwillingly. Who then would not hate the Dionysii in Sicily, and Clearchus in Heraclea, and Apollodorus the butcher of the people of Cassandrea, and Nabis the ruiner of the Lacedaemonians, if indeed those took heart in the sword, while the kings of the wasps took heart in stinglessness and gentleness?

16. The wasps that have stings are said to do this too. Whenever they see a dead viper, they fall upon it and poison their sting. Whence men too seem to me to have learned a lesson, and that not a good one. And indeed Homer bears witness in the Odyssey, saying, "seeking a man-slaying drug, that he might have wherewith to anoint his bronze-tipped arrows"; or, by Zeus, if one must give any heed to the tale about Heracles—that he dipped his arrows in the poison of the hydra—so those too whet their stings with the dipping.

17. Let the fly too have from us the honour of not being left without mention here; for it also is a creation of nature. The flies of Pisa, at the festival of the Olympic games, make, as one might say, a truce both with the visitors and the natives. At any rate, when so many victims are sacrificed and blood is shed and meats are hung up, the flies vanish of their own accord, and cross the Alpheus to the bank opposite. And they seem to differ not at all from the women of the country, save perhaps that those flies are admitted to be somewhat more self-controlled than the women in their conduct; for the women are driven out by the law of the contest and of the temperance belonging to it, but the flies withdraw of their own accord from the sacred things, and during the rites and throughout the appointed time of the games they depart. The contest is dissolved, and they return, as though exiles who have obtained a recall by decree; then the flies flow back into Elis again.

18. The orphus is a sea creature, and if you catch and cut it open, you would not see it die at once, but it lingers in motion, and that for no short time. Through the winter it likes to keep house in its holes; and its haunts are dearer to it nearer the land.

19. The wolf is least apt to go to meet a bull and come at it face to face, but it fears the horns and swerves from their points. And as though it would fight in a straight line it threatens; yet it does not do this, but only makes a show as if about to attack, and then when the bull charges, it twists itself aside and leaps onto its back, and the rival beast holds the beast firmly, and overpowers it, the wolf making up by natural cunning for what it lacks.
20. The sea-ass has its heart placed in its belly, as those skilled in such matters agree with us and teach.

21. The peacock knows that it is the most beautiful of birds, and where its beauty resides, this too it knows, and on it it prides itself and is haughty, and takes confidence in its feathers, which both lend it adornment and send forth fear upon outsiders, and in the summer season provide it with shade from its own resources, not begged nor borrowed. At any rate, if it wishes to frighten anyone, it raises its tail-feathers and then shakes them and sends forth a sound, and the bystanders are afraid, as though frightened by the clang of a soldier from his armour. It lifts its head and nods most haughtily, as though shaking a triple crest. And when it needs to cool itself, it raises its feathers, and inclining them forward displays a kind of natural shade of its own body, screening off the keen point of the sunbeam. And if there is also a wind behind, it quietly parts its feathers; and the breath that flows through, blowing soft and most pleasant breezes upon it, gives the bird refreshment. And when praised it perceives it, and just as a beautiful boy or a lovely woman displays the most advantageous part of the body, so too the peacock raises its feathers in order and in rows, and resembles a flowery meadow or a picture variegated with the many hues of paints; and the labour lies before painters to liken the peculiar work of nature. And it shows how it stands in abundance for display; for it allows the bystanders to take their fill of the sight, and turns itself about, showing diligently the many-formed splendour of its plumage, displaying its own robe above the dress of the Medes and the embroideries of the Persians, and that most haughtily. It is said to have been brought from the barbarians to the Greeks. And being long rare it was then shown for a fee to those who loved beauty, and at Athens at the new moons they received both men and women to view them, and made the spectacle a source of revenue. They valued the male and the female at ten thousand drachmas, as Antiphon says in his speech against Erasistratus. And a double house is needed for their keeping, and guards and attendants too. Hortensius the Roman was judged the first to sacrifice a peacock for a banquet. But Alexander of Macedon, seeing these birds among the Indians, was astonished, and marvelling at their beauty he threatened the heaviest threats against anyone who should sacrifice a peacock.

22. When mice fall into wine-coolers, being unable to swim up and climb out, they bite each other's tails, and so the first draws up the second, and the second the third. Thus indeed most wise Nature taught even these to ally with and help one another.

23. Crocodiles lie in wait for those who draw water from the Nile in the following way. They throw brushwood over themselves, and looking out through it they swim beneath the brushwood. The people come bringing jars or pitchers or water-pots. Then, as they are drawing water, the crocodiles slip out from the brushwood and spring up onto the bank, and seizing them with a most violent snatch they have their dinner. These present remarks of mine have been about the inborn wickedness and cunning of crocodiles.

24. The hare fears dogs, and so too the fox. And these same, by their barking, even rouse a boar from the thicket, and turn a lion, and pursue a deer; but no bird makes any account of a dog, and there is a truce between them. The bustard alone shudders at dogs. The reason is that they are heavy and carry a mass of flesh. So their wings do not lift and lighten them easily, and for this reason they fly low and near the ground, the mass weighing them down. And they are often caught by the dogs. Being conscious of this, whenever they hear barking, they run down into the thickets and marshes, putting these before themselves as a defence, and so rescue themselves from the present danger most readily.

25. Late does a man begin to recognize his parents, being taught and in a way compelled to look upon his father and greet his mother and smile upon his kin; but lambs leap about their mothers from birth, and know both the strange and the familiar, and need to learn nothing at all from the herdsmen.

26. The monkey is a most imitative creature, and whatever you teach it of the things done with the body, it will learn exactly, so as to display it. At any rate it dances, if it learns, and plays the flute, if you teach it. And I myself have seen one holding the reins and laying on the whip and driving. And learning one thing and another it would not disappoint its teacher; so varied and versatile is nature.

27. There are also these peculiar and various natures of animals. Theopompus says that the hares among the Bisaltae have double livers. Ister says that the Meleagrides in Leros are harmed by none of the crook-taloned birds. Aristotle says that the oxen among the Neuri have their horns on their shoulders, and Agatharchides that the pigs in Ethiopia have horns. Sostratus says that the blackbirds in Cyllene are all white. Alexander of Myndus says that the sheep in Pontus are fattened by the most bitter wormwood. The same author says that the goats born on Mimas do not drink for six months, but only look toward the sea and gape and receive the breezes from there. And I hear that Illyrian goats have a solid hoof, not a cloven one. And Theophrastus tells the most marvellous thing: that in the Babylonian land the fish often come up out of the river and then graze on the dry land.

28. The purple coot, besides being most jealous, possesses this peculiarity too. They say it is a lover of its own kind and cherishes the companionship of its mates. At any rate I have heard of a purple coot and a cock reared in a house, feeding on the same food, taking the same walks, and bathing together in the dust. And from this a wondrous friendship grew up between them. And once, when a festival came round, the master of both, having sacrificed the cock, feasted with his household; but the purple coot, having lost its mate and unable to bear the loneliness, destroyed itself by refusing food.

29. At Aegium in Achaea a goose loved a beautiful boy, Amphilochus by name, an Olenian by descent. Theophrastus tells this. The boy was being kept under guard at Aegium together with the Olenian exiles. So the goose brought him gifts. And in Chios, since Glauce the lyre-player was very beautiful—if men loved her, that is nothing strange; but a ram and a goose too, as I hear, loved her. The geese, in crossing Mount Taurus, fear

30. the eagles, and each of them, biting a stone so as not to scream, as though putting a bit in their own mouth, fly over in silence, and for the most part thus escape the eagles' notice. Now the goose, being most hot and fiery in nature, loves bathing and delights in swimming and most of all in the moistest foods—plants and lettuces and the rest, whatever produces coolness within them; and even if it should be wasting with hunger, it would not eat a laurel leaf, nor would it taste oleander, either willingly or unwillingly; for it knows that it will die if it eats any of these. But men through profligacy are plotted against both in food and in drink. Countless ones, at any rate, have swallowed something deadly while drinking, like Alexander, and while eating, like Claudius the Roman and Britannicus his son; and having lain down to sleep they did not rise again, by the use of poison, some having drunk it willingly, others by treachery. As for the fox-goose, its name has been woven from the peculiar and inborn traits of each animal. For it has the form of the goose, but in cunning it might most justly be matched against the fox. And it is smaller than a goose, but braver, and formidable at coming to close quarters. At any rate it defends itself against eagle and cat and the rest, whatever are its adversaries.

31. These too are peculiar to the snake. Its heart is placed at the throat, its gall in the intestines; it has its testicles by the tail; it lays its eggs long and soft; and it carries its venom in its teeth.

32. To the peacock, the aforesaid bird, these traits too are natural and peculiar, which are worth learning. At three years old it begins to conceive and brings forth, and then begins the many-coloured beauty of its feathers. It broods not on successive days, but leaving an interval of two days. The peacock too might lay wind-eggs, as other birds also do.

33. The duck, when it lays, lays on dry ground, but near a lake or marsh or some other watery and dewy place. And the duckling by a certain peculiar and secret instinct knows that it has no share either in flight aloft or in life on dry land. And from these it leaps into the water, and is a swimmer from birth, and needs no teaching, but dives and rises most cleverly, as though it had long been trained in this. But the eagle which they call the duck-killer leaps upon the swimming duck as if to seize it; and the duck, diving, makes itself disappear, then swimming under, peeps out elsewhere. And the eagle is there too, and again the duck dives, and again this happens, and again. And one of two things: either it is drowned in diving, or the eagle withdraws to another prey, while the duck, having safety, swims on the surface again.

34. The swan surpasses men in the greatest matters; for it knows when the end of life comes to it, and moreover, having received from nature this most beautiful gift, it bears its approach with good cheer; for it is convinced that there is nothing painful or grievous in death. But men dread what they do not know, and consider it the greatest of evils. So great is the cheerfulness that abounds in the swan, that even at the close of its life it sings and strikes up, as it were, a funeral song for itself. Such a one, prepared for death heroically and greatly, does Euripides hymn in Bellerophon. At any rate he has made him say to his own soul, "You were ever pious toward the gods, while you lived, and you helped strangers, and never wearied for your friends," and what follows upon this. So the swan too sings a kind of funeral music for itself, giving as provision for its journey either hymns of the gods or some praise of its own. And Socrates too bears witness to it, that it sings not grieving but rather rejoicing; for one who has anything grievous and painful against his soul would never have leisure for song and music. And the swan is brave not only toward death, but also toward battles. It does not begin unjust acts, like a temperate and well-bred man, but from one who has begun it neither withdraws nor yields. Now the other birds are at peace and at truce with one another, but the eagle has often rushed upon this one too, as Aristotle says, and yet never once overcame it, but was always beaten, the swan fighting not only with strength but defending itself also with justice.

35. The heron is clever at eating oysters, and swallows them closed, just as the pelicans do the cockles. And in what is called its crop the heron warms the oysters and keeps them; and they gape open from the heat, and it, perceiving this, vomits up the shells but keeps the flesh, and has its food, consuming whole, by the power of digestion, what has passed within.

36. There is a bird named the asterias, and it is tamed in Egypt, and understands human speech. If anyone, reproaching it, calls it a slave, it grows angry; and if anyone calls it lazy, it bristles and is indignant, as though mocked for baseness and rebuked for idleness.

37. If one holds Cyrenaic juice and takes hold of the torpedo-fish, there indeed he has escaped the effect that comes from it. But if you wish to pull up a sea-dragon with your right hand, it will not follow, but will fight with all its might; if you draw it up with your left, it yields and is caught.

38. I hear Charmis the Massaliote saying that the nightingale loves music, and indeed loves glory too. At any rate, in the solitudes, when it sings to itself, the bird sings a simple song without elaboration; but when it is caught and does not miss its hearers, it sings varied strains and winds out the song softly. And Homer too seems to me to hint at this when he says, "As when the daughter of Pandareus, the pale-green nightingale, sings beautifully when spring is newly come, sitting amid the thick leaves of the trees, and pouring forth, with frequent turns, her many-toned voice." Indeed some write "many-modulated voice" for that which is varied in its imitations, as "unsweet" for that which is not turned to imitation at all.

39. Democritus says that of all animals the lion alone is born with its eyes open, being already in a way enraged and eager from birth for some noble deed. And others have observed that even while sleeping it moves its tail, showing, as is likely, that it is not wholly at rest, nor has sleep encircled and overcome it, as it has the other animals. The Egyptians, having observed something of the sort about it, are said to boast, saying that the lion is stronger than sleep, being ever wakeful. For this reason too, I learn, they assign it to the sun; for the sun, being the most industrious of the gods, is either seen above the earth or goes its lower course without resting. And the Egyptians bring Homer as witness, who says "the unwearying sun." But besides its strength the lion is also intelligent. At any rate it plots against the cattle, going by night to the steadings. And Homer knew this too, saying, "As cattle which a lion has frightened, coming in the dead of night." And it strikes them all with terror by its might, but snatching one it devours it. And when it has filled itself to satiety, it wishes to store some up for another time, but shame holds it from remaining to keep guard, as though it feared hunger from lack of food. So gaping over it, it breathes its own breath upon it, and to this entrusts the guard, while it itself departs; and the other animals, coming and perceiving whose leavings the carcass is, do not dare to touch it, but depart in fear of seeming to rob and cut off anything of their own king's. Now if good hunting and success come to it, it forgets the first kill and, scorning it as stale, departs; but if not, it comes to it as to its own treasure. And when it is over-full, it empties itself by rest and fasting, or again, meeting a monkey and eating it, it empties its belly, purging it with that creature's flesh. The lion, then, was just, and such as to defend a man when someone first does him wrong. At any rate it stands against the one who attacks, lashing its tail and curling it against its sides, then rousing itself as though whetting itself with a goad. But the one who has shot at it and missed it punishes with an equal measure, frightening but harming not at all. When tamed from young, it is most gentle and pleasant to meet, and is fond of play, and endures everything gently to gratify its keeper. Hanno, at any rate, had a lion as a baggage-carrier, and a tame lion accompanied Berenice, differing nothing from her hairdressers. At any rate it brightened her face with its tongue, and smoothed her wrinkles, and shared her table, eating gently and orderly and in human fashion. And Onomarchus the tyrant of Catana, and the son of Cleomenes, had lions as messmates.

40. They say the leopard has obtained a certain wondrous fragrance, hidden from us, but it knows its own advantage, and indeed the other animals know it along with the leopard, and it is caught in the following way. The leopard, when it needs food, hides itself either in thick brush or in deep foliage, and is invisible to meet, and only breathes. So the fawns and gazelles and wild goats and such animals are drawn, as by some spell of the fragrance, and come near; and it leaps out and has its prey.

41. I learn that the ruminant animals have three stomachs, and I hear their names are the reticulum, the omasum, and the abomasum. And cuttlefish and squids feed by two proboscises—for it is no worse so to name them, taking the hint both from their use and from their shape. And when it is stormy and the surge is troubled, they lay hold of the rocks with these same projections, and cling as with anchors most firmly, and remain unshaken and unwashed by the waves; then if it becomes calm, they release and free themselves, and swim again, knowing a lesson not to be despised—flight from the storm and safety from danger.

42. If you wish to learn the names of bees, I would not grudge to tell what I have learned. Some are called leaders, and others sirens, and some water-carriers, and others moulders. Nicander says that the drones are the water-carriers. About the land of the Cappadocians they say that the bees make honey without combs, and tradition holds that this is thick like oil. In Trapezus on the Black Sea I learn that honey is made from the box-tree, and that this is heavy in smell, and makes the healthy go out of their minds, but brings epileptics back to health again. In Media I hear that honey drips from the trees, as Euripides says in his Cithaeron that sweet drops flow from the branches. And I have heard that in Thrace too honey comes from the plants. But in Myconos no bee is bred, and even one brought from outside dies.
43. Aristotle says that about the river Hypanis is bred the creature so called, the "one-day" creature, being born at nightfall and dying as the sun turns to its setting.

44. The cuttlefish has a venomous bite and teeth strongly concealed. The osmylus too and the octopus were biting creatures; and the octopus would bite more violently than the cuttlefish, but discharges less venom.

45. They say that the wild boar does not charge anyone before it has whetted its tusks; and Homer indeed bears witness to this, saying, "having whetted his white tusk in his curved jaws." And I hear that the boar fattens most when it does not bathe, but spends its time in the mire and wallows and drinks muddied water, and delights in quiet and a darker shelter, and in foods that are most flatulent and able to fill it up. And Homer seems to hint at these things. About their wallowing and delighting in the filthier sloughs . . . saying "swine that bed on the ground"; that they fatten on troubled water . . . he says "drinking black water, which nourishes in swine their thriving fat." That they delight in darkness he proves by these words: "beneath a hollow rock they slept, in the shelter from Boreas." And he hints at the flatulence of their food when he says they eat "the heart-cheering acorn." And Homer, knowing that the boar wastes away and ruins its flesh at the sight of the sow, has made the males sleep apart and the females apart. And in Salamis, if a sow falling upon green corn and a flourishing crop crops it, it is a law of the Salaminians to grind out its teeth. And this they say is what is meant by Homer's "corn-wasting sow." But others think otherwise, and say that the sow that has tasted green corn has weak teeth.

46. Nature gave to dogs a herb that counteracts wounds. And if worms trouble them, by eating what is called the green corn they expel them. They are said too, when they need to empty either belly, to eat a certain herb, and to vomit up the part of the food that floats on top, while the surplus is excreted below them, they say. From this the Egyptians too are said to have learned the practice of purging. And partridges and storks when wounded, and ringdoves, gnaw, as the story goes, marjoram, then putting it in their wounds they heal their bodies, and indeed need nothing at all of human medicine.

47. I shall need no older witness here, but I shall tell what I myself have known. A man, having caught a lizard, of those that are exceedingly green but rather full in body, and having pierced it with a sting made of bronze and so blinded the lizard, and having bored an earthenware pot of newly made ware with very fine holes, so as not to shut out the air yet not to give it a way of escape, and having poured in earth, and that very dewy, and put in the creature and a certain herb whose name he did not tell, and an iron ring set with a stone of jet, on which a lizard had been engraved—he covered the pot, sealing on it nine seals, of which he removed a seal each day for nine days. And having effaced the last of all he opens the vessel, and I myself saw the lizard looking, and it had most clear eyes, those that until then had been maimed. And we released it where it had been taken, but that ring the man who did these things said was good for the eyes.

48. To me, O men, it seems most shameful that there should be friendship among animals toward one another, not only among those of the same haunts nor among those of the same kind, but even among those that have no kinship with one another in the common species. At any rate sheep are friendly to goats, and there is friendship between dove and turtledove; and ringdoves and partridges are friendly toward one another; and we have long known that the halcyon and the cerylus long for each other; and the crow is friendly toward the heron, and the gull toward what is called the jackdaw, and the harpe toward the kite. But the crows and the owls wage everlasting and, so to speak, truceless war; and enemies are the kite and the raven, and the redstart against the turtledove, and the brenthus and the gull, and again the greenfinch against the turtledove, and the vultures and the eagles, and the swans and the snakes, and lions against the antelopes and bulls. Most hostile of all were the elephant and the snake, and the ichneumon against the asp, and the titmouse against the ass; for the ass brays, and the titmouse's eggs are broken, and the young fall out unformed; and the titmouse, avenging its young, leaps upon the sores of the asses, and eats them. And the fox hates the hawk, and the bull the raven, and the anthus the horse. And the educated man, who hears nothing in vain, must know that the dolphin too is at odds with the whale, the basses with the mullets, and the lampreys with the conger-eels, and others with others.

49. Bears, when those of the hunters who fall on their faces and draw in their breath are smelt by them, leave them as dead; and this animal seems to loathe a corpse. Mice too hate those that die in their own dwellings and runs, and indeed the swallow casts out a dead swallow. And to the ants too most wise Nature has given the care of carrying out their dead and cleansing their own runs, since this too is peculiar to the irrational creatures—to carry their dead, those of the same kind and nature, more quickly out of sight. And the tales of the Ethiopians, which have no taste of Greek flattery or boasting, say that an elephant, seeing a dead elephant, would not pass it by without scooping up earth with its trunk and casting it on, as though performing some secret holy rite on behalf of the common nature; for not to do this is sacrilege. And it is enough for it to throw on even a branch, and it departs, having not dishonoured the common end of all. And this tale too has come to us. When elephants die of wounds, whether shot in war or having suffered this in the hunt, they take up the herb that is at hand or the dust at their feet, and look up to heaven, and throw up one of the aforesaid things, and in their own voice they wail and lament, as though calling the gods to witness the unjust and lawless things they endure.

50. It is possible to recognize this too as peculiar to animals. We see the tame birds, those reared and kept under our feet, bold among horses and asses and oxen and camels; and if they are reared together with some gentle and tame elephant, they are not afraid, but go even between those very legs. And cocks even fly up onto their backs; so great is their boldness and fearlessness. But a weasel running past instils in them terror and strong fear. And of bellowing and braying they take no account, but at the mere squeak of the aforesaid weasel they shudder. Of geese and swans and ostriches they think little or nothing, but they dread a hawk, though it be very small. The cock by crowing frightens a lion and kills a basilisk; yet it cannot endure either cats or kites. The doves take heart at the cry of eagles and vultures, but no longer at that of hawks and sea-eagles. The flock and the kid and every foal go to the mother's teats the moment they are born, and indeed fill themselves by drawing at the udders; and the parent meddles not at all, but stands still. But all the cloven-footed animals offer their teats to their young lying on their backs—wolves and dogs and lionesses and leopards.

51. Nature has made the animals most various-voiced and, as one might say, of many sounds, just as she has made men also. The Scythian speaks one way and the Indian another, and the Ethiopian has a voice natural to him, and so do the Sacae; and Greek speech is one thing, and Roman another. So too the animals each send forth in its own way the sound and noise native to its tongue; for one roars, another lows, and there is the neighing of one and the braying of another, the bleating and the bleat of goats, and to some belongs howling, to others barking, and to another snarling; and screams and hisses and creakings and songs and melodies and warblings, and countless other gifts of nature, peculiar to the animals, some to some, some to others.

52. Throughout the land of Egypt asps make their dens near the Nile on both banks. And for the rest of the time they keep to their place and love it, as men love their own houses; but when the river is about to rise in the summer season, some thirty days beforehand the aforesaid asps move to the regions farther from the Nile, and creep into the overhanging banks, and indeed take their own offspring with them, having received this gift peculiar to themselves from nature: to know the yearly visitation of so great and so industrious a river, and to guard against the seizure and harm it brings. And the tortoises and the crabs and the crocodiles at the same season carry off their eggs to places untrodden and unreachable by the river; and from this those who chance upon the eggs of the aforesaid creatures already reckon how far the Nile, when it rises, will water their land for them.

53. The river-horses are nurslings of the Nile; and when the crops are at their height and the ears are golden, they do not begin at once to crop and eat them, but passing outside the cornfield they reckon how great a measure will fill them, and then, having calculated what is enough for them, they fall to and retreat step by step as they fill, taking the river's stream at their back. And this has been thought out by them, so that if any of the farmers should come upon them to defend their crops, they might most easily run down into the water, these river-horses watching their enemies face to face, and not from behind.

54. In the Mauretanian land the leopards do not attack the monkeys by main force or by such strength and might as they have. The reason is that the monkeys do not come to close quarters, but flee from them and run up onto the trees and sit there, guarding against their plots. But the leopard, then, was craftier than the monkey. See, at any rate, what kind of snares it contrives and weaves against them. Where a multitude of monkeys sit, there it comes and throws itself down under the tree, and lies on its back upon the ground, and swells out its belly, and lets its legs fall slack, and shuts its eyes, and presses in its breath, and lies there as if dead. The monkeys, seeing their bitterest enemy from above, think it is dead, and what they most wish, that they also believe. Yet they do not yet take heart, but make trial, and the trial is this: they send down one of themselves who seems most fearless, to test and examine the leopard's condition. He goes down not wholly without fear, but having run a little way then turns back, fear having checked him; and he comes down again, and having come near withdraws, and turns back once more, and examines the eyes, and tests whether it lets its breath go. And the leopard, keeping still most resolutely, instils in him little by little a sense of safety. And when he has approached and stayed by it unharmed, the monkeys aloft now take heart, and running down both from that tree and from the others that grow near, gathering in a crowd they go about it and dance round it. Then leaping upon it and mounting it they tumble and dance over it a mocking dance befitting monkeys, and after outraging it in various ways, they show forth the joy and pleasure they have, as over a dead thing. But it endures everything, and then, when it perceives that they are wearied with their dancing and their insolence, it springs up unexpectedly and leaping among them tears some with its claws and rends some with its teeth, and has a most abundant banquet and feast of its enemies. And nature bids the leopard endure patiently and stoutly and nobly, that it may prevail over the enemies who have outraged it, contending most enduringly and having no need to say, "Endure now, my heart." But the son of Laertes uncovered himself a little before the time, unable to bear the insolence of the serving-maids.

55. Among the Indians the elephants, when the Indians compel them to tear up some tree by the roots, do not first set upon it nor attempt the task before they have shaken it and considered whether it can be overturned or is wholly impossible.

56. The deer in Syria are bred on the greatest mountains—Amanus and Lebanon and Carmel; and when they wish to cross the sea, the herd comes to the shores and waits for the dying-down of the wind, and when they perceive it blowing gentle and quiet, then they take heart for the deep. They swim in a row, and hold to one another, those following resting their chins on the loins of those in front; and the last, resting itself on the one before, then brings up the rear. They set out for Cyprus out of longing for the grass there; for it is said to be deep and to provide good pasture. And the Cypriots say that they dwell in a land of good soil, and dare to match their own fields against the cornlands of the Egyptians. Other deer too display this same swimming. The deer of Epirus, at any rate, swim across to Corcyra, and these lie facing each other across the strait.

1. Men need a word to urge and persuade them to be brave, and to drive out cowardice and instil confidence—athletes for the running-track, soldiers for the fight with arms; but animals need no encouragement from outside. They sharpen their own courage for themselves, and rouse and stir themselves up. The boar, when about to go into battle, whets its tusks against the smooth rocks. And to this Homer too plainly bears witness about the creature. And indeed the lion stirs itself up by lashing itself with its tail, and does not allow itself to grow slack or to rest. This too the poet knew, and sings of it concerning the lion. And the elephants strike themselves with their trunks, kindling themselves to the contest when the time for it comes, and they need no one to sing to them and say, "This is no work for sitting or delay," nor do they wait for the verses of Tyrtaeus. And the bull that leads the herd, when conquered by another leader, withdraws himself to another place, and becomes his own trainer, and practices every exercise, rolling in the dust and rubbing his horns against the trees, and in every other way disciplining himself to the training of his strength; and indeed he abstains from love and is temperate, like Iccus of Tarentum, whom Plato the son of Ariston celebrates as having remained, throughout the whole time of his training, ignorant and untried of any intercourse at all. Now for Iccus, being a man and longing for the Olympic and Pythian crowns, conscious of fame and greedy for glory, it was nothing great to sleep with restraint and temperance; for the prizes were both in fact and in reputation glorious—the Olympic wild olive and the Isthmian pine and the Pythian laurel, and to be looked upon while alive and well spoken of when dead. And indeed I hear that the lyre-player Amoebeus, having married a most beautiful wife, abstained from her throughout the whole time during which he went to the theatres to compete. And Diogenes the tragic actor renounced the licentious bed altogether and entirely. And Clitomachus the pancratiast, if ever he saw dogs coupling, turned away, and if at a banquet he heard any licentious and amorous talk, he rose and departed. That men should do these things, either for the sake of gaining money or for the sake of sharing in fame and glory, is no great wonder; but for a bull that conquers a rival bull, what proclamations, O son of Ariston, do they make, and what prizes do they set apart?

2. The irrational animals love often to spare and refrain even from those that have become familiar to them. I hear, at any rate, this tale. A hunter had tamed a leopard from infancy and kept it, loving and cherishing it strongly, as one would a friend or a beloved. So he used to bring it a live kid and give it to it, devising at once both food and a kind of pleasure for the beast in tearing the kid apart, that it might not seem to eat carrion and a dead thing. And when a kid was brought, the leopard held itself in check, choosing to go without food because of fullness. And it did this on the second day too; for it still needed hunger as a remedy. But when the third day came on, it was hungry, and showed this as usual by its voice; yet it did not touch the kid that had been its friend for two days, but let it go and took another. But men have betrayed even their brothers and their parents and old friends, and many men often.

3. That the bear brings forth a shapeless lump of flesh and then articulates it with its tongue and as it were moulds it, has been said above. But what I have not yet said shall be said now, and in a very fitting place. It gives birth in winter, and having given birth keeps to its den, and fearing the frosts awaits the coming of spring, nor would it ever bring out its young before three months are fulfilled. And when it perceives itself to be pregnant, regarding this as a sickness, it seeks a den. Hence indeed the affliction has been called "denning" for the bear. Then it enters not walking but on its back, hiding its tracks from the hunters; for it drags itself along on its back. And having got inside it rests, and in a way wears down its condition, and does this for forty days. And Aristotle says that for twice seven days it remains motionless and still, but for the rest of the time only turns over. So for all forty days it remains without food and without nourishment, and it is enough for it to lick its right paw. And from the excessive wasting its intestine has folded together and closed up. Knowing this, when it comes out it eats what is called wild arum; and this, being flatulent, opens up its intestine for it and widens it, and renders it capable of receiving food. And when it is full again, it eats ants, and is emptied most easily. So have I described the natural emptyings and the timely fillings of bears, which need, O men, neither physicians nor mixtures.

4. When snakes are about to taste autumn fruit, they suck up the juice of what is called the sow-thistle; and this benefits them against being filled with any wind. And when they are about to lie in wait for someone, whether man or beast, they eat the death-bearing roots and the herbs of that kind. Nor was even Homer ignorant of their food. He says, at any rate, how a snake awaits a man, coiling about its den, having first filled itself with much venomous and evil food.

5. When deer have shed their horns, they enter and withdraw into the thickets, guarding against those that attack them, and with reason; for being bereft of their weapons they believe that they have been deprived of their strength for the time. They are said also to take care lest, while their antlers are new, the sunbeam falling upon them before they have set and gained what are called the knobs should rot the flesh.

6. Horses that go into war are suspicious both of leaping over trenches and of vaulting a pit and crossing palisades and stakes and such things. And one may hear Homer too speaking about such matters: how "Hector, going through the throng, besought his comrades, urging them to cross the trench. But his swift-footed horses dared it not, but loudly neighed, standing on the very brink; for the wide trench frightened them, neither easy to leap over near at hand nor to cross."

7. In Egypt, by the lake called the lake of Moeris, where Crocodilopolis stands, the tomb of a crow is shown, and the Egyptians tell this reason. The king of the Egyptians (this one was called Mares) had a crow as a pet, very tame, and whatever letters he wished conveyed somewhere quickly, this bird carried, and it was the swiftest of messengers, and on hearing it knew where it must direct its flight, and what place it must pass by, and where, on arriving, it must rest. In return for which, when it died, Mares honoured it with a monument and a tomb.

8. Each kind of animal possesses also a peculiar name for the care taken in rearing it. There is, at any rate, what one might call colt-breaking, and puppy-rearing, and elephant-tending, and lion-rearing, and bird-rearing, and the like.

9. These too were wise acts of the bear. If it is pursued together with its cubs, it pushes them on as far as it can; but when it perceives that one has given out, it carries one on its back and one in its mouth, and laying hold of a tree leaps up; and the one clings to its back with its claws, while the other is carried in its teeth as it runs

10. up. And when it meets a bull while hungry, it does not fight by main force and in a straight line, but it wrestles, and seizing the neck-tendon it bends it down and tightens its grip. And the bull is pressed and bellows, and at last gives out and lies down, and the bear fills itself. We have recognized that animals are good at learning in this respect too. In the time of the Ptolemies the Egyptians taught the dog-faced baboons letters and dancing and flute-playing and harp-playing. And a baboon would exact payment for these things, and putting what was given into a little pouch hung from it would carry it, like those clever at gathering alms. And that the Sybarites taught horses even to dance, has long been proclaimed. And the docility of elephants to learning and their readiness I have spoken of above. And dogs, too, are capable of serving in the house those who have trained them, and it is enough for a poor man to have a dog as a slave. There were, however, even of such men, some without slaves, like the Troglodytes among the Arabians, and the Nomads among the Libyans, and that part of the Ethiopians who live by the lakes, who have learned to eat nothing at all beyond their food from fish. And the animal remembers what it suffers, and needs for its memory no art—not Simonides, not Hippias, not Theodectes, nor any other of those proclaimed for this profession and this skill. Where the cow has been robbed of its calf, at any rate, coming there it laments its affliction with familiar lowing. And oxen about to go under the yoke, some smile, others retreat step by step. And a horse, when it hears the rattle of bits and the clink of the bridle, and beholds the breast-pieces and frontlets, snorts thereat, and prancing strikes its hooves and is filled with rapture; the shout of the grooms rouses it, and it pricks up its ears and dilates its nostrils, by the memory of the course and by the irresistible spell of habit.

11. The deer gives birth beside the roads, and seems to do this from wisdom; for it fears the wild beasts and their plots, but takes courage at men. And it believes itself weaker than the beasts, but does not doubt that it can escape men. But when grown fat it would no longer give birth beside the roads; for it knows that it is more sluggish at running. So it gives birth in the glens and the woods and the valleys.
12. The land-tortoise, having chewed marjoram, makes nothing of the viper. And if it lacks the marjoram, having eaten rue it is armed against its enemy. But if it fails of either, it is destroyed.

13. The deer, as I hear, is content with what it has, and does not desire more, but is more temperate as to the belly than men. About the Hellespont, at any rate, there is a hill, and deer pasture upon it, and one of their ears is slit, and they do not pass beyond the hill, nor do they desire strange pasture, nor long for other meadows out of need for more abundant grass; but what they have suffices them the whole year through. What, O men, do you say to this—you whom not all that "the stone threshold of the Archer encloses within" could ever fill up until death?

14. The hyena, as Aristotle says, has in its left hand a sleep-producing power, and by merely touching it induces torpor. At any rate it often comes into the steadings, and when it meets someone sleeping, approaching it lays its, so to speak, sleep-producing hand upon the nose, and the man is choked and oppressed. And it digs out the earth beneath his head so far that it bends him back into the hole and makes his throat lie bare and exposed; and then the hyena fastens on and throttles him and carries him off to its den. And it attacks dogs in that manner too. When

15. the circle of the moon is full, it takes the light behind it, and casts its own shadow upon the dogs, and at once silences them, and having bewitched them like the sorceresses it then leads them off in silence, and uses them thereafter for whatever it wishes. The love of a dolphin at Iasus for a beautiful boy, long since sung of, I do not think right to leave without mention from me, and for that reason it shall be told. The gymnasium of the Iasians lies by the sea, and the youths, after their runs and the wrestling-grounds, going down there, wash themselves according to an ancient custom. So as they were swimming, a dolphin fell into a most ardent love with one of them, the most outstanding in beauty. And at first, coming near, it frightened and astonished him, but then by familiarity it drew from the boy a strong friendship and goodwill toward itself. At any rate they began to play with each other, and now they would contest, swimming alongside and racing, now the boy mounting like a rider on a colt would be carried proudly, the lover swimming beneath. And to the Iasians and the strangers what happened was a thing to envy. For the dolphin carried its beloved far out to sea, as far as the boy could be borne in comfort; then it turned back and brought him near the shore, and parting from each other, the one went off to the deep, the other returned home. And the dolphin came to meet him at the time the gymnasium was dismissed, and the boy delighted in the expectation of his friend and in the play with him, and besides his natural beauty he was admired, since he seemed most lovely not only to men but also to the irrational creatures. Yet not long after, this counter-love too was overcome by envy. For it happened that the boy, having exercised more than usual, and being tired, threw himself upon the one that carried him, belly-down, and it chanced that the creature's spine along its back was upright, and it pricked the lovely boy's navel. Then some veins burst beneath, and there followed much flowing of blood, and there the boy died. Now the dolphin, perceiving this from the weight (for he lay upon it not light as usual, since he no longer lightened himself by his breathing), and seeing the sea purple with blood, understood what had been done, and did not dare to outlive its beloved. Using great force, then, like a surging skiff, it cast itself willingly upon the shores, and brought out the corpse along with it, and both lay there, the one dead, the other breathing its last. But Laius, for Chrysippus, O noble Euripides, did not do this, although he was the very first of the Greeks to begin the love of males, as you yourself say and as report teaches. And the Iasians, requiting that strong friendship of theirs, made a common tomb for the lovely youth and the loving dolphin, and set up a monument over it. There was a beautiful boy riding upon a dolphin. And they struck coins of silver and bronze, and stamped on them the figure of the fate of both, and handed it down to memory, honouring the work of so great a god, the people there. And I learn that in the city of Alexander, in the time of the second Ptolemy, a dolphin loved with a love much the same, and at Dicaearchia in Italy. And if Herodotus had known these things, he would, I think, have marvelled less at the tale of Arion of Methymna.

16. When a famine is about to visit, dogs and oxen and pigs and goats and snakes and other animals perceive it, and when a plague is to come they understand it first of all, and earthquake too. And they foreknow also the healthiness of the air and the abundance of crops. And though they have not received the reason that has power both to save and to destroy, yet of the aforesaid things they are not deceived.

17. In the land of the so-called Jews or Idumaeans the natives sang, in the time of King Herod, that a snake of the very greatest size fell in love with a beautiful girl, and visiting her would sleep with the aforesaid girl most amorously. So the girl did not take courage at her lover, though it crept up as gently and tamely as possible. She withdrew, then, and stayed away a month, expecting, of course, that the snake would forget her during the absence of his beloved. But for him the solitude intensified his passion, and he came daily and by night; yet not meeting her as he wished, like a lover unfortunate in his longing, he too grieved. But when the woman returned again, the snake came, and embracing her with the rest of its body, with its tail struck the legs of his beloved sparingly, as one slighted and indeed angry. So He who rules over Zeus himself and the other gods does not overlook even the irrational creatures, but shows by these and by others how he is disposed toward them.

18. Snakes, conscious that they have a thin and long gullet, yet being gluttonous and most omnivorous, as Aristotle says, rise upright and stand on the tip of their tail, and the food slips down for them and passes into the bulk of the body; and being footless they then creep most swiftly. There is one that even shoots itself like a javelin and rushes on, and it has its name from what it does; for it is called the dart-snake.

19. Of the birds that excel in song and music not one has escaped notice, but we know swallows and blackbirds and the race of cicadas, and the chattering jay and the buzzing locust and the murmuring grasshopper, and the

20. cricket that does not keep silent, and besides these the halcyons and the parrots; and of the water-creatures the green tree-frog does not keep silent. And of these some utter mournful and womanish cries, others shrill and piercing; and some, running from branch to branch, sing, as though changing house to house, while others sing in the meadows, as if keeping festival, and living, as one might say, a flowery and delicate life, they hymn, I would say, the coming of spring with their melodies. About swans, and whose servants among the gods they are, I have spoken above. The jay, then, is most imitative of other sounds too, and of the human voice most of all. But the bird called the anthus and the trumpet-bird and the wryneck and the raven are peculiar in such imitations. And the anthus imitates the neighing of a horse, the trumpet-bird the trumpet that shares its name, and the wryneck the slanting flute; and the raven likes to imitate the dropping of rain. Of scorpions the male is most harsh, but the female seems gentler. And I hear that there is a white one, and again a tawny one, and another smoky, and a black one besides; and I have learned of a green and a pot-bellied one, and another crab-like; but the most harsh they sing of as flame-coloured. And I have received by report that there are winged ones too, and some with double stings; and somewhere one was seen with seven joints. The scorpion brings forth not eggs but living young. And it must be known that some say the offspring of these creatures comes not from intercourse with one another, but that scorpions breed amid excessive heat. And what each of them does by smearing its sting, and in what way it kills, you will learn elsewhere.

21. Among the Indians, as I hear, the elephant and the snake are bitterest enemies. So the elephants, tearing off the branches of the trees, feed on them. And the snakes, knowing this, creep up onto them, and wind the lower half of their bodies, the tail part, around the foliage of the trees, while the half that goes toward the head they let down, hanging like a rope. And when the elephant comes to pluck the boughs, the snake leaps at its eyes and gouges them out, then creeping around its neck, drawing with its tail part and tightening with the other, throttles the beast with an unaccustomed and strange noose.

22. Bitterest foes to the lion are fire and the cock, the hyena to the leopard, and the gecko to the scorpion; at any rate, numbness seizes the scorpion when the aforesaid creature is brought near it. The elephant dreads the snake; every beast of burden fears the shrew-mouse; the lobster the octopus. And indeed dogs, when pushed off the roofs, you could not throw down; for they dread the greatness of the danger.

23. What devices, then, nature seems to have given to scorpions too, peculiar to them. The Libyans, suspecting their numbers and their contrivances, devise countless devices against them: wearing hollow boots, and sleeping high up and aloft, and pulling the bed-cords away from the walls, and setting the feet of their beds in jars full of water, and they think they shall thereafter sleep in much safety and peace. But see what the scorpions contrive. If a scorpion can find anywhere to hang itself from the ceiling, it clings there with its claws most firmly and lets down its sting. So the second comes down from the roof, and creeps down by way of the first, and clings to that one's sting with its own claws, and leaves its own sting hanging; and the third clings from there, and the fourth from the third, and the fifth in a row, and those after them creeping down by way of the first. Then the last one strikes the sleeper and creeps up by way of those above, and the one after it, and the third from below, and the rest, until they have all loosed themselves from one another as though undoing a chain.

24. The fox is a crafty thing. At any rate it plots against the land-hedgehogs in this way. It cannot overcome them while they are upright. The reason is that the spines fend it off. But quietly and sparingly using its mouth it turns them over and lays them on their backs, and ripping them open eats easily those that were until then formidable. And the bustards in Pontus they hunt thus. Turning themselves about and ducking their heads to the ground, the foxes raise their tails like a bird's neck; and the bustards, deceived, approach as toward a bird of their own kind, and then, coming near, are caught most easily by the fox, which turns about and attacks by main force. And the little fish it hunts most cleverly. It comes along the bank of the river and lets down its tail into the water; and the fish swimming up are caught and entangled in the thickness of the hairs. And the foxes, perceiving this, withdraw from the water, and coming to the dry places shake their tails, and the little fish fall out, and they have a most delicate dinner. And the Thracians make this hunting a sure index of the firmness of the freezing of the rivers. And if the fox runs across the ice, it not yielding nor giving way under her steps, they take courage and follow. And she makes trial of the safe passage in this way. She lays her ear to the ice; and if she perceives

25. that the stream does not echo beneath nor make any quiet noise down in the depth, then she takes courage in the ice as standing firm, and runs across unflinching; but if not, she would not set foot on it. The poets reverence the daughter of Iphis, and the theatres are filled by them hymning that heroine, since she surpassed all others in temperance, having preferred her own husband to life; but the animals have left no excess of affection unmatched. For the dog of Erigone died upon its mistress, and the dog of Silanion likewise upon its master, and neither by force nor by coaxing departed from the tomb. And for Darius, the last king of the Persians, when in the battle against Alexander he had been struck down by Bessus and lay there, all having abandoned the corpse, the dog reared by him alone stayed faithful, not betraying the one who could no longer feed it, as though it were still alive. Something of the sort Xenophon the son of Gryllus plainly tells, with youthful spirit, about the friends of the younger Cyrus: that his messmates alone stayed by him and perished with him, and that the eunuch who was his sceptre-bearer in honour, Artapates by name, killed himself upon the corpse, scorning a life that would be bereft of Cyrus for him. And to King Lysimachus too a dog willingly shared in the common end, though it could have been saved.

26. The monkey is by some called a mountain-climber, by others, as I hear, a wood-runner, and it is born in the trees and has hair; it is called by some also the flea. Its belly is cut in gently, so to say, as though severed with a thread. It gives most dangerous bites, and trembling follows for the one bitten, and a strong pain comes upon the heart, and the urine is blocked, and the other passage too becomes impassable. And the river-crab, when eaten, seems to be the antidote to the aforesaid.

27. Of cats the male is most lustful, but the female loves her young, and shuns intercourse with the male; for he discharges his seed most hot and resembling fire, and burns the female's parts. Knowing this, then, the male makes away with the offspring they have in common, and she, out of longing for other young, offers herself to him when he is eager to come together. And they say that cats hate and loathe everything that is foul-smelling. For this reason they discharge their own excrement only after digging a hole, in order to make it disappear by throwing earth upon it.

28. They say that the most licentious of fish is the octopus, and that it indulges in lust to such a degree that all the strength of its body flows out and is rendered weak, and it is least able to swim and unable to seek food, and for this reason it feeds others. The little fish, at any rate, and what are called the hermit-crabs and the crabs come upon it and devour it. And they say this is the reason why the octopus cannot live longer than a year's time. And the female octopus too is easily consumed, since it gives birth often.

29. Phylarchus relates that a boy who strongly loved birds received an eaglet as a gift and reared it with varied food and bestowed every care upon it; for he did not rear the bird as a plaything for amusement, but like a beloved or a younger brother—so providently did the boy treat the eagle. And as time went on it kindled them to a strong friendship for each other. It happened that the boy fell ill in body. And the eagle stayed and nursed its rearer, and while he slept kept quiet, and while he was awake stood by him, and while he fasted would not take food. But when

30. the boy died, the eagle followed even to the tomb; and when the body was being burned, it threw itself into the pyre. The fish called the hake has all its other internal organs not very different from those of others, but it is solitary and cannot endure to live with others. And of fish this one alone has its heart in its belly and stones in its brain, which resemble millstones in shape. And at the rising of Sirius it alone goes into its hole, while the others are accustomed to go into theirs in the most frosty seasons.

31. Those who hunt crabs have contrived music as a bait against them. With a little pipe (this is the name of an instrument) they catch them. For some of the crabs have sunk into their holes, and others begin to come at the sound of the tune. And the crabs, hearing it, are persuaded as though by some spell to come forth from their chamber, then, drawn by the pleasure, they advance even outside the sea, and the pipers retreat step by step. And the crabs follow and are caught upon the land.

32. Those who dwell by the lake Mareia hunt the shad there with the clearest of songs and a clapping of shells keeping time with the tune; and the fish, as though dancing to the music, leap up, and fall into the nets, which are spread out for them, and the Egyptians take a fine catch of fish with dancing and play.

33. I learn that the Egyptians by a certain native magic bring down the birds from the sky; and the snakes, having bewitched them from their holes with certain incantations, they then lead out most easily.

34. The beaver is an amphibious animal, and by day it lives sunk in the rivers, but by night it roams on the land, feeding on whatever it meets. So it knows the reason why the hunters come against it with all eagerness and onset, and stooping and biting it cuts off its own testicles and throws them to them, like a prudent man who, falling among robbers, lays down all that he is carrying for the sake of his own safety, exchanging these, of course, as a ransom. And if it has previously cut them off and been saved, and is then pursued again, it raises itself up and shows that it has not the object of their zeal, and so frees the hunters from further toil; for they have less concern for its flesh. And often, even while still entire, having run off as far as possible, then drawing up the part that is sought for, most cleverly and craftily they deceive, as though they had not what they kept hidden.
35. The buprestis is a creature which, if an ox swallows it, the ox is inflamed and bursting dies not long after.
36. Caterpillars feed on the vegetables, and indeed destroy them. But these are killed if a woman undergoing her monthly purgation passes through the midst of the vegetables.

37. Bitterest foes to oxen would be the gadfly and the horsefly. And the gadfly is like the largest flies, and has a firm and large sting, and gives off a buzzing and harsh sound; the horsefly resembles the dog-fly, but buzzes more than the gadfly, though it has a smaller sting.

38. Of those bitten by an asp not one is recorded to have escaped the evil. Hence indeed I hear that the kings of the Egyptians wore embroidered asps upon their diadems, hinting at the invincibility of their rule by the form of the aforesaid creature. There are asps even five cubits long. And most are black or ash-coloured, but you might see a tawny asp too. Those bitten by an asp do not live beyond the fourth hour, but choking and convulsion and hiccupping pursue them, they say. And I hear that the ichneumon destroys the eggs of the asp, as though removing for its own young the future adversaries. And a certain tale says that the Libyan asp even makes men blind by its blast.

39. Must one not then marvel at nature in this respect too, among others? The fathers of the males destroy most of the fawns, lest they multiply and then mount their mothers; for this seems a defilement even among the irrational creatures, and a polluted deed, no doubt. But to Cyrus and Parysatis, O Persians, these things seemed both noble and just; and Cyrus loved his mother wickedly, and was loved by his mother with a like love. And these things, indeed, were done by them—but men, desiring everything and sparing nothing.

40. An island in Pontus named after Heracles is held in honour. So all the mice there revere the god, and whatever is dedicated to him they believe to be dedicated as pleasing to the god, and they would not touch it. So a vine flourishes for the god, and is honoured as an offering to him alone, and the ministers of the deity keep the clusters for the sacrifices. So when the grapes come to ripeness, the mice leave the island, lest by remaining they should at least unwillingly touch what it is better not to handle; then when the season is past, they return to their own haunts. And these are good acts of the Pontic mice; but as for Diagoras and Herostratus and the rest of the catalogue of those hateful to the gods, how would they have spared the clusters or other offerings, men who had chosen somehow to plunder even the names and works of the gods?

41. This is an Egyptian custom. When it rains in Egypt (it rains in fine drops), mice are at once bred. So wandering through the fields these harm the crops, cutting under and shearing off the ears, and indeed by ravaging the heaps of sheaves they grieve the Egyptians. And for this reason they trap them with snares and check them with walls and fend them off with trenches and burn fire in these. But the mice do not even approach the snares from the start, but let them stand idle; and the walls, though smoothed with plaster, they climb, being most apt at leaping, and then leap over the trenches. So when the Egyptians, having given up their devices and contrivances as useless, abandon them and turn instead to prayer and supplications to the gods, then indeed the mice dread the wrath from the gods, and withdraw to some mountain, keeping the order of a square. The youngest go first, and the largest bring up the rear, and turning back they then force the laggards to follow them. And if the youngest, growing weary, hold back, the whole following halts, as is wont to happen in a military force. And when the movement of the foremost begins, then the rest follow too. And those who dwell in Pontus say that the mice do the same there too. And it is believed that from every house which is about to fall they all move out as fast as their feet can carry them. And this too is a peculiarity of mice. When they hear a weasel squeaking or a viper hissing, from the one mouse-hole they move their young, one here, one there.

42. There is an Italian tale, recalling a deed that flourished along with the city of the Sybarites, and which has come to me, that it is no worse to tell. A boy barely past childhood, a goatherd by occupation, Crathis by name, falling into amorous desire, mingled with the most beautiful to look upon of the she-goats, and took pleasure in the union, and whenever he needed love he went to her, and had her as his beloved. And indeed such gifts as he could obtain, such did the goatherd lover bring to the aforesaid beloved, and sometimes he offered her the loveliest sprays of clover, and often gave her smilax and mastich to browse, making his own mouth fragrant for her, should he need to kiss her. And he prepared too a bed for her to sleep in, as for a bride, most delicate and soft. But the leader of the herd, the he-goat, did not behold these things heedlessly, but jealousy stirred him. And he hid his anger for a time, but once, while the boy was sitting and even sleeping, he lay in wait for him; and the boy had buried his face in his lap. So with all his force the he-goat dashed his head against him, and crushed his skull. The deed, then, spread among the natives, and they raised over the boy a tomb not without renown, and from him named the river Crathis. And from the union with the goat a child was born, with the legs of a goat and the face of a man. This one too, the story says, was deified, and the same was held to be a god of the woodland and the glen. So the he-goat teaches that the animals partake of jealousy too.

43. The historians sing of Egyptian galleries, and they too, and the tribe of poets, sing of certain Cretan labyrinths; but the varied paths and windings and circuits of ants in their burrowing they do not yet know. By wisdom they fashion this underground household most winding, rendering the passage difficult or even wholly impassable for the beasts that plot against them. And the earth they dig out, this they throw up around the mouth and make, as it were, walls and bulwarks, so that the water rushing down from heaven may not then easily flood and destroy them all or at least most of them. And they wall off with certain partition-walls the chambers that divide the burrows from one another, and that most skillfully, and there would be three areas, as in a stately house.
