At any rate, when they come near the trench which those hunting them are accustomed to dig, whether by some natural understanding or, by Zeus, by a secret prophetic sense, they are checked from advancing farther, and turning themselves about they then stand their ground, as in war, most stoutly, and try to overturn the hunters and, having forced their way through them, to procure their safety by flight, becoming the stronger over their adversaries. There then arises, at that moment, a fierce battle, and slaughter on both sides. The manner of this battle is as follows. The men hurl strong spears, aiming at them, while the elephants seize whoever comes within reach, and dashing him to the ground and trampling him and wounding him with their tusks, they bring upon him a most pitiable and most painful end. The beasts advance, in their fury, spreading out their ears like sails, after the manner of the great ostriches, which spread their wings and either flee or advance; and the elephants, curving up their trunks and folding them under their tusks, like the ram of a ship borne along with a great surge, fall upon them with most violent rush and overturn many, trumpeting a piercing and shrill note like a trumpet. And as those caught are trampled and crushed by the knees, a great crash of bones being shattered is heard even from afar, and as their eyes are squeezed out of their faces and their noses crushed and their foreheads broken, the distinctness of their appearance is lost, and they often become unrecognizable even to their nearest kin. But others are unexpectedly saved in this way. The hunter is caught, but the beast in its rush overpasses him, and drives its knees into the ground, and fixes its tusks fast into a bush or a root or some such thing, and is held, and only with difficulty pulls them out and frees them; and in the meantime the huntsman slips out and gets away. So in such a battle the elephants often prevail, but often too are defeated, when the men bring against them terrors devised by stratagem and varied fears. For trumpets sound, and they make a din and a clatter, striking their spears against their shields, and some fire they kindle upon the ground, and some they raise aloft, and other fire they sling, hurling blazing brands and shaking violently against the faces of the beasts long torches of fire at its height. And the beasts, fearing these and confounded, are pushed back, and sometimes are even forced to fall into the trench which till then they had guarded against.

11. Hegemon, in his Dardanian verses, says of Aleuas the Thessalian many things, and among them that a serpent fell in love with him. That this Aleuas had golden hair is a marvel he tells in the saying; for me let it be fair. And he says that Aleuas herded cattle on Mount Ossa, as Anchises did on Ida, and pastured the cows by the spring called Haemonia. The spring too would be Thessalian. A serpent of the greatest size, then, fell in love with Aleuas, and crept up to him, and kissed his hair, and licking the face of its beloved with its tongue cleaned it, and brought him many gifts of its hunting. And if a ram was overcome by Glauce the lyre-player, and a dolphin at Iasus by a youth, what prevents a serpent too from falling in love with a beautiful herdsman, since it has become, with its keen sight, a good judge of conspicuous beauty? It was, then, peculiar to animals to fall in love not only with one of their own kind and nature, but even with what was least akin to them, provided it was beautiful.

12. The pareias, or parouas—for so Apollodorus would have it—is reddish in colour, fair to look upon in the eye, broad of mouth, not dangerous to bite, but gentle. For this reason they dedicated it as sacred to the most humane of the gods, and those who first traced these things out gave it the name of attendant of Asclepius.

13. In Ethiopia the scorpions called Sibritae—for so the natives are likely to call them—I hear feed on lizards and asps and millipedes and water-beetles and every creeping thing, and whoever treads upon their droppings, I have learned, breaks out in sores. About Corcyra there are born the so-called hydrae, which turn upon their pursuers and, breathing out a strange breath, then check them in their rush and turn them back. The typhlops, which they also call typhline and besides "the deaf one," has a head much like a lamprey's, so one account says, but exceedingly small eyes. And one of its two names it has from this; the other, "deaf one," because it is dull of hearing. It has a strong hide, very slow to be cut through. The acontias they say is an amphibious snake, and spends much of its time on dry land, and lies in wait for every creature. The cunning of its plot is of this kind. It hides somewhere unseen along the highways, and often, having crept up onto a tree, then coiling itself up and hiding its head in the coil, it eyes quietly the passers-by; then it launches itself at whatever passes, whether it be an irrational animal or a man. It is a leaping creature, able to spring across even twenty cubits, if need be; and as it leaps it at once fastens on.
14. Wolves, if they happen upon an ox that has fallen into a deep marsh, harass it from outside and frighten it,

15. not allowing it to swim across and set foot on the land, but in time they compel it, writhing and twisting, to be choked to death. Then one of them, the most accomplished, leaping into the water and bending toward it, takes hold of the ox's tail and drags it outward; and another, taking hold of that one, drags him; and the third the second, and the fourth this one, and the thing described is done down to the last, who stands outside the water. And in this manner, having drawn out the ox, they make a meal of it. And if they catch in ambush a calf that has strayed, they leap upon it, and taking hold of its muzzle they drag it; and it pulls against them, and there is much contest over it, the wolves trying to force it, and the calf making it a struggle not to yield. But when they see it straining hard against them in this way, they let go; and the calf, by the force of its own backward pull, is overturned, and the wolves fall upon it and tear open its belly and eat it. When elephants are unable to cross a trench, one of them, the largest, throws himself into it, and stands across it, and bridges the gap, and walking over him the rest go to the far side and escape—first, however, rescuing him too. And the manner of his rescue is this. One from above stretches out his foot, and offers that one his trunk to wind around; and the others throw in brushwood and logs as quickly as possible, on which, climbing and having his foot held very firmly and carefully, he is pulled up most easily. There is in India a tract of land, and it is called Phalacra, the Bald Place. The cause of the name is that whoever tastes of the grass that grows there loses both his hair and his horns. The elephants, therefore, of their own will do not approach this tract, but turn away when they come near it, fleeing all that is harmful, like prudent men—the elephants.

16. The sponge is steered by a small creature, not like a crab in form, but rather like a spider. For the sponge is no soulless thing, nor without a share of blood—it is an offspring of the sea, and clings to the rocks, just as other things do, but has a certain motion of its own, and needs, as one might say, something to remind it that it is alive. For when it lies still, through a kind of natural porousness, and is quiet, then, when something falls into its openings, it is pricked by the spider-like creature, and seizes what has fallen in, and gets its food. And when a man approaches to cut it off, being stung by its companion creature it bristles and contracts itself, and becomes the cause of much labour and toil, by Zeus, to the gatherer.

17. We have spoken, then, of elephants separately, and shall speak of them more. Just as they are masters of their way of life, so, in what manner they have a share of self-control, it is most fitting to say. For they do not come to union with the female as though in wantonness or lust, but like those who need a continuation of their race and beget offspring, that the line of descent from one another may not fail them, but that they may leave seed behind. Once, at any rate, in their lifetime they call to mind love, when the female too submits; then, each having filled his mate, he thereafter knows her no more. And they do not couple openly, nor in the sight of the others, but having withdrawn; and they set before themselves either dense trees or some thick wood or a hollow and deep place that affords them abundant concealment. That they are just, I said above, and their courage too has already been told; and now this present matter has demonstrated their self-control. But their hatred of wickedness too, whoever has leisure to learn it, let him incline his ears and hear. A tame elephant had a keeper, and he had a wife older than himself, but rich. So, being in love with another woman, and eager that his wife's property should become that other's, this hot-headed man strangled her and buried her near the elephant's stall, and married the other. There, then, the elephant, taking hold with its trunk of the newly arrived woman, led her near the dead one, and digging her up with its tusks and laying the body bare, showed by the very deeds those things which it could not say, teaching the woman the character of the man who had married her—the elephant that hated wickedness.

18. Anchovies—some call them encrasicholi, but I have heard a third name for them too, for there are those who call them "wolf-mouths." They are little fishes, prolific by nature, and very white to look at. The fishes that go in shoals eat them most of all. So, when frightened, they run together, and each holding to its neighbour, by that close packing it escapes being easily plotted against. So great, indeed, does their union become when they have run together, that not even passing ferry-boats split them; and indeed, if anyone should wish to pass an oar or a pole through them, they are not torn apart, but hold to one another as if woven together. And if you put down your hand, you may, as from a heap of grain or beans, draw them out by force, so that they are often even torn apart, and half of the little fishes are taken while the rest are left. For you will hold the tail-part, while the head remains with the others; or you will carry a head home, while the rest remains in the sea. Their dense and continuous shoal is called a "haul," and one haul has often filled fifty fishing-boats, as the seafarers say.

19. The sow recognizes the voice of the swineherd, and obeys when he calls, even if it has strayed; and the proof of this is near at hand. Off the Tyrrhenian coast some malefactors brought to land a pirate ship, and coming up they happened upon a steading, and the steading was a swineherds', and it had many sows. These, then, they seized and threw into the ship, and casting off the cables they set about their voyage. The swineherds, while the pirates were present, kept quiet; but when the men had got out to sea, as far as the carry of a shout, then the swineherds called the sows back to themselves with their accustomed cry. And the sows, when they heard, crowding themselves to one side of the ship, overturned it. And the malefactors were at once destroyed, while the sows swam back to their own masters.

20. They say that the stork too is jealous. At Crannon in Thessaly a man who had married a beautiful woman named Alcinoe, leaving her at home, set out on a journey abroad. Now Alcinoe consorted with one of the servants. The household stork, perceiving this, did not endure it, but avenged his master. Leaping upon her, it blinded the woman's eyes. Earlier I made mention of the jealousy of a purple coot, then of such a dog; and now of a stork doing the same as they against a marriage gone sick.

21. Sheep change their colours through the change in their drink, according to the peculiar nature of the rivers; and the season of the year at which this befalls them is the time of their mating. So they turn from white to black, and again change the colour the other way. This is wont somehow to happen about the river in Antandria and the one in Thrace, whose name the Thracians who dwell beside it will tell. But the Scamander at Troy, since it makes the ewes that drink of it yellow, has had set upon it, alongside its original name Scamander, another name, Xanthus, from the acquired colour of the sheep.

22. Animals are good at remembering a kindness in this respect too. At Tarentum there was a woman in other respects worthy of esteem, and chaste, moreover, toward her husband; Heracleïs was her name. While her husband lived she tended him most carefully; but when he ended his life, the woman aforesaid came to hate the haunts of the city and the house in which she had seen her husband dead, and as her grief moved her she moved her dwelling to the tombs, and remained, enduring hardship, by the grave of her one-time husband, showing herself faithful to him who was beneath the earth. And once it was summertime, and as young storks were making their first trial of their own flight, one, the youngest, still not in command of his wings, slipped down and broke one of his two legs. So Heracleïs, seeing the fall and learning of the injury to the foot, pitied the nestling, and taking it up with much care she bound up the hurt, and treated it with fomentations and plasters, and brought it food and offered it drink, and in due time, when it had grown strong and grown its swift wings, she let it go free. And it, knowing by some natural and wonderful sense that it owed a ransom for its life, went away. Then, when a year had passed, she happened to be warming herself in the sun as spring was dawning, and the stork that had been healed by her, seeing its benefactress, slackened the rush of its wings, and bringing itself down in a lower flight came near, and gaping disgorged a stone into the lap of Heracleïs, and spreading its wings settled itself upon the roof. At first, as was natural, she wondered, and being disturbed was at a loss, unable to make out what had happened; but she put the stone away somewhere within, and then, waking by night, she sees it giving off a kind of light and gleam, and the house was lit up as though a torch had been brought in—so great was the radiance that rose and was born from the stone. And taking up the stork and stroking it she observed the scar from the wound, and recognized that this was the very one that had met with her pity and her care.

23. A lobster, if you should take it and carry it very far away, leaving a mark from where you caught it, you will find again in the same place from which it was taken. I mean, if you carry it along the seaside and then set it down somewhere near, so that it can creep into the sea.

24. Agreus is its name, a winged creature by nature, of the clan of blackbirds, black in colour, musical in voice. It is called Agreus, "the hunter," and rightly; for by its song it catches the tender young of other birds as they fly to it, charmed by its fine music. Knowing, then, the advantage that is bred in it, it seems to use the gift of Nature for pleasure and for food at once; for in hearing itself it is gladdened, and in hunting what comes to it it fills itself. If anyone should catch this bird and shut it up in a little cage, his pains profit him nothing; for he has a voiceless bird, which avenges itself upon its captor for its slavery by silence.

25. Above I told of the kindness that the trochilus-birds render to the crocodiles, which Herodotus too mentions in his Egyptian account; but what I did not say, though I knew it, shall now be told, that another too may learn. The trochilus is one of the marsh birds, and roams along the banks of rivers and feeds, picking up whatever it chances upon; and the crocodile too feeds it in the way I have said. And the bird repays it by looking out for it when it sleeps and keeping watch over it; for when it lies and slumbers the ichneumon plots against it, and fastening on its throat has often choked it; but the trochilus cries out and strikes it on the nose and rouses it and sets it on against its enemy. Whether, then, one ought to praise the bird for being so thoughtful of a beast omnivorous and gluttonous, we shall consider; but I have told what is peculiar to these creatures.

26. The stingray—I do not now mean the one of the air, but the one in the sea—when it wishes, swims, and again, rising up, flies. It has a sting, of which I made mention above too, that brings death. Now that it stings both irrational animals and men and destroys them at once is not yet a marvel; but what is worthy of astonishment shall be told. If you bring the sting to the largest tree, very flourishing and well-grown and exceedingly luxuriant in its foliage, and prick the tree, not long after it casts off its leaves; and as these fall to the ground the whole trunk withers, and looks as if it had been struck by the sun.

27. The elephant is born coming out head first, and the size of the newborn is that of the largest piglet. To one mother several little elephants follow, they say. And if you should wish to touch the calves when they are newly born, the mothers are not at all vexed but allow it; for they understand that no one touches them to harm or to punish them, but that all do so caressing and fondling them. For who would injure so small a creature? But when, being hunted, they fall into the trench, and see that escape is now impossible for them, they take forgetfulness of their former spirit that went with freedom, and when men hold out food they readily accept it, and when they offer water they drink, and when men pour wine into their trunks they do not refuse the pledge of friendship.

28. The fish called ellops men hold to have been called by the poet "the sacred fish." A certain account says that it is rare, and is caught in the sea off Pamphylia, though there too only scantily. And if it is caught, the fishermen adorn themselves with garlands over their good fortune, and they garland the boats too, and put in to shore with clapping and pipes, bearing witness to their catch. But others hold not this, but the anthias, to be sacred. The reason is that, wherever this fish appears in the sea, that place must surely be free of beasts, and there is a truce for the fishes against everything that hunts in the water, and the fishes themselves, taking courage, spawn. But to scrutinize the secrets of Nature is not for me, and reasonably so, since a lion fears even a cock, and the basilisk fears the same, and the elephant a pig; and as for the causes, those who have much leisure, in seeking them, will despise the time spent, yet will not come at last to the end of their search.

1. The lion, when it is already advanced in age and has grown heavy with years, is least able to hunt, and gladly rests in cavernous or bushy haunts, and does not venture even against the weakest of beasts, mistrusting its years and mindful of its body's weakness. But those born from it, taking courage in the prime of their age and in their inborn strength, go out to the hunt, and take along the one now grown old, urging him on; then, leaving him behind at the middle of the road they must travel, they set about the hunt themselves, and when they have got as much as will suffice both for themselves and for him who begot them, with a noble and piercing roar the young call the aged one, the sons their father, as hosts call a guest to the feast. And he comes quietly and at a walk, and as it were creeping, and embracing his young, and fawning a little with his tongue, as though praising them for their good hunting, he sets to the meal, and feasts with his sons. And Solon does not command these things to the lions, but Nature teaches them, Nature that cares nothing for human laws; and she becomes an unalterable law.

2. The eagle, the king of birds, the other birds fear and cower before when it appears—not only while it survives and lives, but even if one should mix its feathers with those of other birds, the eagle's remain whole and untouched, while the others rot away, not enduring the company of those.

3. Mice are in any case a prolific creature, and bring forth many at a single birth; but if they happen to taste salt as well, then indeed they bear a great many, far more than usual. The crocodiles, when they have laid their eggs, test the genuine from the spurious in the following way. If, the moment it is hatched out, the young one seizes something, it counts thereafter as belonging to the race, and is loved by its parents, and is believed to be one of the crocodiles and is reckoned among them; but if it is sluggish and lazy and does not catch from somewhere either a fly or a gnat or an earthworm or a young lizard, the father tears it to pieces as worthless and counterfeit and in no way belonging to him. And it seems that, like these beasts, the eagles too test their genuine offspring by the ray of the sun, and love their young by judgment and not by feeling.

4. I hear that the teeth of the asp—which one might rightly call venom-bearing—have, as it were, very thin coverings wrapped about them, like membranes, by which they are enwrapped. So when the asp fixes its mouth upon someone, they say the little membranes part, and the venom is poured out, and again those membranes run together and unite. And the sting of the scorpion, they say, has a kind of hollow fold, not

5. very visible because of its extreme thinness. And they say that the poison both exists and is engendered there, and at the same moment as the blow goes forward through the sting and flows out. And the opening through which it issues you will not see either, observable as it is. But if a man spits saliva upon it, the sting is blunted and numbed and becomes powerless to strike. The bitch, even if she bears many puppies, yet the first that comes from the mother and is eldest of the litter convicts the father; for it is born most like to him in every way, while the rest are as it may chance. Nature seems to philosophize in this, preferring the sower to the receiver.

6. Of the shell-backed and shell-skinned creatures this too is peculiar. They are wont to become somewhat emptier and lighter as the moon wanes. And among the shell-backed, the purple-fish and whelks and sea-snails and their kindred prove what I say; among the others, the rock-crabs and crayfish and lobsters and crabs and whatever is akin to these. It is said too that the young of beasts of burden born while the moon wanes are feebler than the others and weaker; and indeed those skilled in these matters advise that what is born in this part of the month should not be reared, for it is of no worth. At the new moon, as I learn, animals either utter something with their natural voice or fall down; but the lion alone, as Aristotle says, does neither of these.

7. Aristotle says that the bass is keenest in hearing, and likewise the chromis and the saupe and the grey mullet. And I learn that the bass knows well that there is a little stone in its head. And in winter this becomes very cold, and pains it severely. For this reason, in that season of the year, it warms itself, and contrives this remedy against the chill from the stone, a most effective one. And the chromis does the same, I have learned, and the sea-bream and the maigre; for these too have a similar stone. There were parasites, it seems, even among the kinds of fish. The one called the "louse," at any rate, nibbles at the dolphin's catch; and the dolphin is pleased with it and willingly shares. For this reason it is very fat, as though stuffed full from a rich and abundant banquet. And Menander's Theron prides himself that he led men by the nose and made them his own manger; while Cleisophus even bound up one of his eyes with a bandage, doing a favour to Philip, whose own eye had been struck out in the siege of Methone. But there is, it seems to me, friendship and fellowship between the louse and the dolphin; for to flatter, as also other evils, a man knows, but the irrational creatures do not know it.

8. The elephant has this strong love too toward its offspring. The hunters of these beasts dig trenches, into which these animals fall, and some are taken and some are killed. And what the manner of such trenching is, and what its shape, and how great its depth, and what the approaches are—you will learn elsewhere; but I come to uncover and to prove their affection. A mother, seeing her own calf fallen into one of the trenches, neither hesitated nor lingered idly, but rushing with all the impulse she had, eagerly and with overwhelming feeling, she thrust herself down headlong upon her young, and both met the same end together; for the calf, crushed by the mother's weight, was shattered, while she perished darting down headlong. Ridiculous, then, are those who

9. are in doubt whether there is a natural affection toward offspring. The seals give birth on the land, but little by little they bring their pups to the wet, and give them a taste of the sea, then lead them back to the place of their birth, and again

10. lead them down to the sea, and quickly lead them out; and when they have done this many times, in the end they make them most accomplished swimmers. And easily does the pup slip into the sea-life, instruction leading it on, while Nature compels it to love its mother's ways and habits and customs. The eagle is a grasping creature, and they make their food by plunder, and eat flesh; for they snatch hares and fawns and a goose from the yard and other things. But one alone among them, the very one that is called "of Zeus," touches no flesh, but grass suffices it; and though it has heard nothing of Pythagoras of Samos, yet it abstains from living things.

11. If one merely touches the venomous spider, they say, it kills him without his even being severely pained. And that the bite of the asp too is most gentle Cleopatra proved, when, as Augustus drew near, she tested painless death at her banquets, and found that by the sword it was painful, the wounded confessing this, and that by drugs it was distressing—for they brought on a kind of convulsion and forced the heart to suffer—but that the death from the bite of the asp was gentle, and, to put it in Homer's words, "feeble." There are some creatures that kill merely by being touched and by their belching too, such as the centrines and the toad.

12. You will tell me that the fox is a cunning creature—I mean the one nourished from the land; but hear too the devices of the sea-fox, and learn what sort of things she too does. For either she does not approach the hook at all from the first, or, having swallowed it, at once turning inside out the inner part of herself, she turned it outward, unrolling her body like a tunic, and in this manner, of course, she thrust out the hook.

13. Men say that there are certain love-charms; and the frog gives, as a token of amorous union, a kind of cry to the female, like a lover singing some serenade, and this cry is called the ololygon, as they say. And when he has won the female, both wait through the night; for they cannot come together in the water, and by day they shrink from coupling on land. But when night falls, with much security they come out and enjoy one another. And when frogs cry more loudly and more clearly than usual, they signify a visitation of rain.

14. That if one touches the torpedo-fish the affliction named after it seizes his hand—this too I heard, when I was a child, my mother often saying. And from wise men I learned that even if one touches the net in which it has been caught, he is wholly numbed. And if one should put it alive into a vessel and pour in seawater, then, if it is pregnant and the time of its labour has come, it gives birth. And if one pours the water in the vessel over a man's hand or foot, the hand or the foot must be numbed.

15. Animals do not always have the same power in their blows or in their bites, but it is often heightened by some cause. The wasp, at any rate, when it has tasted a viper, is harsher in its sting; and the fly that has come upon some such thing is bitterer to bite and gives pain; and indeed the bite of the asp becomes wholly incurable if it has eaten a frog. And the dog, if it bites while healthy, makes a wound and kindles pain; but if it bites while rabid, it destroys. A seamstress mending a little tunic torn by a rabid dog, having somehow bitten the tunic with her mouth to stretch it, contracted the madness and died. And the bite of a fasting man is grievous and hard to cure. The Scythians are said, besides the poison with which they smear their arrows, to mix in human serum as well in their poisoning, the part that somehow floats upon the blood, which they know to be a secretion of it. Theophrastus too is sufficient to attest this.

16. When the snake casts off its old age—it does this at the beginning of spring—then too it cleanses the mist of its eyes and the dimness of its sight, this also being as it were an old age of the eyes; and rubbing and stroking each eye against fennel, it then becomes free of this affliction. For it grows dim-sighted through hibernating in winter in a recess and in darkness. So the fennel, gently warming the creature's sight, numbed by the cold, clears it, and makes it keener of vision.

17. When the halcyon perceives that she is pregnant, then she makes a nest for the reception of her chicks, neither needing mud and a roof and houses, as the swallow does, and entering uninvited as a stranger, and troubling the early morning with her chatter and cutting short the sweetest of sleep; nor again does she hold to the aforesaid task with her body alone in open places, but weaving and gathering together the spines of the needlefish, with a kind of secret bond of orderliness she encompasses her work. For some of them she binds straight, and others crosswise—you would say it was a woman skilled in weaving interlacing the woof with the warp—and she makes the work gently rounded and hollow, fashioning it like the weave of a fish-trap. And when she has woven the thing described, she carries it to the sea, where, as the wave breaks gently upon it, the lapping that comes upon it proves the halcyon's work; for the part that is not watertight she mends again against the water that falls in. But the parts that are fitted together, even if you strike them with a stone, you could not pierce. And if you should wish to cut through them with iron, they would not yield, being so well and finely woven together, no less than the linen corselet which they sing that Amasis dedicated to Athena of Lindus. And the mouth of this trap is to no other creature either passable or even very visible, but it admits her alone. Nor would even any of the sea flow in through it; so watertight is it. There, then, the halcyon rears her chicks too, borne upon the waves, as they say.

18. Near the Nile there grows a plant, and it is called wolf's-bane, and it is not falsely named, and reasonably so; for when a wolf treads upon it, it dies in convulsions. For this reason those Egyptians who revere this animal forbid this plant to be brought into their country.

19. If a domestic fowl falls into wine and is drowned, they say it does no harm either to the wine or to those within the house; but if it falls into water, it makes the water foul-smelling and works a bad odour about the air. But if a gecko slips into wine and is then drowned, it does no harm at all; whereas if it falls into oil and dies, it makes the oil foul-smelling, and whoever tastes of it breaks out swarming with lice.

20. That the horn of a deer, when burned as incense, drives away snakes is clear. And Aristotle says that the stone that occurs in the river Pontus—this river is in the country of the Sinti and the Maedi—when burned as incense drives away the same creatures, and indeed he describes the nature of the stone as follows. If one pours water upon it, it kindles into flame; and if you should wish to fan the burning stone with a fan to make it blaze higher, it is quenched. And burned as incense it gives off, they say, a smell heavier than bitumen. With these things Nicander too agrees.

21. The island of Pharos long ago—the Egyptians say what I am about to say—was filled with snakes many and various. But when Thonis, the king of the Egyptians, had received as a trust Helen, the daughter of Zeus—for Menelaus, wandering about upper Egypt and Ethiopia, had entrusted her to him—then Thonis fell in love with her, and when he was offering violence to Helen to compel her to amorous union, the daughter of Zeus, the story says, told each of these things to the wife of Thonis, who was called Polydamna; and she, fearing lest the stranger should surpass her in beauty, secretly removed Helen to Pharos, and gave her a plant hostile to the snakes there, of which the snakes, when they perceived it, sank down into the ground. And Helen planted it, and in time it grew up and gave off seed hostile to snakes; and indeed in Pharos no such creature any longer came to be. And those skilled in such matters say that the plant was called helenion.

22. Starfish are a sea creature, and they too are soft-shelled, and are enemies to oysters; for they dine on them. And the manner of their plot against them is this. The oysters often gape, needing coolness, and besides to be fed by anything that may fall into them; so the starfish insert one of their own limbs into the middle of the shells, each of them, and fill themselves with the flesh, the shells being kept from closing together again. Let this be told by us as peculiar also to starfish.

23. The Lernaean hydra, Heracles' labour, let the poets sing of, and the compilers of ancient myths, among whom is Hecataeus the chronicler; and let Homer too sing of the nature of the Chimaera with three heads, that Lycian monster of Amisodarus, king of the Lycians, a creature reared for the destruction of many, varied and unconquerable, by Zeus. And these things seem to have been set apart for the realm of myth; but the amphisbaena is a two-headed snake, both above and at the tail-end; and as it goes forward, however the need of its progress draws it to its course, it leaves the one part to be tail, and makes the other its head. And again, if it needs to go backward, it uses its heads in the opposite way to that in which it used them before.

24. There was, it seems, a kind of frog, and it is called the angler, and it takes its name from what it does. It has, above its eyes, baits—long, as one might say, eyelashes—and to the end of each a little ball is attached. It is aware, then, that it has been equipped by Nature, and besides whetted, with these lures against the other fish. So, hiding itself in the muddier and more silt-filled places, it lies quiet, holding out the aforesaid hairs. The smallest of the fish, then, swim toward these eyelashes, thinking the spherical orbs at the tips to be bait; and the angler, lying in wait, keeps still, and when they have come near, it draws the hairs into itself—and they are drawn in by certain hidden and unseen ways—and the little fish, having come close in their gluttony, are a meal for the frog aforesaid.

25. The crayfish is an enemy to the octopus. The reason is that, when the octopus throws its tentacles about it, it pays no heed to the stings that grow upon its back, but pouring itself around it, throttles it to suffocation. The crayfish knows this clearly, and flees from it. And the nature of the crayfish is this. When it is without fear, this fish goes forward, slanting its horns this way and that, so that the water, coming against its swimming, may not check its horns and hinder it from going forward; but if it flees, going backward it lets them down entirely. The reason is that, rowing as with oars and stirring like a ferryboat, it draws far away. And if there should be a battle of crayfish with one another, raising their horns and then falling upon each other like rams, they dash their foreheads together. The contest of the lamprey and the crayfish I have told above.

26. The dewy and moist calamint, they say, drives away snakes strongly, and so does the chaste-tree. This too the Attic women spread beneath them in their bedding at the Thesmophoria. And the chaste-tree seems both to be an enemy to venomous creatures, and is besides a check upon amorous impulse, and seems to have got its name from this. The same venomous creatures fear too the plant called rosemary.

27. From Theophrastus I have heard these things too. This man records a certain plant, and calls it by the name "woman-slayer," which, if one should place it upon a scorpion's back and leave it there, the scorpion is at once withered. And the same man says that the same scorpion will revive, if you should sprinkle white hellebore upon it. But I praise the woman-slayer, and the white hellebore least of all. The reason is that I hate scorpions, but love men. And Callimachus sings that in the land of Trachis there grows a tree, and it is called smilos, which the creeping things, when they come near and merely touch it, then die.

28. That the sow has flesh more pleasant than other flesh has long been believed. And experience teaches this too, very clearly. Whenever it eats a salamander, it itself is unharmed, but it kills those who taste of it.

29. The Euphrates, which flows between the Parthians and the Syrians—what else it has beyond other rivers, remarkable, I shall tell at another time; but what the Parthians and the Syrians know of it, and what is in tune with these accounts, shall be told. At the first sources of this river there are born certain snakes, and very hostile to men—but not to the natives and those reared among them, while to strangers and foreigners they are in no way hostile. And they are honoured by causing death to these.

30. The lion, when it walks, does not go straight forward, nor does it let the marks of its tracks be simple, but now it goes forward, now it goes back, and again it holds to its forward course, and indeed it darts in the opposite direction. Then it confounds its road, and makes it impossible for the hunters to go along its trail and easily to find the lair where it rests and dwells with its cubs. And these too are the lions' peculiar gifts of Nature.

31. Imagine for me a good herdsman, skilled in pasturing. Now the herdsman loves the sheep, and loves the goats too, but hates the hiccup. This is a disease that often befalls a man, and repletion brings the hiccup upon these animals too. So the herdsmen plant near the folds of the aforesaid animals a certain plant hostile to this affliction, and this plant wards off the evil from them. And those who have tried it say that this plant is good for men too against the same affliction.

32. Those whose business it is to gather henbane and its juice dig pits round about and loosen the roots, but they do not pull them up with their own hands, but having caught or bought some winged creature, they tie one of its two feet to the plant. And it, writhing, then pulls the plant up. And both are profitable for the uses men have of them. But if one should not pull it up in this way, he gets in another fashion what he thinks a fair and useful treasure he has taken.

33. As for southernwood, what good things it does, and how it gives passages to the breath, and indeed is a cleanser of the lung, this is not the time to tell; but at any rate it is an enemy to a noxious creature, and destroys the tapeworm, which, when it goes on further, becomes a beast engendered in the entrails, but reckoned among human diseases—and that among those most incurable and impossible to be brought to a cure by a mortal hand. To attest this Hippys too is sufficient. And what the writer of Rhegium says is of this kind. A woman had a tapeworm, and the most skilled of the physicians despaired of curing her. So she came to Epidaurus, and begged the god that she might be freed of the affliction that dwelt with her. The god was not present; the sacristans, however, laid the woman down where the god was wont to heal those who needed it. And the woman lay quiet, as she had been bidden, while those who served the god did what was needful for her cure, and they took her head off from her neck, and one of them put in his hand and drew out the tapeworm, a great thing of a beast. But to fit and restore the head to its former joining they were no longer able. So the god arrives, and was angry with them, that they had attempted a task too great for their own skill; but he himself, by some irresistible and divine power, restored the head to the body, and raised up the stranger. And not at all, O lord Asclepius, most humane of the gods, do I set southernwood against your skill—may I never go so mad—but it came to my mind, and I made mention of your beneficence and your astonishing cure. And that this plant too is your gift one must not even doubt.

34. The nautilus is itself also an octopus, and has a single shell. So it swims up, turning the shell about the lower part, that it may not draw in the brine and so push itself down again; but when it is on the waves, when there is calm and a peace of the winds, it turns the shell on its back—and it floats like a ferryboat—and putting out two tentacles on this side and that, and stirring them gently, it rows and pushes forward its connatural ship. But if there is a wind, having first stretched out the oars it makes them longer rudders, and raising up other tentacles, between which is a very thin membrane, it spreads this and makes it a sail. So it sails in this manner when it is without fear; but if it is frightened by any of the larger creatures, sinking the shell it fills it, and slips down by the weight, and having hidden itself it escapes its enemy. Then, when it is at peace, it springs up and sails again. And from these things it has its name.

35. To three hundred fathoms, they say, the things in the sea are visible to men, but no further. Whether fishes swim still below this, or beasts too, or whether these regions are untrodden even by them, and the sea gods and the spirits of the deep have been allotted the place, and indeed the lord of the watery element—neither do I busy myself to inquire, nor does anyone else tell.

36. There was, it seems, a fish accustomed to the rocks and feeding among them, of the mullet kind, and yellow to look at. A double name is current about it; for some call it adonis, and others exocoetus, the "out-sleeper." For when the wave is calmed in fair and gentle weather, then it runs itself aground, riding upon the impulse of the wave, and spreads itself out upon the rocks, and sleeps a deep and most peaceful sleep. And it knows well that from all the rest it is under truce, but it dreads those birds that are and are reckoned bred of the sea. So if one of these appears, it leaps up and springs by some natural dance and, as one might say, a most secret caper, until, leaping off the rock and then falling among the waves, it is saved. And they like to call it adonis, since it has both land and sea for friends, the first who, it seems to me, gave it the name hinting at the life of the son of Cinyras, which was divided between two divinities, the one beneath the earth and the one above the earth being in love with him.

37. The branch of one plant grows upon the trunk of another, often belonging to it not at all. The cause Theophrastus tells, having traced it out most naturally: that the little birds, feeding on the bloom of the trees and then perching upon the plants, void their droppings. So the seed, falling into the hollows and openings and clefts of them, and watered by the rains from heaven, then makes grow again those things from which it sprang. Thus you will observe a fig-tree growing in an olive, and in another tree another.

38. The "sheep" lurks in the recesses of the sea, and the so-called hepatoi, and those which the fishermen like to call the "fitting ones." And they are the greatest in nature to look at, but sluggish in swimming, and they coil about their lurking-places, whence indeed they do not leave their own retreat. And they lie in wait for those of the weaker fishes that swim past. Among these too the "ass-fish" would be reckoned; and this ass-fish fears most of fishes the rising of Sirius.

39. There is born in the cornfields of wheat and in the poplars and in the fig-trees besides the tribe of the cantharid-beetles, as Aristotle says; in the chickpeas the tribe of caterpillars; in the vetch certain spiders; in the leeks the so-called leek-cutter. There is born too in the cabbage a kind of grub, and its name is from the haunts in which it lives; it is called the cabbage-grub. The apple-tree too breeds something; and this often destroys the fruit of that plant, but for those still of an age to bear it might even be good for fruitfulness. And the manner another will tell.

40. Each of the animals knows in what part it possesses its strength, and in this it takes courage, and when plotting uses it as a weapon, and when in danger as a means of defence. The swordfish, at any rate, defends itself with its snout as with a sword, whence indeed it has its name; the stingray with its sting; the lamprey with its teeth, and very reasonably; for it has a double row of them.

41. The mice in the house are a timid and weak creature, and they fear a noise, and shudder at a weasel's squeak; and the field-mice too are timid. But of the domestic ones the sea-mice are bolder. Small is their body, but their daring is irresistible; and they take courage in two weapons, a tough hide and the strength of their teeth; and they fight even with the larger fishes and with the fishermen most skilled at hunting them.

42. Tunny perceive the change of the seasons, and know the turnings of the sun most keenly, and have no need at all of those skilled in the heavens. For wherever the beginning of winter overtakes them, there they stay quiet and remain content, and abide until the coming of the equinox. And Aristotle attests this. And that they see with one of their eyes, but no longer with the other, Aeschylus too agrees, saying, "casting his left eye aside, like a tunny." And they go into the Pontus, and take the land on their right side, the side with which they also see; and going out again they swim along the land on the opposite side, taking, most providently, the guard of their body on the side of the eye that sees.

43. For the rock-crabs the first shell breaks, and just as the snakes their old age, so indeed do these too cast off their shell. And when they perceive it parting from their flesh, they go everywhere maddened and seek more food, that, when bulk has been added to them, they may swell and break their shell off themselves. And when they have slipped out of it and become free, they lie relaxed upon the sand, like dead things; for they are afraid for the hide that is growing upon them, which is still wet and tender. But little by little, gathering themselves and in a way coming back to life, they first taste the sand. And to such a degree are they without daring and least courageous as long as a membrane covers them as an outer shelter; but when it begins to harden and to pass into the nature of a shell, then they cast off their cowardice, taking courage as in a weapon, in the shelter of their covering and, as one might say, in full armour.

44. The Troglodytes are a celebrated race of men, and they have taken their name from their way of life. The snakes fear them. The reason is that the men eat them. And the snakes, when they mate with one another, give off a most heavy smell.

45. When a field borders on the sea and fruitful plants stand beside it, the farmers often catch, in the summer season, octopuses and squids that have come out of the waves and crept up through the trunks and fallen upon the branches and are gathering the fruit, and they arrest them and bring a charge against the thieves. And in return for what the aforesaid creatures gathered, the masters of the plundered fruit feast on them in turn.

46. Rhyades is the name of a sea creature wise at discerning the passage of the seasons. At the beginning of winter, at any rate, they stay quiet, fleeing the frosts, and gladly warming themselves by remaining together in brotherly equal shares; then in spring these begin to swim and to take longer journeys, and they feed not only on what falls in their way, but also on what they seek out and trace.

47. If one should crush sea urchins while they are still alive and in their shells and presenting their spines, and scatter them into the sea, leaving one fragment here and another there, they come together again and unite and recognize the kindred fragment, and clinging together grow into one. And they become whole again by some wonderful and peculiar nature.

48. To make the increase of their animals greater for themselves, their keepers rub the parts of the females—of ewes and goats and mares—at the time of mating, filling their hands with salt and natron. From this an appetite for love arises in them more strongly. Others anoint the same parts with pepper and honey, others with natron and the seed of the nettle; and some now anoint with horse-parsley and natron. From this irritation, then, the female flocks become incontinent of themselves, and go mad after the males.

49. Of the greatest sea-monsters not one approaches the beaches and shores and the so-called "scaly" and shallow places, but they inhabit the open seas. And the greatest are the lion and the hammerhead and the leopard and the blowers and the saw-fish and the so-called maltha; and this last is a hard creature to contend with, and unconquerable. The ram too is a dread animal and one that brings danger, even if it appears from afar, by the disturbance of the sea and the surge that it works. And the hyena—no good sight is this for seafarers. Of the "dogs," their difference and their strength I have told above.

50. The castorides are a sea creature, and on the headlands and the jutting rocks they let out a certain dread wailing, and howl most heavily. Whoever, then, hears this sound, escape is impossible for him, and not long after he dies. And the whale comes forth from the sea and warms itself in the ray. But the seals come out rather at dusk; though indeed even at midday they sleep out of the sea. This too Homer knew, and in the Odyssey he made Menelaus describe to Telemachus and Pisistratus this resting-place of theirs, when Menelaus recounted to them the events at Pharos and concerning Proteus the sea divinity, and the prophecy which that Proteus I spoke of prophesied to him.

51. About the red mullet I have spoken above; but what I did not say, I shall now tell. At Eleusis it has honours from the initiates, and the account of this honour is twofold. Some say it is because it spawns three times in the year; others, because it eats the sea-hare, which is deadly to man. Perhaps I shall say something about the red mullet again.

52. They fly when they are afraid, and spring out of the sea, the squids and the sea-hawks and the flying-fish. And the squids dart up to the greatest height with their fins, and lighten themselves aloft, and are borne along in shoals, in common, like birds; the flying-fish make their flight lower; while the hawks are borne a little above the brine, so that one can scarcely judge that they are not swimming but flying.

53. Fishes wander and roam, some in masses, like herds of cattle or ranks of soldiers going in squadrons and battalions, and some go in order in a column, and others—you would say they are companies. Others are numbered into tens and swim together in this way; and some swim by pairs. Others keep house in their lurking-places and live out their lives there.

54. I learn that those skilled in herding, when they wish their animals to put on fat, take away their horns. And when they wish to make the he-goats more eager for mating, they anoint their nostrils with perfume, and their beards too they anoint with the same. And again they check excessive appetite, if one ties up the middle of their tails with a thread. Aristotle says that mares cast their foals if they smell overmuch the wick of a lamp that has been put out. And I hear that against the house-dogs, that they may not run away, this device has been contrived. Having measured their tail with a reed, they anoint the reed with butter, and then give it to them to lick all round. And they remain, they say, as though bound.

55. These too are peculiar to the dog. They do not bark if anyone approaches carrying with him the tail of a weasel—a weasel which he has hunted, and having cut off the aforesaid tail then let it go alive. And an ass will not bray, if you hang a stone from its tail, as they say.

56. In the summer season, when the sun is very strongly at its height, the elephants anoint one another with thick mud, and this affords them coolness, and is more pleasant to these animals than any cavernous house or any tree overshadowing them with branches. These follow the scent strongly, and have a most keen perception. They go forward, making a way for one another, and the first—for they go in a column—perceiving the grass underfoot, and understanding from his touch of it that men have passed through, pulls up the grass and gives it to the one behind to smell, and that one to the one after him; and this passing-on, as one might say, goes through them all. And indeed, when it reaches the one bringing up the rear, he sounds out loudly, and they, as though soldiers receiving a watchword, then turn aside into the glens and thickets of the mountains, or the more hollow parts of the marshes, and indeed those of the plains that are thick with bushes. In any case, whatever men tread, this they flee; for they regard this animal as their bitterest enemy. And when their pastures fail them, some dig up the roots and feed on these too, while others go off seeking fodder. And the first of them who happens upon the prize turns back and calls his fellows and leads them to the find.

57. In the most violent winter, when the sea is in tumult, and the winds blow down harsh and violent, the fishes shudder at the sea that is at once their nurse and their friend. And some of them heap up the sand with their fins, and overshadowing themselves they keep warm beneath it, while others slip under some rock, and in shelter from the cold rest very gladly; and others, running down into the recesses of the deep, then turn aside the upper turmoil, going below and into the depth; for it is not, they say, so much above that the wave swells and beats in its rage. But at the beginning of spring, when the air has become bright, and the plants begin to flourish, and the meadows are thick with their native growth, the fishes, perceiving that the things of the deep are calm and fair, run up and leap, and swim near the land, as though come home from abroad.

58. These three become the greatest of animals from the smallest: of the water creatures the crocodile, of the winged the great ostrich, and of the four-footed the elephant. Juba says that his father had a Libyan elephant many years old, descended from the higher members of its race; and that Ptolemy Philadelphus had an Ethiopian one, and that it too, having lived from far back, became most gentle and most tame, partly from its fellowship with men, partly from being broken in; and he sings that Seleucus Nicator possessed an Indian elephant, and indeed says that this one lived on to the reign of the Antiochi.

59. Those fishes which have a river neighbouring on their native sea, or some lake, when they are about to spawn, swim out of the brine, choosing the water that is unbroken by the waves and least troubled and beaten by the winds. For the peace of the waters is good for them to receive their offspring and to keep their young unharmed and unplotted-against, both in other ways and indeed through the absence and scarcity of beasts; and lakes and rivers somehow tend to have this freedom. For this reason the Euxine Sea too abounds in many fishes; for it has not learned to nourish monsters. And if anywhere it nourishes a seal and very small dolphins, yet from all the others the fishes there are in shelter.
60. The sea-needles, being thin, and not having a womb capacious of embryos, do not endure the growth of the young within, but burst, and in this way they do not bear but cast forth their offspring.

61. It is said that the traces and tokens of the asp's bites are not very clear or easy to discern. And I learn the cause is this. The poison from it is most sharp and swiftest to run through. So the asp fastens on, but the venom does not stay on the surface, but slips down into the inner passages, and vanishes from the surface and the skin beneath the eye, and is thrust within. For this reason too the death of Cleopatra was not very easily recognized by those about Augustus, but late, when two punctures, hard to see and hard to detect, were observed, by which the riddle of the death was discovered. And besides, the traces of the asp's trail appeared, evident to those who have the knowledge of the movement of these animals.

62. When Pompeius Rufus was aedile of the Romans, at the Panathenaea a man who was a drug-pounder and one of those who rear snakes for shows, with many others of the same craft standing by, put an asp to his arm as a proof of his skill, and was bitten. Then with his mouth he sucked out the venom. But not having water to gulp down after—for there was none at hand, although it had been prepared for him, the vessel having been overturned by a plot—since he neither washed out the poison nor rinsed it away, he ended his life, after the second day, I believe, in no pain at all, the venom having quietly rotted away his gums and his mouth.

63. When spring is at its height and the earth is flowering, the animals are filled with amorous frenzy and call to mind their matings, and are eager to couple with one another, both the mountain creatures and those that dwell in the sea and those that travel aloft. And of the fishes some rub off their eggs upon the sands, eggs that are dense and clinging to one another, while others, as they swim, then cast forth a very great quantity of eggs, and those swimming behind swallow most of them. And indeed the males go before and shed their milt, and the females following, gaping very greedily, fill themselves; and this is their mating. And that certain fishes even dwell together with their females as wives, and guard them, and that a kind of jealousy is kindled even in the kinds of fishes, I have told above.

64. Aristotle says, and Democritus before him, and Theophrastus too in the third place says it, that fishes are not nourished by the salt water, but by the fresh water mingled with the sea. And since this seems somehow incredible, the son of Nicomachus, wishing to confirm what was said by the very facts, says that there is a drinkable water in every sea, and that it is proved thus. If one should make a vessel of wax, hollow and thin, and let it down empty into the sea, fastening it somewhere so as to be able to draw it up, when a night and a day have passed he draws it up filled with sweet and drinkable water. And Empedocles of Acragas too says that there is a sweet water in the sea, not visible to all, but nourishing to the fishes. And he gives a natural cause of this sweetening of the water in the brine, which you will learn from his work.

65. Those initiated to the Two Goddesses would not, they say, eat the dogfish; for it is not a pure dish, since it gives birth through its mouth. But some say that it does not give birth this way, but that, fearing some of those that plot against its young, it swallows them down and hides them, and then, when the one that frightened it has passed by, disgorges them again alive. And the red mullet the same initiates would not taste, nor would the priestess of Hera at Argos; and the reasons I know I have told somewhere above.

66. The matings of the viper and the lamprey, and how they consort with one another—she coming forth from the sea, and he creeping out of his hole—I have not forgotten that I told in what went before. But what I did not say I would now say. When the viper is about to consort with her, that he may seem gentle, as befits a bridegroom, he vomits up and casts out his venom, and so, hissing softly, he calls his bride, as though striking up a kind of pre-nuptial wedding song. And when they have accomplished together the rites of their amorous eagerness, she rushes off to the waves and the sea, while he, sucking up his venom again, returns once more to his own haunts.

1. Of Myra in Lycia there is a gulf, and it has a spring, and there is a temple of Apollo there, and the priest of this god scatters about the flesh of calves sacrificed to the god, and the orphus-fish swim up in shoals and eat the flesh like invited banqueters. And those who have sacrificed rejoice, and believe that the feasting of these fish is for them a good omen, and they say the god is gracious, because the fish have been filled with the flesh. But if they cast it out upon the land with their tails, as though dishonouring it and judging it abominable, this is believed to be the wrath of the god. And the fish recognize the voice of the priest too, and when they obey, they gladden those by whom they have been summoned, but doing the contrary, they grieve them.

2. At the old Bambyce (it is now called Hierapolis, since Seleucus named it thus) there are sacred fish, and they swim in troops and have leaders, and these eat first of the food thrown to them. And they keep their friendship toward one another most of all fish, and they are always at peace, either because the goddess breathes concord upon them, or because, being filled with the food thrown to them, they thus remain without taste and without knowledge of devouring one another.

3. The Egyptians say (and they do not at all persuade me, but they say nevertheless) that a lamb both eight-footed and two-tailed was born in the time of that famous Bocchoris, and that it broke into speech. And they sing that the lamb had two heads, and they say the same was four-horned. Now to Homer, who gave a voice to the horse Xanthus, it is fair to grant pardon, for he is a poet; and Alcman too, imitating Homer in such things, would not bear blame, for he has a sufficient excuse toward respect in being the very first to dare; but how is it possible to give heed to Egyptians boasting such things? Still, the peculiarities of this lamb have been told, even if they are fabulous.

4. This too I know I have heard about hawks. Before the Nile spreads over Egypt and rises onto the ploughlands, they cast off the feathers that are already growing old, just as the branches of plants cast off their dry leaves, and the hawks grow fresh and fine plumage, as the trees their blossom. There were, it seems, several kinds of hawks, and Aristophanes too seems to hint at this. At any rate he says: "But we sent three thousand hawks, mounted archers. And every one comes with hooked talons, kestrel, buzzard, vulture, owl, eagle." They are distributed and assigned to many gods. The partridge-catcher and the swift-winged is, they say, a servant of Apollo; the sea-eagle and the falcon they assign to Athena; of Hermes they say the dove-slayer is the plaything; of Hera the long-winged, and the so-called buzzard of Artemis. To the mother of the gods the merlin, and another to another god. So the kinds of hawks are very many.

5. The Egyptians, then, revering and deifying various kinds of animals, incur ridicule among most people; but the Thebans, being Greeks, revere, as I hear, the weasel, and they say it was the nurse of Heracles — or rather not the nurse at all, but that when Alcmene was in labour and unable to give birth, the weasel ran past and loosed the bonds of her travail, and Heracles came forth and was now creeping. And those who inhabit Hamaxitus of the Troad revere the mouse; from this, they say, they also call the Apollo honoured among them Sminthian. For still the Aeolians and the Trojans call the mouse "sminthos," just as Aeschylus too in his Sisyphus: "But there is some field-mouse, sminthos, thus monstrous." And in the Sminthium tame mice are reared, receiving public maintenance, and white mice lurk beneath the altar, and beside the tripod of Apollo a mouse stands. And this fable too I have heard concerning this worship. The crops of the Aeolians and the Trojans were assailed by many myriads of mice which, coming upon them, mowed them down unripe and rendered the harvests unfinished for the sowers. So when they inquired of the god at Delphi, he said that they must sacrifice to Apollo Sminthian, and they, obeying, were freed from the plot of the mice, and their wheat came to the appointed harvest. And they add these things too. When the colonists sent out from home to a settlement of Cretans were overtaken by some misfortune, they begged the Pythian god to show them a good place, profitable for their settlement. An oracle came forth: where the earthborn should make war on them, there they should remain and raise a city. So they come to this Hamaxitus and encamp to rest, and an unspeakable multitude of mice creeping up gnawed through the handles of their shields and ate through the strings of their bows; and they conjectured that these were the earthborn, and indeed, coming to be at a loss for their weapons of defence, they settle this place, and found a temple of Apollo Sminthian. So the mention of the mice has led us to a piece of theology, but we have been no worse for ourselves for having heard such things too.

6. Dolphins, it seems, are mindful of their dead too, and in no way betrayers of their fellows when they have departed from life. At any rate, having gone beneath one of their own that has died, they then carry it borne up to the land, trusting that men will bury it, and Aristotle bears witness to this; and another multitude follows, as though honouring it, or, by Zeus, even fighting on its behalf, lest some other sea-monster run up and, seizing the corpse, then devour it. So those who are just and have a sense of music bury them out of reverence for the dolphins' love of music; but others say that they neglect them, with no concern from Muses or Graces. And forgive, dear dolphins, the savagery of men, since even the Athenians cast out unburied the good Phocion. And Olympias too lay naked, she who bore the son of Zeus, as she herself boasted and as he too declared. And the Egyptians, having killed the Roman Pompey, surnamed the Great, who had done so much and won most august victories and celebrated three triumphs and saved the father of his murderer and restored him to the kingdom of the Egyptians, left him cast out, deprived of his head, beside the sea — him too, as they often leave you. For this all-devouring creature, man, does not spare even you, but they dare to make even you into salt-fish, and they do not perceive that they are doing this in anger against the Muses, the daughters of Zeus.

7. Lions they revere in Egypt, and a city is named after them; and it is worth telling the peculiarities of the lions there. They have temples and abundant places of resort, and they have beef every day, and it lies torn in pieces, bare of bones and sinews, and as they eat the Egyptians sing over them in the Egyptian tongue. And the burden of the song is, "Let no one of those looking on bewitch you," and the song is, as one might say, in place of amulets. Many of them are deified among them, and dwellings facing one another are set apart for them. And some windows opening toward the dawn, others toward the evening, make their abode more agreeable to them. They have also gymnasia for the sake of health, and near are wrestling-floors, and the well-fed calf is their adversary. And having exercised against this, if it overthrows it (it does this slowly, from idleness and lack of hunting), it gorges itself and returns to its own den. And the creature is intensely fiery, and from this the Egyptians dedicated it to Hephaestus too; and the fire from outside it shrinks from and flees, they say, owing to the abundance of the fire within. And since it is exceedingly fiery, they say it is the house of the Sun; and when the sun is hottest and most summery in itself, they say it draws near to the Lion. Moreover, those who inhabit the great city of the Sun rear these lions in the gateways of the god's temple, as having a share, the Egyptians say, of a more divine portion. For indeed, standing over those to whom the god is gracious in a dream, they foretell certain things, and those who have sworn falsely they punish, not with delays but at once, the god breathing his just anger upon them through them. And Empedocles too says that the best transmigration of a man is, if his lot should lead him into an animal, to become a lion; if into a plant, a laurel. And what Empedocles says is this: "Among beasts they become mountain-couching, ground-bedded lions, and laurels among the fair-leaved trees." And if one must, of the wisdom of the Egyptians who turn even such things into nature, take account (and one must), they assign the front parts of this animal to fire, but the hinder parts to water. And the double-natured sphinx the Egyptian craftsmen carving and the Theban myths boasting try to show us as of two forms, glorifying it by the mixture of the maiden's face and the lion-like body. This Euripides too hints at, saying: "Curling her tail beneath her lion-footed tread, she sat." And indeed they say the Nemean lion fell from the moon. At any rate the verses of Epimenides say: "For I too am of the race of fair-haired Selene, who, shuddering terribly, shook off the wild beast, the lion, in Nemea, bringing him up at the bidding of revered Hera." But let us assign these things to the myths; the peculiarities of lions have been told both above and now sufficiently.

8. There is a creature, the moth, which delights in the brightness of fire and flies to lamps when they are at their height, and falling upon them by its rush it is then burnt up. Aeschylus too, the poet of tragedy, mentions it, saying: "I greatly fear the foolish doom of the moth."

9. The wagtail is a winged creature, weak in its hinder parts, and for this reason they say it is unable to weave a nest privately or by itself, but lays its eggs in those of others. From this the proverbs of the countryfolk called beggars "wagtails." It moves its tail-feathers, like the halcyon in Archilochus. Aristophanes too mentions this bird in his Amphiaraus, saying: "Wag your loins from the tips like a wagtail, of an old man, and you will work a good charm." And in his Old Age: "the wagtail-stepping rhythm of one stooping." And Autocrates in his Drummers: "as the dear maiden daughters of the Lydians play, lightly leaping their hair, and clapping with their hands, before Ephesian Artemis the fairest, and lifting one hip downward and the other again upward, as a wagtail leaps."

10. Mice that die by themselves and from no plot, their limbs flowing away from them, depart little by little from life. From this the proverb says "according to a mouse's destruction," and Menander mentions it in his Thais. They used to say "more talkative than a turtle-dove"; for the turtle-dove both utters sound unceasingly through its mouth, and already, as they say, very much also from its hinder parts. The same poet mentions this proverb too in his Necklace. And Demetrius in his play Sicily mentions that the turtle-doves talk with their rump too. They say that mice are most lecherous, and they bring forward Cratinus as witness, who says in his Runaway Women: "Come now, let me flash for you, out of a clear sky, the lewdness of Xenophon's mouse." And still more they used to say the female was raging mad for venery. And again in Epicrates' Chorus: "But the accursed bawd quite took me in, swearing by the Maid, by Artemis, by Pherrephatta, that she was like a heifer, like a virgin, like an unbroken filly. But she was a whole mouse-warren." And wishing to call her lecherous to excess, he named her a whole mouse-warren. And Philemon: "a white mouse — when anyone — but I am ashamed to speak — the accursed creature cries out so loudly at once that it is often impossible to escape notice."

11. The Egyptians revere a black bull too, and they call it Onuphis. And let Egyptian accounts tell us the name of the place where it is reared; for it is harsh. Its hairs grow the contrary way to those of others; for these things too are peculiar to it. And this was the greatest of cattle, beyond even the Chaonian, which the Thesprotians and the Epirotes call "larini," tracing them in their genealogy from the breed of the cattle of Geryon. And this Onuphis feeds on Median grass.

12. The dolphin was the swiftest and most leaping of fish, and indeed of all land creatures too. At any rate it leaps over even a ship, as Aristotle says, and he tries to add the cause, and it is this. It holds its breath, just as the underwater divers do; for they too, having braced the breath within like a bowstring, then let the body go like an arrow. And what is compressed within, he says, pushes and shoots them forth.

13. The physa is an Egyptian fish worthy of wonder. For it knows, they say, when the moon wanes, and knows its waxing too. And indeed its liver waxes together with the goddess or wanes together with her, and at one time it is well-nourished, at another thinner.

14. The catfish is found about the Maeander and the Lycus, the Asian rivers, and in Europe about the Strymon, and it is like the sheatfish in form. And it is by nature the most loving of its young of fish. At any rate, whenever the female has spawned, she is released from care for the young, as a woman in childbed; but the male, appointing himself to the guarding of the offspring, remains, warding off everything that plots against them. And it is able even to swallow a hook, as Aristotle says.

15. The frog hates the water-snake and fears it strongly. So by its loud croaking it tries to terrify it in return and frighten it back. And there is the malice of the crocodile in hunting man and other animals. The path by which it knows men come down to the river, either for drawing water or for watering a horse or a camel, or, by Zeus, even to board a boat — this path it sprinkles by night with much water, and filling its mouth it pours often over the path, wishing to make it slippery and rendering its prey easier for itself; for those that slip do not keep their footing on the bank, but they are carried down, and it darts up and, catching them, dines. And I shall say a little about crocodiles now too. This beast is not at peace with the whole tribe of trochilus-birds (many are their kinds and names, harsh and grating to hear, and for this reason I leave them out); but only the so-called slack-beak does it have as comrade and friend; for this one can without pain pick out the leeches for it.

16. Democritus says that the sow and the dog are prolific, and he adds the reason, saying that they have many wombs and the parts receptive of the seed. The semen, then, does not fill them all from a single impulse, but these animals couple twice and three times, so that the continuity may fill the parts receptive of the offspring. And he says that mules do not bear young; for they do not have wombs like those of other animals, but of a different shape, least able to receive the seed; for the mule, he says, is not a work of nature, but a contrivance and theft, as one might say, of human ingenuity and an adulterous daring. "It seems to me," he says, "that an ass forced a mare by chance, and that men, having become learners of this violence, then went on to the habit of breeding them." And especially the asses of the Libyans, being very large, mount mares not maned but shorn; for a mare that has its own splendour through its mane would not, the wise in these matings say, endure such a mate.

17. Democritus says that embryos are aborted more in southern weather than in northern, and reasonably; for the bodies of pregnant women are made loose by the south wind and gape apart. So, the frame being relaxed and not knit together, the embryos, warmed and heated, slip this way and that and are aborted more easily; but if there be frost and the north wind blows, the embryo is compacted, but is hard to move and is not troubled as by a swell, and being unbuffeted and in calm it is strong and firm and lasts to the natural time of bearing. So in cold, the Abderite says, it holds together, but in warmth for the most part it is cast out. And he says it is a necessity, when the heat abounds, that both the veins and the joints gape apart.

18. The same man says that the cause of the growth of horns in deer is this. Their belly, he agrees, is very hot, and he says that their veins, which run through the whole body, are very loose, and that the bone enclosing the brain is very thin and membranous and porous, and that veins, very thick, rise up from there even to the top of the head. So the food, and the most fruitful part of it, is distributed very swiftly. And the fat, he says, is poured round them on the outside, but the strength of the food leaps up to the head through the veins. From there, then, the horns grow forth, watered by much moisture. So the moisture, being continuous and flowing on, pushes out the earlier matter. And the part that projects, the moisture outside the body, becomes hard, the air fixing and horn-forming it, but the part still shut up within is soft. And the one hardens by the chill from outside, but the soft part remains so by the warmth within. So the growth of the new horn pushes out the older as something alien, the part within pressing and wishing to thrust this up and swelling and throbbing, as though hastening to be born and come forth. For the moisture, fixing and rising up, is unable to keep still, but itself becomes hard and is thrust upon the earlier matter. And most of the horns are pressed out by the strength within; but some, caught by branches and hindering the swift course, the beast, driven by its rush, has knocked off. And some slip out, and others nature brings forward ready to peep out.
19. The gelded oxen (Democritus says) grow crooked and thin and long horns, but the entire ones thick at the root and straight and less

20. drawn out to length. And he says these are broad-browed much more than the others; for the veins being many there, the bones are widened by them. And the growth of the horns, being thicker, leads this same part of the animal toward breadth too; but the geldings, having a small circle at the seat of the horns, are less broadened, he says. And the hornless bulls, not having the honeycomb-like part (so Democritus names it) on the crown (he would mean the spongy part), the whole bone being resistant and not receiving the confluences of the humours, become bare and without a share of their weapons of defence. And the veins along this bone, being less nourished, become thinner and weaker. And the neck of the hornless ones too must be drier; for its veins too are thinner. And so they are less robust. But all the Arabian cattle that are female in kind, yet well grown in their horns, in these the great influx of humours, he says, is the nourishment of the noble growth for the horns.
