And those too are hornless which have the bone receptive of the moisture more solid and least receptive of the humours. And to speak in sum, the influx is the cause of growth to the horns; and this the veins channel, being very many and very thick and pregnant with as much moisture as they can hold.

21. Peculiar to animals is kindness toward man too. An eagle, at any rate, reared an infant. And I wish to tell the whole story, that it may be a witness of what I have proposed. When Seuechorus was king of the Babylonians, the Chaldeans said that the child born of his daughter would take away the kingdom from his grandfather. He shuddered at this, and, to put it with a touch of play, he became an Acrisius toward the girl; for he guarded her most bitterly. But secretly the girl (for fate was wiser than the Babylonian) conceived by some obscure man and bore a child. So those guarding her, in fear of the king, threw it from the citadel; for there the aforesaid girl was shut up. The eagle, then, with very keen sight, seeing the child's fall while it was still in the air, before the infant was dashed against the earth, came beneath it and put its back under it, and carries it to a certain garden, and sets it down very carefully. So the keeper of the place, beholding the beautiful little child, loves it and rears it; and it is called Gilgamos, and becomes king of the Babylonians. And if anyone thinks this a myth, I agree, having examined it to the best of my power and found it so; yet Achaemenes the Persian, from whom the nobility of the Persians descends, was, I hear, a nursling of an eagle.

22. In Crete there is a temple of Artemis so called, "of Rhoccaea." There the dogs go raging mad violently. So whenever they fall into this disease, they then throw themselves headlong from the height into the sea.

23. In the land of Elymais there is a temple of Anaitis, and there are tame lions there, and they greet and fawn upon those who pass into the temple. And if you call them while you eat, they come like invited banqueters, and taking whatever you hold out, they then depart modestly and orderly.
24. In the Red Sea there is a fish, they say, and its name is the watery palm, and it has black lines, and between them it is dotted with dark-blue drops.

25. The horse-mackerel there is equal in length to the one found in our sea, and bands resembling gold run round it, descending from the gills to the tail, and through the middle of them a band resembling silver divides them. Its mouth gapes, and the lower jaw is bent toward the upper; it has green eyes, and gold-like eyelids run round them. And the so-called charax is a nursling of the same sea. It has fins, and as far as the eye can see those on either side resemble gold, and those on the back it has gold-like too. Lower down there are bands purple in colour, and conceive the tail-part of it as gold-like too, and purple spots mark the middle of its eyes to beauty. And the toxotes that is found in the same sea is like the sea-urchin in form, but it has spines firm and long.
26. The Libyan porcupines prick those who touch them bitterly, and indeed work grievous pains. And even of the dead the wounds from their spines prove troublesome, they say.

27. There is in the Red Sea also an "ape," not a fish, but a cartilaginous creature, and this too not large. In colour the sea-ape resembles the land one, and its face too is ape-like. Over the rest of its body is thrown a shell, not fish-like, but such as is the tortoise's. It too is somewhat snub-nosed, as indeed is the land one. The rest of the body is flat in shape like the torpedo, so as to be, one might say, a bird with its wings spread; and as it swims it resembles one flying. It differs from the land ape in this too. It is spotted, and the broad parts along the nape are tawny, like gills. And it has a long mouth at the tip of its face, the fish being likened in this too, fittingly, to the form of the land ape.

28. The nightingale through the summer changes its colour to a different form, and alters its voice; for it does not sing in many tones and variously, but otherwise than through the spring. The blackbird sings in summer, but in winter it chatters and utters a confused sound, and having changed its colour like a garment, from its former black it is somewhat yellow. The thrush in winter is more starling-coloured to look at, but in summer shows a variegated neck. And these fish too change their colour: thrushes and blackbirds and wrasses and sprats. And jackals, as Aristotle says, are bare through the summer, but shaggy through the winter.

29. In Bubastus of Egypt there is a lake, and it nourishes a very great multitude of sheatfish, and these are tame and the gentlest of fish. And men throw to them fragments of bread, and the fish frisk up and leaping, one before another, pick out the food thrown to them. This fish is found in rivers too, as in the Cydnus of Cilicia; but this one is small in size. The reason is that a transparent and clear stream, and cold besides (such is the Cydnus), does not nourish it abundantly, but it delights more in a turbid one full of mud, and there it grows fat. The Pyramus and the Sarus nourish fatter ones, and these too are Cilician. The same would be reared in the Orontes of the Syrians too, and indeed the river Ptolemaeus nourishes very great ones, and the lake of Apamea.

30. Tame fish, obedient to a call and gladly receiving food, both are and are reared in many places, as in Epirus, in the city that still stands, which they called of old Stephanepolis, in the temple of Fortune, in the cisterns on either side as one goes up; and in Helorus of Sicily, which was of old a fort of the Syracusans; and in the temple of Labrandean Zeus, in a spring of transparent water, and they have little gold necklaces and earrings, golden too. The temple of this Zeus is seventy stades distant from the city of the Mylasians. The statue has a sword hanging at its side, and he is honoured under the names Carian and Stratian; for the Carians first devised a market of war, and served for silver, and fastened handles to their shields, and fixed crests on their helmets. And they were called by this name from Car the son of Crete and Zeus; and Zeus Labrandeus got this title from raining "labros" and abundant. And in Chios too, in the so-called Harbour of the Old Men, there is a multitude of tame fish, which the Chians rear for the consolation of old age for their elders. And in the land between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris a spring is celebrated as being transparent to the depth and casting up water white to look at, and there comes from it a river named Aborrhas. And the natives sing over the name a sacred story too, and the story is this: Hera, after her marriage to Zeus, bathed there, as the Syrians say, and to this day the place breathes fragrance, and all the air round about is blended with it there. And there frisk shoals of tame fish.

31. The peculiarities of animals not even the gods disdain to know. I hear, at any rate, that Eurysthenes and Procles, the sons of Aristodemus the son of Aristomachus the son of Cleodaeus the son of Hyllus the son of Heracles, wishing to take wives, came to Delphi and asked the god with whom of Greeks or barbarians they might form an alliance and then seem to have married well and prudently; and the god answered them to go back to Lacedaemon, and to return by that road by which they had come. And in whatever country there should meet them the most savage animal carrying the gentlest, there they should arrange their marriages; for thus it would be better for them. And they obeyed, and they come to the land of the Cleonaeans, and a wolf meets them carrying a lamb that it had snatched from some flock. They conjectured, then, that these animals were what the oracle meant, and they married the daughters of Thersander the son of Cleonymus, a man of repute. And if the gods know the gentlest animal and the most savage, it is not unfitting for us either to know their natures.

32. The land of the Indians bears many and various things. And some are evidences of a happy and wondrous productiveness, but others are not enviable nor such as to be worthy of praise or longing. And concerning the profitable or the luxurious and costly things I have said some, and others shall be told, with the help of the gods; but for the present I am set to tell how the land displays a brood of serpents. It bears many and various ones, and what is left over is past counting for the inexperienced. These serpents, then, harm both men and the other animals. But the same land bears also herbs that ward off the bites, and the natives have experience and wisdom of them, and have learned what drug is the antidote to which serpent, and they help one another as quickly as possible, trying to cut short the spreading of the venom over the body, which is very sharp and swift. And these things the country sends up to them for their necessary aid very readily and abundantly. But a serpent that kills a man, as the Indians say (and they bring forward as witnesses many of the Libyans and those of the Egyptians who dwell about Thebes), can no longer go down and creep into its own home, the earth not receiving it, but casting it out of its own bosom, as one might say, an exile. And from then on it goes about a wanderer and a vagabond, and is wretched in the open air both through summer and through winter, and neither does its mate any longer come near it, nor do its own offspring recognize their father. Such a punishment, then, for the slaying of man was shown by nature even to the brute beasts, by the forethought of the divine, according to my recollection; and it has been told for the instruction of him who understands.

33. Dogs, it seems, are more useless than geese at guarding, and the Romans detected this. The Celts were warring against them, and having very strongly pushed them back, they were in the city itself, and Rome had been taken by them except the Capitoline hill; for it was not easily accessible to them. The places that seemed able to receive an assailant with a plot were fortified. And it was the time when Marcus Mallius, being consul, was guarding the aforesaid hill committed to him. This is the man who both crowned his son with a garland for valour, and yet killed him because he had left his own post. When the Celts saw that all sides were impassable for them, they resolved, in the dead of night, lying in ambush, then to fall upon men sleeping most deeply, and they hoped it would be accessible to them by the unguarded part, where there was quiet, the Romans having believed that the Gauls would not attack from there. And indeed by this both he himself and the citadel of Zeus would have been most ingloriously taken, had not geese chanced to be present; for the dogs kept silent before the food that was thrown them, but it is peculiar to geese to cry out at things thrown to them for food and not to keep still. So they roused Mallius, screaming, and the guard about him. For this the dogs pay penalties among the Romans even now, every year, in memory of that ancient betrayal, but a goose is honoured on appointed days, and goes forth in a litter very ceremoniously.

34. And these things too about animals are not beside the Muse to tell. The Scythians, from lack of wood, boil whatever they sacrifice with the bones of the animals themselves. And the Phrygians, if anyone among them kills a plough-ox, the penalty for him is death. The Sagaraeans hold a contest of camels for Athena every year with reverence for the goddess, and these camels among them are very fleet and swift. The Saracori have their asses neither as burden-bearers nor as grinders, but as warriors, and on them they endure the dangers of battle, just as the Greeks do on horses. And whichever of their asses seems to be the most braying, this one they bring as a sacred offering to Ares. Clearchus of the Peripatetic school says that the Argives alone of the Peloponnesians do not kill a serpent; and on the days which the same people call "lamb-days," if a dog comes into the marketplace, they kill it. In Thessaly the man about to marry, sacrificing the marriage-feast, brings in a war-horse wearing its bridle and the whole panoply of war; then, when he has finished the rite and poured libation, leading the horse by the rein he hands it over to the bride. What this means, let the Thessalians tell. The people of Tenedos rear a pregnant cow for Dionysus the man-render, and when she has calved they tend her like a woman in childbed. But the new-born calf they sacrifice, having put buskins on it. And the one who has struck it with the axe is pelted with stones by the people, and flees as far as the sea. The Eretrians sacrifice mutilated victims to Artemis at Amarynthus.

35. I have learned, besides what I have already related, that there were dogs loving their master, those of Xanthippus the son of Ariphron. For when the Athenians were removing to the ships, at the time when the Persian kindled the great war against Greece, and the oracles said it was better for the Athenians to abandon their fatherland and embark on the triremes, the dogs of the aforesaid man were not left behind either, but removed together with Xanthippus, and swimming across to Salamis they expired. And Aristotle and Philochorus tell these things.

36. The Crathis sends forth water that makes white. At any rate, the sheep that drink of it, and the cattle and all the four-footed herd, as Theophrastus says, become white from black or tawny. And in Euboea too the cattle are born white almost all, from which the poets called Euboea "Argiboeon," land of white cattle.

37. A cock fell in love with a royal cupbearer (and the king was Nicomedes of the Bithynians), and the cock's name was Centaur, and Philo tells this. And a jackdaw too fell in love with a beautiful boy. And I have learned that certain bees are amorous, even if most are chaste.

38. They paint and mould the sphinx winged, with all the diligence and labour about the handiwork. And I hear too that at Clazomenae there was a winged sow, which ravaged the land of Clazomenae; and Artemon tells this in his Annals of the Clazomenians. From this a place there is called and celebrated as "of the winged sow." And if this seems to anyone a myth, let it so seem; but for my part what was said about an animal and not left unnoticed has not grieved me by being told.

39. To Halia, as she passed by Sybaris into a grove of Artemis (the grove was in Phrygia), a divine serpent appeared, very great to look upon, and consorted with her. And from this the so-called Ophiogeneis, the Serpent-born, sprang of the first stock.

40. The Delphians honour the wolf, the Samians the sheep, and the Ambraciots the lioness; and the reasons for each honour it is not beside this study to tell. For the Delphians a wolf tracked out sacred gold that had been stolen and buried on Parnassus; for the Samians too a sheep found such gold that had been stolen, and from this Mandrobulus the Samian dedicated a sheep as an offering to Hera; and the former Polemon tells, the latter Aristotle. The Ambraciots, since a lioness tore in pieces their tyrant Phaylus, honour the creature as having become for them the cause of freedom. And Miltiades buried in the Ceramicus the mares that thrice won at Olympia, and Euagoras the Laconian too buried magnificently his Olympic-victor horses.

41. The Ganges that flows among the Indians, taking its beginning from its springs, is twenty fathoms deep and eighty stades broad; for it still goes forward with its native water unmixed with another; but as it goes on, the others falling into it and sharing their water with it, its water reaches a depth of sixty fathoms, and it widens and overflows to four hundred stades. And it has islands greater than Lesbos and Cyrnus, and it nourishes sea-monsters, and from their fat they make an unguent. And there are tortoises in it too, and the shell of these is not less than a cask holding even twenty amphorae. And it breeds two kinds of crocodiles. And some of them harm not at all, but others most voraciously eat flesh and most unsparingly, and they have on the tip of the snout a projection like a horn. These men use as ministers for the punishment of evildoers too; for those convicted of the greatest crimes they throw to them, and they have very little need of an executioner.

42. The wise in things of the sea let down as bait for the parrot-fish, as Leonides says, coriander and especially leeks, and these are good catching and easiest to take; for the parrot-fish swims toward them, bewitched as by seasonings. And the leaves of beet take the red mullet; for the creature delights in this vegetable, and by it is caught and most easily enslaved.

43. Of the hunting of water-creatures there are four kinds, they say: net-fishing, harpooning, weel-fishing, and hook-fishing besides. And net-fishing is wealth-bringing, and resembles the taking of an army and the capture of certain prisoners, and it needs varied equipment, such as broom-cord and white flax and another black, and galingale and cork and lead and pine and thongs and sumac and stone and papyrus and horns and a six-oared ship and an axle and pegs and a windlass and a drum and iron and wood and pitch. And various kinds of fish fall into it, and shoals various and many. Harpooning is the most manly of the rest, and needs the most robust hunter. There must be present a straight fir-pole and broom-cord ropes and torches of the most resinous pine; and it needs a small boat and vigorous rowers and good arms. Weel-fishing is the most deceitful hunting and terribly treacherous, and seems least fitting for free men. It needs dry rushes and withy and a stone and bedding-weights and sea-weed and rushes and cypress foliage and corks and wood and bait and a small boat. Hook-fishing is the cleverest and most becoming to free men. It needs horsehair, of colours both white and black and tawny and grizzled; and of the dyed they approve the grey-green and the sea-purple; for all the others are bad, they say. They use also the stiff bristles of wild boars and turpentine, and very much bronze and lead and broom-cord and feathers, especially white and black and variegated. And the fishermen use also crimson and purple wools and corks and wood; and they need iron and other things, among them well-grown and dry reeds and soaked rushes and a polished fennel-stalk and a rod of cornel-wood and goat's horns and hide. And one fish is taken by one of these, another by another, and I have already told their hunting.

44. By these two accounts an Indian and a Libyan, differing in race, shall speak: the Indian will tell the things of his country, and the Libyan as much as he too knows; and what both accounts sing is this. Among the Indians, if a full-grown elephant is caught, it is hard to tame, and longing for freedom it thirsts for slaughter. And if you grip it with bonds too, it is kindled still more to anger, and will not endure to be a slave and a prisoner. But the Indians coax it with food too, and try to tame it with varied and enticing baits, setting before it whatever fills the belly and charms the spirit. But it is vexed with them and disdains them. What, then, do they devise? They bring against it a native music, and sing over it with a certain instrument familiar too; and the instrument is called the skindapsos. And it lends its ears and is charmed, and its anger is softened, and its spirit draws back and is calmed, and little by little it looks toward the food too. Then it is released from its bonds, but remains bound by the music, and dines eagerly, a dainty banqueter; for from longing for the strain it would no longer stand off. And the mares of the Libyans (for one must hear the other account too) — the flute-playing takes them so far. They are softened and tamed, and cease from their insolence and frisking, and they follow the herdsman wherever the strain leads them away, and when he stops they too stop; and if he raises the strain higher, tears are shed from them for pleasure. The cowherds of the horses, hollowing out a branch of oleander and making a flute and breathing into it, then thus pipe to the aforesaid mares. And Euripides too speaks of certain "shepherd hymenaeals"; and this is a strain which casts the mares into love and amorous frenzy, and maddens the males to mate with them. So horse-marriages are accomplished in this manner, and the strain seems to sing a wedding-hymn.

45. That the tribe of dolphins is fond of song and of the flute, Arion of Methymna is a sufficient witness, both from the statue at Taenarum and from the epigram written upon it. And the epigram is: "By the escort of the immortals, this conveyance saved Arion the son of Cycleus from the Sicilian sea." And a hymn of thanksgiving to Poseidon, witness to the dolphins' love of music, Arion wrote, paying these too, as it were, a ransom for his life. And this is the hymn: "Highest of gods, lord of the sea, gold-tridented Poseidon, earth-holder, through the teeming brine; round you the swimming beasts dance in a ring with their fins, with light tossings of their feet lightly leaping, snub-nosed, bristle-necked, swift-running whelps, the music-loving dolphins, sea-nurslings of the maiden Nereid goddesses, whom Amphitrite bore; you who brought me to the land of Pelops, to the Taenarian shore, as I wandered in the Sicilian sea, carrying me on your arched backs, cleaving the furrow of the Nereid plain, an untrodden path, when treacherous men cast me from their hollow sea-faring ship into the sea-purple swell of the deep." Peculiar to dolphins, surely, in addition to what has been said above, is their love of music too.

46. A certain Tyrrhenian account is current that says the wild boars and the deer among them are caught by nets and dogs, as is the law of hunting, but with music fighting on the hunters' side, and the more so. And how, I will now tell. They throw round the nets and the rest of the hunting-gear, all that lies in wait for the animals; and a man stands by skilled in the flute, and tries as much as possible to relax the strain, and lets be whatever is intense in the music, but whatever is sweetest in flute-song, this he plays. Stillness and quiet easily carry it across, and to the heights and the glens and the thickets and, to speak in sum, to all the lairs and beds of the beasts the strain flows in. And at first, as the sound passes into their ears, they are struck and somewhere too filled with fear; then a pure and irresistible pleasure of the music takes hold of them, and enchanted they have forgetfulness even of offspring and homes. And yet the beasts love not to wander from their accustomed places. But the Tyrrhenian creatures, little by little, as though by some persuading spell, are drawn, and as the strain bewitches them they come and fall into the snares, mastered by the music.

47. The anthias-fish, when they are struck and caught, are the most pitiable of sights, and as they die they seem to lament themselves and in a way to supplicate, like men fallen among pitiless and most murderous robbers. For some of them, trying to escape, are then entangled in the nets, and as they try to leap over the ambush, the spear-point overtakes them; and others, fleeing this death, leap out onto the land that is until then hostile to fish, choosing the end of life apart from the sword, and very gladly.

1. I am told that an eagle foretold to Gordius the kingship of his son Midas. While Gordius was ploughing, the eagle flew down, perched upon the yoke, and spent the whole day there; nor did it leave before evening, when Gordius gave over his ploughing at the hour when oxen are unyoked. And when Gelon of Syracuse was still a boy, an enormous wolf sprang into the schoolroom and snatched the writing-tablet from his hands with its teeth. Gelon leapt up from his seat and pursued it, not cowering before the beast but clinging fast to his tablet. But as soon as he had got outside the schoolroom, the building collapsed and buried the boys together with their teacher, while by divine providence Gelon alone survived. And here is the marvel: a wolf did not kill a man but saved one — the gods not disdaining to use even creatures without reason, to reveal a kingdom to the one and to save the other from impending danger. This love of the gods, then, is also a property peculiar to animals.

2. The Carians catch the sea-bream in this way. When the south wind blows gently and sends a softer breeze, when the swell has subsided and laps quietly upon the sands, then the fisherman has no need of a rod at all. He takes a switch of juniper, a very strong one, fastens a line to its tip, and threads upon the hook a half-salted fish with a mouth like a wolf's, and lets it down into the sea. He sits at the stern of his boat and works his bait, while a boy rows gently for him, deliberately learning beforehand to keep the stroke slow, and brings the boat in toward the land. Many sea-bream leap about, darting up out of the burrows where they live, and gather around the hook; for the fish, long since dead but dressed up to catch them, draws them on as though by a magic charm. Then, when they have come near the shore, they are easily taken, bound fast by the greed of their bellies.

3. Fish have many haunts: some live among the rocks, some in the sands, others among the grasses. For there are indeed sea-grasses, and some of them are called moss, others vines, and certain ones grapes, and others seaweed. There is even a kind of sea-grass called cabbage; and certain growths among them are called lichen and hairs. The food of these is different for different fish, and one accustomed to its own native and kindred grass would not, one might say, taste of another.

4. You may hear fishermen speaking of a fish called the callionymus. About it Aristotle says that it has a large gall-bladder lying upon its right lobe, and that its liver is carried on the left side. Menander also bears witness to this, in the Messenia I think, where he says, "I declare you have more gall than a callionymus"; and Anaxippus in the Man under Judgement, "If you provoke me and make all my gall boil up like a callionymus's, you will see I am no whit different from a dogfish-swordfish." Now there are some who say it is good to eat, but the greater number contradict them. The poets who have taken pains to give a lawful place in their verse to fish that are of some account do not readily mention it in their banquets of fishes — Epicharmus in The Marriage of Hebe and in Earth and Sea and besides in The Muses, and Mnesimachus in The Isthmian Victor.

5. The sea-frog also, like the birds, lays an egg. For it does not bring forth living young within itself; for even at birth its young have a head both large and rough, and on this account it is least able to receive its offspring back in fear; for they would gall and injure it if they re-entered. And likewise, when born and going forth, they would do much the same. So sea-frogs are neither easy in childbirth for the bringing of living creatures to birth, nor are they good refuges for their young. The eggs of frogs do not agree with the nature or peculiar character of other eggs; theirs too is rough, and has scales, and to one who touches it will seem resistant.

6. Octopuses too in time grow to great size, advancing toward the bulk of sea-monsters, and they too are reckoned among them. At any rate I am told that at Dicaearchia in Italy an octopus grew to a prodigious bulk of body and came to scorn and despise its food in the sea and the pastures there. This creature would even go forth onto the land and plunder some of the things on shore. Now there was a hidden conduit that carried the refuse of the said city out into the sea; up this the octopus would swim, climbing into a certain house by the shore, where there was a cargo belonging to Iberian merchants and salted fish from those parts stored in stout vessels. Then, wrapping its tentacles about the earthenware and squeezing it, it would break the jars and devour the salt fish. And when the merchants came in and saw the broken pottery, and found a great quantity of their cargo gone, they were astounded and could not guess who was plundering them: for the doors were seen to be untampered with, the roof unbroken, and the walls not dug through; yet the remains of the salt fish, left over by the uninvited guest, were plainly to be seen. So they decided to leave the boldest of their household indoors, armed, to lie in wait. That night the octopus crept up to its accustomed feast, and wrapping itself about the vessels — like an athlete in the wrestling clinch gripping his adversary firmly and very warily — it then crushed the pottery; for the octopus, one may say, was as easy a robber as ever was. It was the time of the full moon, the house was lit up, and everything was clearly visible. But the man would not set upon it alone, fearing the beast — for indeed the enemy was too great for one man — and at dawn he related to the merchants what had been done; and they, hearing it, would not believe him. Then some, remembering the magnitude of their loss, ventured the risk and hastened to engage the foe, while others, thirsting for the strange and incredible spectacle, shut themselves in along with them as volunteer allies. Then in the evening the thief came again and made for his accustomed table. At this point some blocked off the conduit, others armed themselves against the enemy, and with sharpened cleavers and razors they cut through its tentacles, as vine-dressers and woodcutters cut the topmost branches of an oak. And having lopped away its strength they brought it down at last, late and with difficulty, after no little labour; and — the strangest thing — merchants hunted a fish on dry land. So the malice and craftiness of this creature has been revealed to us as a property peculiar to it.

7. The Indians heal the wounds of captured elephants in this way. They bathe them with warm water, just as Patroclus did for the wound of Eurypylus in the fair pages of Homer; then they anoint them with butter. If the wounds are deep, they soothe the inflammation by applying and inserting pieces of pork, warm and still bloody. Their eye-diseases they treat by warming cow's milk and pouring it into them; the elephants open their eyelids, and being helped they take pleasure and feel it, just as men do. And they keep flushing them so long as they keep the rheum running; the proof that the inflammation has ceased is this. As for whatever other diseases befall them, dark wine is their remedy. But if a creature is not delivered from its sickness by this medicine, it is past saving.

8. For an elephant of the herd, though tamed, water is its drink; but for one trained for war the drink is wine — not the wine of the vine, but one they make by craft, one from rice, another from cane. They also go out to gather flowers for them; for elephants are lovers of fragrance, and they are led into the meadows to be broken in by the sweetest of scents. The elephant chooses out the flower, judging by its smell, and the trainer, holding a basket, holds it out as the beast gathers and casts in. Then, when it has filled the basket, it bathes, as though it had been plucking fruit, and delights in the bath like the more luxurious sort of men. Afterward, on returning, it longs for the flowers, and cries out if they are slow in coming, and will not take its food before someone brings it what it gathered. Then, taking the flowers from the basket with its trunk, it strews them over the edge of its manger, devising in this way, through their sweet scent, a relish for its food, so to speak. It also scatters many of the flowers over the place where it lodges, eager to win a sleep made sweet. The Indian elephants were nine cubits in height and five in breadth. The greatest of the elephants there are those called the Prasian, and second to these would rank the Taxilan.

9. To hold and check an Indian horse as it springs and bolts forward was not within every man's power, but only of those trained in horsemanship from boyhood. For it is not their custom to govern these horses with a bit, to keep them in rhythm and steer them, but with spiked muzzles; for the horses have an unruly tongue and an untried palate. Nevertheless these masters of horsemanship compel them to wheel about and turn round in a circle, revolving on the same spot. Whoever would do this needs both strength of arm and a thorough knowledge of horsemanship.

10. Those who have reached the height of this skill try to wheel and drive a chariot about in the same way; and it would be no contemptible feat to turn a team of four ravenous horses round with ease. The chariot carries two fighters beside the driver. The war-elephant, upon what is called its little tower, or indeed upon its bare and unencumbered back, carries three warriors, two hurling missiles on either side and the third behind, and a fourth who holds the goad in his hands and with it steers the beast, as a skilled steersman and master of the ship steers a vessel with the rudder. The hunting of leopards would be a Moorish practice. They have a building made of stones, resembling a kind of cage; this is the first enclosure. As for the second, further in, they hang from a longish cord a portion of rotten and stinking flesh, and they set up a flimsy door of reeds and certain canes, and through it the smell of the said flesh streams out and disperses. The beasts catch the scent — for somehow they take pleasure in foul smells — for the air bearing those odours strikes upon them, whether they are on the mountain-tops, or in a ravine, or even in a glen. Then, inflamed at meeting the smell, and by its overpowering urge, the leopard rushes headlong to the beloved banquet, drawn on by it as though by a magic charm. It falls upon the door, overturns it, and lays hold of its ill-fated dinner. For along with the said cord a very cunning snare has been woven in, which is set in motion as the flesh is eaten and closes about the greedy leopard. And she is caught — the unhappy creature paying the penalty for her ravenous belly and her loathsome feasting.

11. Hares are caught by foxes too, and by craft no less but even more; for the fox is clever at deceiving and knows tricks. Whenever by night it comes upon the track of a hare and perceives the creature, it steps up silently and with noiseless foot, holding back its panting, and coming upon it in its form tries to take it as one secure and unsuspecting. But the hare is not given to luxury, nor does it sleep heedlessly; the moment it perceives the approaching creature it leaps up from its bed and runs. And it accomplishes its course very swiftly, while the fox too darts upon its track and keeps to the chase. The hare, having run a long way and thinking itself now the stronger and beyond capture, plunges gladly into a thicket and rests; but the fox comes up and does not let it stay still, but rouses it again and drives it off on another course, blown along by the wind. Then this second course, no less than the first, is run to its end; and when the hare longs to rest once more, the fox comes up and, shaking the bush, works wakefulness upon it. And the hare runs off again, and the fox is not left behind. When course follows course upon it without break, and sleeplessness succeeds, the hare gives up, and the fox, coming upon it, takes it — not by speed, by Zeus, but mastering it by time and by craft. Now this account, running ahead, has been put off concerning the hare's running, and the rest it will be more seasonable to tell in what follows. So I return to the point from which I digressed. This, then, was the reason for scattering its offspring and rearing them apart, one here, one there. The hare is exceedingly fond of its young, but it fears the plots of hunters and the raids of foxes, and shudders no less at the assaults of birds, and at the voice of ravens and eagles most of all; for with these among winged creatures it has no truce. It hides itself either in a leafy bush or in deep standing corn, or sets some other necessary and unassailable shelter before itself.

12. I have heard an account from a hunter who in other respects too was a good man, the kind who would not lie, and I have believed him, and for that reason it shall be told. He said that the male hare also gives birth, and at the same time begets and is in labour, and does not lack a share in either nature. And he said it rears its young after bearing them, and that it brings forth perhaps two or three; and he affirmed this, and indeed he added that crowning instance to the whole account. A male hare, he said, was caught half-dead, and its belly was swollen as though it were pregnant. He admitted that it was cut open, and that a womb was found, and three leverets. These at first lay motionless when taken out, and lay there like mere lumps of flesh; but when, warmed by the sun and gradually heated, they had lain a while, they came round and revived, and one of them stirred and afterward looked up, and presently even put out its tongue and opened its mouth in longing for food. So, as was natural, milk was brought to such little creatures, and little by little they were reared — a proof, as it seems to me, of the marvellous nature of the parent that bore them. Yet I cannot persuade myself not to believe the account; and the reason is that the man's tongue knew neither falsehood nor boasting.

13. The hare is also knowing about winds and seasons; for there is something clever in it, though not gracious. In winter, then, it makes its bed in spots that face the sun; for it is plain that it gladly takes warmth and is hostile to cold; but in summer it inclines toward the north out of longing for cool. Its nostrils are its gauge of the difference of the seasons. The hare does not close its eyes when it sleeps — this it has alone among animals — nor are its eyelids overcome by sleep; they say it sleeps with its body, but at that time sees with its eyes. I write what the skilled hunters say. Hares feed by night, partly perhaps from a desire for strange food, but I should say it is for the sake of exercise, so that even then, when it holds out vigorously against sleep and stays active, it may keep up its speed. It loves the way back exceedingly, and is overcome by attachment to every familiar spot; and for this reason it is mostly caught, since it cannot bear to abandon its accustomed haunts.

14. The hare, when pursued by hounds and horsemen, runs — if it comes from level ground — more swiftly than mountain hares, being small of body and slender; and on this account it is not unlikely that it should be light. At first it skips up from the ground and leaps, and slips easily and smoothly through bushes and through every marshy place; and if the grass anywhere is deep, it passes through that too with ease. And just as they say the lion's tail can rouse and spur him on, so for the hare its ears serve as signals of speed and rousers of its course. It lays them back along its shoulders, and uses them, like spurs, to keep from idling and shrinking. It does not run a single straight course, but swerves this way and that, and twists here and there, confounding the hounds and deceiving them. Wherever it sets out and wishes to turn aside, in that direction of swerving it inclines one of its ears, as though steering its course by it. Nor does it spend its strength without stint, but watches the onset of its pursuer; and if the hound is sluggish, it does not let loose its whole speed, but holds something back, so as to run ahead of the hound, yet not to give out from the strain of the running itself. For it knows it is the better, and sees that it is the moment not to over-tax itself. But if the hound is very swift, then —

15. — the hare runs at the full stretch of its legs. Indeed, when it has got a long way ahead and left hunters and hounds and horses far behind, it leaps up onto some high hill and, raising itself upon its hind legs, looks out as from a watchtower at the contest of its pursuers, and seems to me to laugh at them as the weaker. Then, taking courage from this as having the advantage, and gladly seizing as it were a moment of peace and calm, it settles down and lies sleeping. The mountain hare is not so swift as those that dwell on the plains — unless indeed those mountain hares too have a plain lying below them, on which they come down and range; for they dwell on the mountain, but exercise there, often running together with those from the plains. In the plains, then, they are wont to be hunted, and some are stirred up while others lie hidden; and then, when from the customary chase the hidden ones are roused, not one escapes. But when they are on the point of being caught, turning a little aside from the plain track they leap up into the steep and mountainous ground, hastening as toward their own native and accustomed haunts; and going off in this way they are gone, having met with unexpected safety. For climbing the heights is by nature hostile to horses and hounds, since their feet fail them and are easily worn away. The hounds suffer this still more; for their feet are fleshy and have nothing resistant against the rock, as horses have their hoof. But the hare is the opposite: its feet are shaggy by nature, and so it endures rough ground. But hares whose haunts are in thickets and brush are sluggish in running and slow to flee; for such are fattened and, through idleness, not practised in running, and least of all do they stray far from the brush. The hunting of these is as follows. At first they slip through the small bushes, where the covert is not continuous; but the denser ones, since they cannot pass beneath, they naturally leap over. Some bushes are continuous and woven through one another; where these are, the hare — being often forced to do this, and not being given to leaping because of the weight of its body — soon tires and gives out. The hounds at first stumble and miss it; for they do not see it through the thickness of the wood, but they too leap over the bushes, led by the scent; yet at last they catch sight of it and pursue and give no quarter, while the hare, from the unbroken leaping, tires and gives out and is thereupon caught. Hares run up steep heights with ease, for their hind legs are longer than their front; but they do not run down so well, for the contrary disposition of their legs hinders them. There is also another hare, small by nature, that never grows large: its name is the coney. I am no coiner of names, and so in this treatise too I keep the name given it from the first, which the western Iberians bestowed upon it, among whom it is both bred and found in great abundance. Its colour, compared with the others, is dark, and it has a short tail; in other respects it is like in appearance to those described. It differs also in the size of its head, for its head is more slender, exceedingly fleshless, and shorter. It is whiter than the rest. They have year-round irritants in their nature, by which they are stung and driven wild when they rush upon the females. There is a bone in its heart, and to know what that bone is good for shall be another's concern.

16. The Italians and Sicilians like to call the hunting of tunny the "monster-fishery"; and the places where they store their great nets and the rest of their hunting gear are called "monster-hunting stations," since they wish to distinguish the tunny's size as belonging among the sea-monsters. I am told that the Celts and Massaliotes and all the Ligurian folk hunt tunny with hooks; these are made of iron, and are very large and thick to look upon. And let what I have now said about tunny, in addition to what was said before, be enough for me.

17. About the islands called Tyrrhenian those engaged in fishing hunt the monstrous fish of those waters, which they call the aulopias; and it is no bad thing to describe its peculiar features. In size the largest aulopias is inferior to the largest tunny, but in strength and fighting power it would bear off the first prize when set against them. For the tunny too is a valiant tribe of fishes, but to one who faces it and contends with it eagerly it yields the mastery after its first onset, its blood congealing within it, and being spent it is very swiftly caught. But the aulopias holds out for a long while when one sets upon it with force, and stands against the fisherman as against an adversary, and prevails for the most part, pressing itself harder down and bending its head and thrusting toward the deep; for it is strong in the jaw and powerful in the neck, and has excellent vigour. When it is taken, it is most beautiful to see, with its eyes open and round and large, such as Homer sings of in oxen; and its jaw, though strong as I said, yet also lends to its beauty. Its back imitates the colour of the deepest blue, but it is girt with a white belly; and a line of golden colour begins from its head and, running down to the tail-end, finishes in a circle. I am willing to tell the crafty way they hunt them, which I know from hearsay. Choosing out in advance the spots where they suppose the aulopiae to gather, they then catch with their bait-nets many small crows-fish; and mooring their boat upon anchors and continually making a certain noise underwater, they stretch out the crows-fish, fastening them tight with cords. These, hearing the noise and seeing the bait, swim up from this side and that, gather, and circle round the fishing-boat, and grow so tame at the din and the abundance of food that they remain even when men stretch out their hands. They endure a human touch — in my judgement, enslaved by the feeding, but, as the hunters say, also trusting in their strength. Among them there are tame ones too, which the fishermen recognize as benefactors and companions, and have a truce with them. Other strangers follow these as leaders, and these newcomers, as one might call them, they both hunt and kill; but toward the tame ones, which are like decoy doves, there is for them no hunting and a truce. Nor would so great a want ever come upon a skilled fisherman that he should take a tame aulopias by treachery; for if it is caught by chance, for certain reasons, it even causes grief. It is caught either by being pierced upon a hook or by being wounded to death. We see that fowlers too will not kill any of the decoy birds, either for sale or for dinner. And there are other ways of hunting these fishes as well.

18. In the royal palace of the Indians, where the greatest of their kings dwells, there are many other things worthy of wonder, so that one should set against them neither the Memnonian Susa and its sumptuousness, nor the magnificence at Ecbatana; for those would seem mere Persian boasting if compared with these. To go round the rest in my account does not belong to this treatise; but in the parks there are reared tame peacocks and pheasants made gentle to the hand, and these have their place among the trees that have been cultivated, which the royal keepers think worthy of the needful care. For there are shady groves and pasture grown together, and branches woven into one another by a certain art of arboriculture. And the most august thing about the beauty there is that the trees themselves are of the evergreen kind, and never grow old or shed their leaves; some are native, others brought from elsewhere with great care, which adorn the place and give it splendour — except the olive; for the land of the Indians does not bear it, neither produces it of itself, nor rears it when it comes from elsewhere. Other birds too come there, free and unenslaved, and arriving of their own accord they have their roosts and resting-places among the trees. There too the parrots are reared and throng about the king. No Indian eats a parrot, though they are very many in number; the reason is that the Brahmans believe them sacred, and indeed they honour them above all birds. And they add that they do this with good reason; for the parrot alone most eloquently imitates the human voice. There are also in this palace beautiful artificial lakes, and they hold fish of the greatest size and gentle; and no one hunts them except the king's sons while they are still children, fishing and playing in the calm and least dangerous water, and at the same time learning to swim.

19. In the Ionian Sea, off Leucas and the sea by Actium — where they call the region Epirus — there are, one might say, countless schools of grey mullet and very great numbers of them. They are hunted in a most astonishing way; and the manner of the hunting is this. The fishermen there, watching for a moonless night, after supper put out two to a boat, when there is no swell but the sea is calm and unbroken; then quietly and little by little they row forward. One man works the boat with his oar, bringing the skiff along at a walking pace, as one might say; the other, reclining on his elbow, weighs down his own side of the skiff and tilts it so far that its rim comes near the water. The grey mullet and the striped mullet of like kind, whether delighting in the night or rejoicing in the calm, leave their hollows and burrows and swim up, showing the tips of their faces above the water, taking so much of their upward swim that they come near the shore. The hunters, seeing them, row on, and the wash of the skiff begins gently to ripple. So the fish, fleeing the land and turning back, push themselves into the tilted side of the boat, and passing within are caught.

20. Of the sea-monsters, those that are exceedingly huge and prodigious in size swim in the midst of the open sea, and are even struck by thunderbolts. Besides these there are certain other rare creatures of the kind, and their name is "wheels." These swim in schools, chiefly on the right of Thracian Athos, in the gulfs as one sails from Sigeum; one may also meet them along the mainland opposite, by what is called the tomb of Artachaees and the Acanthian isthmus, where the Persian's cutting is to be seen, by which he cut through Athos. These monsters, which they call wheels, are said not to be valiant; but they show a crest and exceedingly long spines, so that these are often seen above the water. On hearing the noise of oars they wheel about and coil up, thrusting themselves as far down as possible; and from this they have got their name. They come up again unrolled and rolling the other way.

21. About Tritons the fishermen say they cannot give a clear account or strong proof; yet a report widely current says — yes, by Zeus, much is told — that there come to be in the sea certain monsters of human shape, in all that reaches from the head down to the waist. Demostratus, in his discourses on fishing, says that at Tanagra he saw a salted Triton. In all else, he says, it was like the figures sculptors fashion and painters draw; but its head, ruined by time, was not very clear, nor such as one could easily make out and recognize. "And when I touched it," he says, "rough scales fell off, and very resistant ones at that." One of the magistrates assigned by lot to govern Greece and entrusted with the office for a single year, wishing to test and prove the nature of what was seen, took off a little of the skin and consigned it to fire; and a heavy smell from the burning thing struck the nostrils of those present. Yet, he says, we could not determine whether the creature was by nature a land or a sea animal. But the trial did not pay him a good wage. For not long after he ended his life, crossing a narrow strait in a small skiff. And the Tanagraeans said, as Demostratus tells, that he suffered this in requital for the impiety he had committed against the Triton, alleging as proof that, while it was breathing out its last, it was taken from the sea and gave off an ichor like in smell to that of the Triton's skin when he burned and set fire to it. From where this Triton wandered, and how it was cast up here, let the Tanagraeans and Demostratus tell. As for these matters, I reverence the god, and it is right to believe so great a witness; and the Apollo at Didyma would be sufficient to prove it to anyone whose mind is sound and whose understanding is strong. He says, then, that the Triton is a sea-creature, and what he says is this: "A nursling of Poseidon, a watery monster, loud-voiced Triton, swimming, met the rush of a hollow ship." If, then, he who knows all things says that Tritons exist, we need not be perplexed about it.

22. When the king of the Indians goes forth to give judgement, the elephant is the first to do obeisance to him, having been taught this, and performing it both mindfully and obediently. There stands beside it the man who gives it the reminder of its lesson by a stroke of the goad and by a certain native call, which elephants are appointed by some secret nature to understand — a thing very peculiar to this creature. Moreover it sets in motion a certain warlike movement, as though showing that it preserves this lesson too. Twenty-four elephants attend the king as guards, by relief, like the rest of his sentinels, and the keeping of the watch is a lesson to them, and they do not nod off; for they are taught this too by a certain Indian art. Hecataeus of Miletus says that Amphiaraus the son of Oicles lulled the watch to sleep and suffered what he relates. But these elephants are wakeful and not overcome by sleep, and are the most trustworthy of the guards there after men.

23. As for me, with all the eagerness I had, examining and tracking these matters and what bears on them to the farthest point, I have learned that the centipede also is a kind of sea-monster, this too the greatest of monsters; and one cast up on shore no one would be bold enough to look upon. Those who know sea-creatures precisely say that these are seen afloat, and that the whole of what is the head juts out above the surface, and that they show hairs projecting from their nostrils, very tall ones, and a broad tail like that of a crayfish. The rest of its body too is seen floating on the waves, of such size as to be set against a full-sized trireme in bulk. They swim with many feet, ranged in a row on this side and on that, like oar-blades hung along (if it is somewhat harsh to hear), rowing themselves along. Those skilled in these things say that the wash sounds gently beneath them, and they persuade by what they say.

24. Xenophon says this too about hounds. One ought often to lead them into the mountains, but less into cultivated land; for the beaten paths from the worked fields trouble them and throw them off. It is better, he says, to lead them onto rough ground, and he teaches this further gain besides — that they become good of foot and better leapers by training their bodies. He says that the tracks of a hare are seen long in winter because of the length of the nights, but not so in summer, for the contrary reason. And it is plain from what has been said what the contrary reason means.

25. Horses and elephants the Indians honour as creatures useful both in arms and in war, and very greatly so. To the king, then, they bring sheaves which they cast into the mangers, and fodder, and they display it fresh and unspoiled. And if it is such, the king commends them; but if not, he punishes most severely the keepers of the elephants and the grooms of the horses. Nor does he dishonour the other creatures, but he accepts these too when they are brought to him as gifts. For the Indians despise no creature, neither tame nor wild. At any rate the subjects who are held in honour bring as gifts cranes and geese, fowls and ducks, turtle-doves and besides francolins, partridges and "spindali" (this last is like the francolin), and besides these, smaller than the aforesaid, "boccalides" and fig-peckers and the so-called millet-birds. They display them spread open, testing the depth of their fatness. And they bring a wealth of fattened deer and antelopes and gazelles and oryxes and the asses that have a single horn, of which I made mention somewhere above; and various kinds of fish too they bring.

26. There is also a sea-cicada. The largest of them resembles a small crayfish, but it has not large horns like those, nor stings. To look upon, the cicada is darker than the crayfish, and when it is caught it is like one chirping. A few small wings have grown beneath its eyes, and these too would be like those of the land cicadas. Most people do not eat it, holding it sacred. I am told that the Seriphians even bury one when it is caught dead; but if it falls alive into their net they do not keep it, but give it back to the sea. They make lament over them when they die, and they say that they are the plaything of Perseus son of Zeus.

27. The "hyena" is a fish that shares its name with the land hyena. If you place its right fin beneath a sleeping man, you will throw him into great disturbance; for he will see certain fearful sights and apparitions and phantoms, and other dreams in no way kindly or friendly. Again, if you cut off the tail of a horse-mackerel while it is alive, and then let the horse-mackerel go free again into the sea, but hang the said tail upon a pregnant mare, before long the embryo will be cast and the mare will miscarry. Again, when a youth, longing for the hairs of his chin, is at a loss for the longest time, the blood of a tunny smeared on makes the youth smooth before his time. The torpedo-fish and the "lung" do the same; for the flesh of these, rotted in vinegar and smeared on the chin, works, they say, the banishment of the hairs. What against this can those mischievous sophists of Tarentum and Tyrrhenia say, who tracked down and tried out that cunning pitch, to mark off men from women?

28. The gilthead is the most cowardly of all fishes. In the ebbings of the sea, when the season runs with Arcturus, the sea retreats about the headland, and bare sand is left behind, and ships often stand upon the land widowed of water. So the natives, sharpening green and leafy shoots of poplar like stakes and fixing them in the sand, withdraw; then the returning wave drags along an irresistible multitude of the said fish, and ebbs again, and many gilthead are left behind in shallow water, wherever a low hollow place is found. Then, cowering beneath the branches, they keep still; for being shaken and stirred by the wind that strikes them they take fright, and neither gasp nor leap up. So one may seize them like captives and strike them — a populace of cowardly fish, one might call it — with whatever comes to hand. At any rate not only experts catch them, but even a layman who chances to be by, and children and women too.

1. In the Ionian Sea, near Epidamnus, where the Taulantii dwell nearby, there is an island called Athena's, and fishermen live there. There is also a lake on the spot, and shoals of tamed and domesticated mackerel are reared in it. The fishermen throw food to these, and there is a truce between them, and the fish are free and have been granted exemption from being hunted, and they live on to a great age, and even old mackerel dwell there. Yet they do not feed in idleness, nor are they ungrateful for their keep; rather, when they have taken their morning food from the fishermen, they then go off to the hunt themselves, as though paying for their nurture. Going forth from the harbour they set out against the foreign mackerel, and when they meet them, as it were a troop or a battle-line, they swim up to them as to fellows of their own kind and nature; and neither do those flee these, nor these turn away from those, but they come together. Then the tame ones, surrounding the newcomers and forming a ring and packing themselves close, cut off a great multitude in the middle and do not let them slip away, but wait for their keepers; and in return for the food on which they were fed they feast the fishermen in turn. For the fishermen come up and take the foreign fish and work a great slaughter. The tame ones then go off in haste to the harbour, and slipping into their own hollows await their afternoon meal. And the fishermen come bringing it, if they wish to have fellow-hunters and faithful friends. And this is done day by day.
2. If you give a man suffering in the liver and afflicted with jaundice the gall of a parrot-fish to eat, he will be saved, as the skilled fishermen teach.

3. Fish are caught even without weels and hooks and nets, in this way. Many sea-gulfs end in certain shallows, and these can be waded into. So when there is calm and a peace of the winds, the expert fishermen lead many men there, and bid them walk and trample the sand, pressing down their soles as hard as they can. Then deep footprints are left behind, which, if they are kept — provided the sand does not collapse and confuse them, and the water is not stirred up by wind — the fishermen wait a little, then, wading in, find lying at rest in the hollows of the steps and in the footprints the flat fish: plaice and turbot and sole and torpedo-fish and the like.

4. About the sea-urchin I have spoken above, and now too I will tell what I have further heard. It is good for the stomach; for one who was before a poor eater and loathed everything whatever, this restores. It is also an emptier of the bladder, as those skilled in these matters say. And if you smear it on a body that is scaly with itch, it makes whole one who before was suffering the said disease. Burnt in its very shells, it cleanses away the foulness of wounds. And the ash of a land-hedgehog burnt, mixed besides with pitch and smeared on the bald parts, makes the hairs that were before fugitive (to add a little jest) grow up again. Drunk in wine it is good for the kidneys, and saves those who are dropsical when it is drunk, as I have already said. And the liver of this hedgehog, dried in the sun, heals those who are seized

5. by the disease called the elephant's. The female elephant — the wise ones celebrate that her tusks are the more valuable, and they teach us this too. In the land of Mauretania the elephants are wont to shed their tusks invariably in the tenth year, just as deer shed their horns, only deer do so every year. These elephants, then, choose out level and dewy ground in preference to the rest, and set their tusks into it, crouching down on bended knees, exceedingly eager to be rid of them. They thrust them so far in as to hide them completely; then, smoothing the place with their feet, they leave it standing guard over their treasure. And since the ground is most fertile, it very quickly grows grass over it, and conceals the sight of what has been done from those who pass that way. But those who track down these hidden hoards, and have a certain cunning against the elephants' stratagem, bring water in goatskins, and then scatter the filled skins about in different places, while they themselves remain there. And one of them sleeps, another drinks, and one perhaps, even while sipping from his cup between draughts, sings a little, and through his song calls to mind the girl he loves. Nor should I be surprised if one of them also makes advances to a handsome youth who is present and a partner in the search; for the Moors are both beautiful and tall, and have a manly look, and apply themselves to the works of hunting, and indeed they inflame many to love, being still mere boys and of that age. So if the tusks lie buried near, by some secret and marvellous attraction they draw that water out of the skins, and prove them empty. Thereupon, with mattocks and pickaxes, they dig up the place, and have their quarry, having tracked it by scent without hounds. But if the skins stay full where the hunters of these tusks set them down, they go off to another hunt, and indeed carry off the skins and water again, the instruments of the said chase.

6. The elephant is said to have a double heart and to think with two minds, raging with the one and growing gentle with the other; and I follow Moorish accounts in saying this. For the same men celebrate this too, that there are lynxes there. They say the lynxes are even more snub-nosed than the leopard, but shaggy at the tips of their ears. This beast is a terrible leaper, and powerful to grip its prey most forcibly and firmly. Euripides too seems to bear witness to this beast, even when he does not name it, where he somewhere says: "He comes upon his shoulders bearing a weight, either of a boar or of the misshapen lynx, a hard-to-bear creature." But what he means by "hard-to-bear" it is better to ask the critics.

7. About the great ostrich one might say this too. When it is killed, its stomach is found, when cleaned out, to hold stones, which the ostrich swallows and keeps and digests in time within its gizzard. These stones would also be good for men's digestion, and the bird's sinews and fat are good for men's sinews. The ostrich is caught by horses; for it runs in a circle, but circling round on the outer side, while the horsemen cut across by the inner circle, and going round a shorter course they catch it in time, when it gives out from running. It is taken also in this way. It makes a low nest on the ground, scooping out the sand with its feet. The very middle of it is hollow, but it builds the edges round about high, walling them off in a manner, so that the rain from heaven may be kept out by the rims and may not flow into the nest and flood the ostrich's chicks, which are tender. It lays even more than eighty eggs, yet does not hatch them all at once, nor do they all come to the light at the same time; but some are already hatched, others are still forming within the eggs, and others are being kept warm. So when the ostrich is engaged in this, a man who is not foolish but practised in such hunting, having observed it, fixes sharpened spear-points about the nest, setting them upright on their butt-ends, and the iron gleams; then he withdraws and lies in wait for what happens. So the ostrich comes back from feeding, loving its chicks strongly and thirsting for their company. At first it looks about this way and that and rolls its eye, fearing lest someone see it; but then, overcome by longing and goaded, spreading its wings like a sail, borne along at a strained pace and with a rush, it leaps into its own nest, and most pitiably, entangled and impaled upon the spear-points, it dies. So the hunter comes up and has taken the offspring along with the mother.

8. There is a city in the western regions of Italy; its name is Patavium. They say the city is the work of Antenor the Trojan. He founded it, having been saved from his home when he departed after his fatherland Ilium was taken, the Greeks having shown him respect, since he had saved Menelaus when he came on embassy with Odysseus concerning Helen, though Antimachus advised that they be killed. And Antimachus gave this advice having received Alexander's gold, splendid gifts, as Homer says. Now another city neighbours this Patavium, and they call it Vicetia, and a river flows past it named the Eretaenus, and this river passes a good deal of country and then falls into the Eridanus, and shares its water with it. Now in the Eretaenus there are eels of the greatest size, and by far fatter than those elsewhere; and they are caught in this way. The hunter sits upon a jutting rock in some bay-like spot, where the stream spreads out wider, or he sits upon some tree that has been thrown roots and all near the bank by a strong wind, which rots beneath but is useless to cut up and burn. So this eel-fisher, taking his seat, and taking the gut of a newly slaughtered lamb, three or four cubits long and very fat, lets one end of it down into the water, and it is whirled about, turning in the eddies; but the other end he holds in his hands, and into it has been inserted a piece of reed, as long as a sword-hilt. The food does not escape the eels; for they delight in this gut. And the first one that comes up, goaded by hunger and gaping wide, fixes in its teeth, which are curved and hooked and hard to disengage, and continually leaps about and tries to drag the bait down. The man, perceiving from the trembling of the gut that the eel has hold, puts into his own mouth the reed to which the gut is attached, and blowing down it with all his might, inflates the gut very strongly, and from the inrushing breath it swells and grows distended. So the wind slips down into the eel and fills its head with breath and fills its throat, and stops up the creature's breathing. And unable to breathe, nor yet to draw out from the entrail the teeth fixed in it, the eel is choked, and is hauled up, caught by the gut and the breath and the reed as a third agent. Now this is done day by day, and many eels are caught by many fishers. Let these things too be told by me as peculiar to these fishes.

9. That the sea-lion resembles the crayfish in a way, we too know; but we see that it is slighter in the build of its body, and somewhat tinged with blue, and that it is sluggish and has very large claws, like in shape to those of crabs. It is said by the more skilled fishermen to have certain membranes attached to its shell, beneath which membranes are tender little pieces of flesh, and these are called the fat of that lion. And men derive this benefit from them: it cleanses muddy complexion from the face, and mixed with oil blended with roses and made into an ointment it lends to beauty and brightness. I have also heard this further: that the lion on land is greatly afraid of the strange look of the sea-lion, and cannot bear its smell; and that the same lion fears the cock, I have said above. They say too that, when its shells are crushed and the powder cast into water, the land-lion that drinks it is delivered from a sickness troubling its belly. Let these too be told by me as peculiar to the sea-lion.

10. The Moorish asses, swiftest to run, are at their first onset most keen, so that one might think there was some rush of a breeze, or, by Zeus, the very wing of a bird; but they soon tire, and their feet give out, and their breath fails, and they forget their swiftness and stand fettered, and let fall plentiful tears — not, it seems to me, so much over their coming death as over the weakness of their feet. So the men, leaping down from their horses, then throw nooses about their necks, and each, fastening the captive to his horse, leads it off as a prisoner. That the Libyan horses are small to look at but swiftest to run, I have said above.

11. The herd of Libyan oxen was indeed beyond number, and the wild and free among them are swiftest. The hunters often go astray pursuing one and fall in with others that are fresh; for one slips into a thicket or a glen and vanishes, while others appear, like it, and deceive the eye. And if one should set about pursuing one of them, his horse will give out before the ox; for he will catch in time the one already tired, but those that are just beginning their run, his horse having worn itself out beforehand, he will not catch. Many are caught and killed every year, yet their breeding succeeds them most abundantly. The bulls roam together with the calves in common, and the females too, some pregnant, some newly delivered. If one should catch a calf still young, and not kill it at once, he will have a double gain; for he has caught its mother along with it, by doing what it is not absurd to relate. He ties the calf with a rush-rope and leaves it and withdraws; and the mother, worn with longing for her young and inflamed and goaded, wishing to loose it and lead it away, drives her horns at the rope to fray and burst the bonds. And whichever of her horns she thrusts into the twist of the rush-rope is held fast, and fettered along with the calf she remains, not having loosed it, but having flung about herself an inescapable bond. So the hunter takes out her liver for himself, cuts out the udders still swelling, flays off the hide, and leaves the flesh as a feast for birds and beasts. But the calf he carries home whole; for it is most pleasant to eat, and will furnish curd for the cheese-making, yielding rennet.

12. The sea-dragon is like the other fishes in the rest of its body, but in its head it resembles the land-dragon, and in the size of its eyes (for these too are large), and indeed its jaws also present somehow the form of those of land-dragons. It has scales too, and they are rough, and seem not far from the dragon's skin, if one should touch them. There grow upon it dangerous stings, and the stings bear venom, and they are no good thing to one who touches them.

13. It would be for me to tell also what is peculiar to animals. The king of the Indians eats for his dessert such things as the Greeks ask to nibble — the fruit of the ground-palm; but he dines on a certain grub bred in that plant, roasted, sweetest of all, as the Indian accounts say; and those who tell of so great a pleasure from eating it win even me over by what they say. He has these too as side-dishes: the eggs of swans and those of land-ostriches and of geese. Now in other respects I do not blame him; but as for swans, which are servants of Apollo and most tuneful, as the report that goes about says, to plot against their offspring and destroy their eggs, dear Indians — no more of that.

14. As for the Libyan gazelles and the young deer there, my heart bids me speak of them now. The gazelles are swiftest, and yet they do not escape the Libyan horses. They are taken also with nets. They are grey in the belly, and this colour goes up into the flanks; and along either side of the belly black bands run down. For the rest of their body they are tawny, long in the legs, black in the eye, their heads adorned with horns, and their ears are very long. The creature called

15. by the poets the "young deer" is swiftest to run, like a storm, but to look upon it is red-haired and very shaggy, and it has a white tail. Its eyes are likened to a dye of blue. Its ears are full of the thickest hairs. Its horns are facing each other and fair, so that, fair as it is, it both meets the hunt and at the same time both frightens and is harmed. This young deer displays the swiftness of its feet not on land alone, but, falling into a river's current, rowing as it were with the hooves of its feet, it then cuts through the stream. It delights also to swim in a lake, and there too it gets its food, dining ever on flourishing reed and galingale. So at the beginning of spring it lightens its filled belly, and lets down its udders, and indeed the young deer rears its own offspring. The murry, I learn, is a fish. From what it drew that name I cannot say; but it has been called so. They say it is a sea-snake. Whichever of its eyes is taken out and made into an amulet rids a man of dry ophthalmia; and they say another eye grows again for this murry. But one must let the fish go alive, or you keep the eye in vain.

16. The wild goats that tread the Libyan heights are in size like oxen to look upon, but their thighs and breasts and necks bristle with the thickest hairs, and with these their chin too. Their foreheads are curved and rounded, their eyes flashing, but their legs are stunted. Their horns, after the first joining together, stand apart from each other and slantwise; for they are not at all upright like those of the other mountain goats, but go down crosswise and reach toward the shoulders. So very long are they. From the topmost ridges, which both herdsmen and the sons of poets like to call "crags," they leap easily to another peak; for these are the best leapers of all goats. And even if one should fall farther than where there is anything to receive it, so as to be beyond its reach, yet such strength resides in its limbs that it remains unharmed when it has come down. At any rate it breaks nothing, even if it falls upon a cleft rock, neither horn nor skull; for these are strong and like the resistance of the rock. Most of them, then, are taken on the very heights with nets and javelins and foot-traps, by the cunning that is in huntsmen generally and in goat-hunting especially; but they are hunted also in the plains, and there they are too weak to flee. So even one who is slow of foot will catch them. Both the hide and the horns are useful; for the hide, in the fiercest winters, keeps the cold from coming near herdsmen and woodcutters; and those horns are good for drawing up and drinking from a river flowing by, or some spring rising in the summer season, and serviceable for quenching thirst; for it lets you drink at a draught no less than the largest cups, until you have cooled your breath and quenched all that smoulders and inflames within. So if the inside be cleaned out by one skilled in scraping horns, one of the two would easily hold three measures.
17. There are also tortoises bred in Libya, the most curly-shelled to look upon, and these are mountain tortoises, and they have a shell good for lyres.

18. When a mare gives birth, a piece of flesh, not large but small, grown out of the foal, hangs attached — some say to its forehead, some to its loins, others to its genitals. This the mare bites off and makes away with, and this little piece of flesh is called the "horse-frenzy." It is done out of pity and mercy of nature toward horses. For if, they say, that piece were always and right through attached, the males and females among them would be kindled to a frenzy of unrestrained mating. Let it be, if you please, a gift given to horses by Poseidon the Horse-god or by Athena the Horse-goddess, that their race may endure and not be destroyed by a madness of lust. Horse-keepers know this well and rightly, and if ever they need the said piece of flesh for some plot against a person, to kindle love in him, they keep watch over the pregnant mare, and when she gives birth they at once snatch away the foal and cut off the said flesh, and put it into the hoof of a mare; for there alone could it be well kept and stored up. The foal they sacrifice at sunrise; for the mother no longer suckles it, the token having been taken away and it having lost the ground of her affection; for it is from biting off that flesh that the mother begins to love her young strongly. And whoever, by some plot, tastes that little piece of flesh is held by a love most unrestrained, and is parched and cries out, and rushes uncontrollably even upon the basest favourites and upon a woman past her prime and ugly, and bears witness to his disease, and tells those he meets how he is goaded. And his body wastes and pines, while his soul is driven by erotic madness. I am told, then, that even at Olympia the bronze mare, with which horses fall in love and go mad and wish to mount, and neigh an erotic neigh when they see it, has within it, in the bewitched bronze, a plot derived from this horse-frenzy lying hidden, and that by some secret device of the craftsman the bronze plots against living creatures; for there could not be such accuracy that horses seeing it should be thus deceived and goaded by the work itself. And perhaps those who say this say something, and perhaps they say nothing; but what I heard about these matters too I have told.

19. It is said that in Libya there is a lake of boiling water, and in this water, they say, fish live and swim, and when food is thrown in they leap up toward the food. But if one should throw them into cold water, they die; this too I have heard besides.

20.
